title: Sharp One-shot Bounds And Optimal Exponents Of Universal Randomness Extraction
authors: Hao-Chung Cheng Bartosz Regula
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce techniques for the study of randomness extraction against quantum side information (privacy amplification) by relating this problem to variants of hypothesis testing tasks with quadratic constraints. Building also on the recently introduced measured smooth entropy approach of [Regula and Tomamichel, arXiv:2603.04493], we precisely determine the optimal scaling of the error of quantum privacy amplification in several regimes. Our results apply to the standard operational security criterion based on trace distance and focus in particular on universal classes of hash functions. On the technical side, our investigation reveals connections with operator space theory methods used in non-commutative Khintchine inequalities. As one application, we give a one-shot converse bound that shows the leftover hash lemma of [arXiv:2603.04493] to be tight up to a constant factor for all strongly 4-universal hash functions. This allows us to evaluate the asymptotic i.i.d. error exponent of universal randomness extraction for all rates, matching the bound of [Dupuis, arXiv:2105.05342] and improving also earlier classical asymptotic results of [Hayashi, arXiv:1010.1358]. We furthermore give new one-shot achievability and converse bounds on the error in the strong converse regime, which we show to match up to a constant factor. This establishes the exact strong converse exponent of quantum privacy amplification under 2-universal hash functions, complementing the converse bound of [Shen, Gao, and Cheng, arXiv:2202.10263].
tldr: The paper derives sharp one-shot bounds and optimal error exponents for universal randomness extraction against quantum side information, connecting privacy amplification to hypothesis testing and measured smooth entropy.
motivation: Randomness extraction with quantum side information is central to quantum cryptography, but tight one-shot and strong-converse characterizations for universal hash functions were incomplete.
method: The authors relate privacy amplification to hypothesis-testing variants with quadratic constraints and use measured smooth entropy plus operator-space/noncommutative Khintchine techniques.
result: They obtain a tight one-shot converse for strongly 4-universal hashes, evaluate the asymptotic i.i.d. error exponent for all rates, and establish the exact strong converse exponent for 2-universal hash functions up to constant factors.
conclusion: The work significantly sharpens the theory of quantum privacy amplification and universal randomness extraction, with direct relevance to composable quantum cryptography and quantum entropy measures.

title: When Does A Noisy Bell Pair Attain The Rains Bound?
authors: Stefano Pirandola Matthew Barber
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two entangled Bell-diagonal qubit states with the same singlet fraction have the same Rains bound. We prove that their attainable rates under operations preserving the positive partial transpose can nevertheless differ: the bound is attained if and only if one of the Bell probabilities vanishes. Every mixed entangled isotropic state, in every finite dimension, lies strictly below its bound. This refutes the attainment suggested by finite-block numerics, and places the two-way quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel strictly below its relative-entropy bound.
tldr: The paper proves that Bell-diagonal qubit states with equal singlet fraction can have different attainable rates under PPT-preserving operations, and that the Rains bound is attained only in a special limiting case.
motivation: The Rains bound is a central relative-entropy-based upper bound on entanglement distillation and quantum channel capacity, but whether it is attainable under physically relevant operations was unclear.
method: The authors analyze Bell-diagonal qubit states under operations preserving positive partial transpose, proving attainability conditions and applying the result to isotropic states and the qubit depolarizing channel.
result: They show the Rains bound is attained if and only if one Bell probability vanishes; every mixed entangled isotropic state in finite dimension lies strictly below its bound, implying the two-way quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel is strictly below its relative-entropy bound.
conclusion: The work refutes finite-block numerical suggestions of attainability and clarifies the gap between the Rains bound and achievable rates under PPT-preserving operations.

It proves that two states with identical singlet fraction (and hence identical Rains bound) can have different attainable rates: the bound is achievable if and only if at least one of the Bell probabilities vanishes. For isotropic states in any finite dimension, the authors show that every mixed entangled state lies strictly below its Rains bound, contradicting earlier finite-block numerical suggestions of attainability. As a corollary, the two-way quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel is strictly less than its relative-entropy bound. The work combines rigorous analytical arguments with a counterexample to numerical intuition, highlighting the gap between the Rains bound and actual PPT-preserving distillable entanglement.

title: Structure-factor Witnesses Of Thermal Entanglement: Exact Optimal Covariance Criteria For The Xy Chain
authors: Julia Math\'e, Ayaka Usui, Otfried G\"uhne, Giuseppe Vitagliano
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Which entanglement witness is optimal for a thermal many-body state, and what does its structure reveal about the equilibrium physics? We address these questions for the spin-[MATH] XY chain in a transverse field, using the covariance-matrix criterion (CMC), which requires only one- and two-spin correlations. We show that for thermal states the optimal CMC witness is fixed by the minima over momentum of the three static spin structure factors, which are accessible to scattering experiments and can be evaluated directly in the thermodynamic limit. The optimal witnesses select the collective spin modes with the smallest thermal fluctuations, with their form dictated by symmetry rather than by criticality. They certify entanglement, and can also bound entanglement measures, up to temperatures of the order of the exchange coupling, including in states without any pairwise entanglement. A systematic investigation of entanglement in small chains reveals that the CMC is nearly as powerful as a moment-matrix hierarchy supplied with all spin correlations, and close to the XX point it detects thermal states that are PPT across every bipartition. In addition, we observe that the same witnesses can also certify entanglement generated by a sudden quench from a thermal state in which none is detected.
tldr: The paper derives optimal covariance-matrix entanglement witnesses for thermal states of the transverse-field XY chain, showing they are determined by minima of static spin structure factors over momentum.
motivation: It is often unclear which entanglement witness is optimal for a given thermal many-body state and what its structure reveals about equilibrium physics; this work addresses that for the XY chain.
method: The authors use the covariance-matrix criterion, requiring only one- and two-spin correlations, and show that for thermal states the optimal witness is fixed by momentum minima of the three static spin structure factors, which are experimentally accessible and computable in the thermodynamic limit.
result: The optimal witnesses select collective spin modes with minimal thermal fluctuations, certify entanglement up to temperatures of order the exchange coupling, can bound entanglement measures, nearly match a full moment-matrix hierarchy, detect states that are PPT across every bipartition near the XX point, and can certify quench-generated entanglement.
conclusion: Structure factors provide experimentally relevant, symmetry-dictated optimal witnesses for thermal entanglement in XY chains, connecting entanglement detection to measurable equilibrium correlations.

A systematic study of small chains reveals that the CMC is nearly as powerful as a moment-matrix hierarchy with all spin correlations, and close to the XX point it detects thermal states that are PPT across every bipartition. title: Robust Certification Of Non-projective Qubit Measurements Without Inputs
authors: Sumit Rout, Pawe{\l} Horodecki, Some Sankar Bhattacharya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) beyond projective simulation (aka non-projective measurements) offer advantages over projective measurements, motivating their certification directly from observed statistics. Here, we show that this certification can be achieved robustly without input randomness, using only the joint outcome distribution of two measurement devices. We consider two spatially separated observers whose only shared resource is an uncharacterised two-qubit state. Each observer performs a local measurement. In the projective-simulable case, the measurement device privately randomises over qubit projective measurements and applies arbitrary classical post-processing to their outcomes. In the noiseless regime, we identify three- and four-outcome anti-correlations that certify that both local measurements lie beyond projective simulation. To establish noise robustness, we develop a non-linear covariance witness that combines the geometry of projective measurements with a contraction bound valid for every two-qubit state. For the correlations generated by identical qubit trine measurements or identical qubit SIC-POVM on noisy qubit singlet, we obtain exact critical white-noise fractions of (1/4) and (1/3), respectively. Below these thresholds, no pair of projective-simulable measurements on any two-qubit state can reproduce these correlations. We present explicit projective simulations that attain the thresholds and cover the remaining noise range. Finally, the same method yields a strictly positive noise tolerance for certification whenever both observers apply the same extremal qubit POVM with three or four non-zero effects to a depolarised qubit singlet. These results establish a general analytic framework for certifying non-projective qubit measurement resources without input randomness.
tldr: The paper presents an analytic, noise-robust framework for certifying that qubit measurements lie beyond projective simulation (i.e., are genuinely non-projective POVMs) using only the joint outcome statistics of two local measurement devices, without any input randomness.
motivation: Non-projective POVMs offer advantages over projective measurements, but certifying them from observed statistics typically requires trusted inputs or assumptions; the authors aim to remove input randomness and make the certification robust to noise.
method: Two spatially separated observers share an uncharacterised two-qubit state and each perform a local measurement; the authors identify three- and four-outcome anti-correlations that witness non-projective-simulability and develop a non-linear covariance witness combining projective-measurement geometry with a contraction bound valid for all two-qubit states.
result: Exact critical white-noise fractions of 1/4 for identical trine measurements and 1/3 for identical SIC-POVMs on a noisy singlet are derived, with explicit projective simulations attaining these thresholds, and strictly positive noise tolerance is shown for any extremal three- or four-outcome qubit POVM on a depolarised singlet.
conclusion: The work establishes a general analytic framework for input-free, robust certification of non-projective qubit measurement resources, extending self-testing-style reasoning to POVM certification.

title: Extrinsic Thermodynamic Geometry, Symmetry, And The Cost Of Constraint
authors: David A. Sivak Jordan R. Sawchuk
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driving a stochastic system in finite time costs excess work; exactly how much depends on which system parameters, and hence which paths in distribution space, a controller can access. In the friction-tensor formalism for slow driving, the space of equilibrium distributions is a Riemannian manifold and constraints on a controller define submanifolds. Whether a constrained controller is forced onto suboptimal paths is a question of the extrinsic thermodynamic geometry of the submanifold, which we develop for discrete systems. We show that submanifolds with zero extrinsic curvature can be identified from symmetries of the transition network, before any optimization. A minimum-work protocol on such a submanifold is therefore stationary in the excess work even when the constraints are lifted. The stationarity of symmetric optima holds exactly, beyond slow driving. In the slow-driving regime, we show that the ambient curvature transverse to a symmetric submanifold determines whether nearby symmetry-broken protocols have lower excess work. This curvature, which separates into independent contributions from each pattern of symmetry breaking, thus acquires an operational meaning as a measure of the thermodynamic incentive to break a given symmetry. A thermodynamic comparison theorem provides an inexpensive test of local minimality that weighs the extremal curvatures along the symmetric protocol against its excess work. There is no need for such tests under certain convexity conditions on the transition rates and control parameters, which guarantee that a symmetric optimum is a global optimum. These results certify the global optimality of a five-parameter protocol previously observed to match 15-parameter full control of a four-spin Ising system, and explain why partial symmetry breaking is optimal for the same system under local-field control.
tldr: The paper develops an extrinsic thermodynamic geometry framework for constrained finite-time driving of stochastic systems, showing how symmetries and curvature determine whether constrained optimal protocols remain optimal.
motivation: Finite-time driving incurs excess work, and controller constraints may force the system along suboptimal paths in distribution space. The authors ask when a constrained minimum-work protocol is globally optimal or when symmetry breaking lowers thermodynamic cost.
method: They treat the space of equilibrium distributions as a Riemannian manifold and controller constraints as submanifolds. Using the friction-tensor formalism, they analyze extrinsic curvature, transition-network symmetries, and a thermodynamic comparison theorem to test local and global optimality.
result: Symmetric submanifolds with zero extrinsic curvature yield stationary minimum-work protocols even beyond slow driving, while transverse ambient curvature quantifies the incentive to break symmetry. Convexity conditions certify global optimality, and the framework explains the optimality of a five-parameter protocol for a four-spin Ising system.
conclusion: Extrinsic thermodynamic geometry provides an operational geometric meaning for curvature and practical criteria for assessing constrained optimal control in stochastic thermodynamics.

In the friction-tensor formalism, the space of equilibrium distributions forms a Riemannian manifold, and controller constraints define submanifolds. The authors introduce the extrinsic curvature of these submanifolds to quantify whether a constrained controller is forced onto suboptimal paths. They show that submanifolds with zero extrinsic curvature can be identified from symmetries of the transition network before any optimization, implying that a minimum-work protocol on such a submanifold is stationary in excess work even when constraints are lifted. This stationarity holds exactly beyond the slow-driving regime. In the slow-driving limit, the ambient curvature transverse to a symmetric submanifold determines whether symmetry-broken protocols yield lower excess work, providing an operational meaning to curvature as the thermodynamic incentive to break symmetry. A thermodynamic comparison theorem offers a cheap test of local minimality, and convexity conditions on transition rates and control parameters guarantee global optimality of symmetric optima. The results certify the global optimality of a five-parameter protocol for a four-spin Ising system and explain why partial symmetry breaking is optimal under local-field control.

title: Nisq Preparation Of Conditional Thermal States For Precision Thermometry
authors: Emery Doucet, Reece Robertson, Nicholas Donatelli, Shou-I Tang, Sebastian Deffner, Akira Sone
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to prepare thermal states on gate-based quantum computers is an important building block for quantum computation, both with regard to the implementation of certain classes of quantum algorithms as well as to the study of quantum thermodynamics in and out of equilibrium. A useful generalization of the standard notion of a thermal state which appears naturally in the study of quantum work distributions is the conditional thermal state, which is conditioned on the use of an accessible pointer basis associated with a measurement apparatus. Among other uses, it has been proven that conditional thermal states can outperform ordinary thermal states in quantum thermometry. In this work we demonstrate the preparation of conditional thermal states of few-qubit systems implemented on IonQ's cloud-based quantum computers across a range of temperatures. To validate their performance advantage in thermometry, we measure the sub-quantum Fisher information (a lower bound on the quantum Fisher information) of the prepared states, which can be computed via a constant-depth quantum circuit without tomography.

method: Few-qubit conditional thermal states are prepared across a range of temperatures on IonQ hardware, and their thermometric performance is assessed by measuring the sub-quantum Fisher information using a constant-depth quantum circuit without tomography.
result: The authors successfully prepare conditional thermal states on NISQ hardware and experimentally verify their thermometry advantage through sub-quantum Fisher information measurements.
conclusion: Conditional thermal states are feasible on current cloud quantum computers and provide a practical route toward precision thermometry and broader quantum thermodynamic studies on NISQ devices.

title: Gauge Symmetry Permits Extremely Low-depth Random Unitary Circuits
authors: Yunfei Wang, Yuqing Li, Junqi Wang, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Junyu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous global symmetries can obstruct logarithmic-depth symmetric unitary [MATH]-designs and pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) through long-range correlations. We ask whether gauge symmetries impose analogous limitations. For [MATH] lattice gauge theories, we identify a randomization scale [MATH], the minimum patch size needed for matter to screen every allowed boundary-flux mismatch, and a diffusive scale governing boundary-flux correlations. Glued circuits built from gauge-symmetric unitaries with subdiffusive support are efficiently distinguishable from gauge-symmetric Haar-random unitaries, whereas local controlled designs can be glued into global approximate designs when overlaps exceed the diffusive scale multiplied by a logarithmic factor. Our analysis suggests incomplete screening limits design guarantees to constant order, whereas strictly locally random systems with complete local screening ([MATH]) admit a local tensor-product description, permitting superpolynomial design orders and logarithmic-depth designs and PRUs. We construct a toy model of charged black-hole evaporation in which insufficient screening makes uninterrupted complete discharge exponentially unlikely in [MATH], whereas strict local randomization removes this screening obstruction. This motivates a quantum-information analogue of the weak gravity conjecture, requiring the available charged spectrum to support complete local screening in addition to superextremality. We conjecture that this condition allows gauge-symmetric systems to scramble as rapidly as unconstrained ones and support this by constructing logarithmic-depth approximate strong designs and strong PRUs.

title: Optimal Controlled Quantum Instrument For Monitored Many-Body Dynamics
authors: Jimin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-selecting rare trajectories of monitored quantum dynamics requires exponentially many repeated experiments. We extend Bayes' rule to monitored many-body dynamics and bias the quantum trajectories by nonlinear functions of the post-measurement state. For functions that are constant on the sets of a suitable finite partition of the post-measurement states, we construct a quantum instrument on the system and an additional register that produces the biased trajectories at the optimal rates without post-selection. This optimal controlled quantum instrument has a natural tensor-network representation as the left canonical form of the system--register tensors. We illustrate the construction with two examples: a precessing qubit, biased by its spin component along the field, and free fermions with gain and loss, biased by the particle number, where the biased trajectories undergo a phase transition. We also argue, under one assumption, that biasing a measured Majorana chain by its von Neumann entropy leads to entanglement transitions.

motivation: Post-selecting rare monitored quantum trajectories requires exponentially many repeated experiments, so the author seeks a direct quantum-instrument construction that produces biased trajectories at optimal rates.
method: The author extends Bayes' rule to monitored many-body dynamics, biases trajectories via nonlinear functions of post-measurement states, and constructs a system-register quantum instrument with a left-canonical tensor-network representation.
result: The construction is illustrated for a precessing qubit biased by its field-aligned spin component and for free fermions with gain/loss biased by particle number, where the biased trajectories show a phase transition; an argument is also given that entropy-biasing a measured Majorana chain can lead to entanglement transitions.
conclusion: The work provides a post-selection-free, rate-optimal measurement-instrument framework for studying biased monitored many-body dynamics and entanglement transitions.

title: Using A Static Spacetime Subsystem Code To Calculate Floquet Code Distance
authors: Milad Marvian Ethan Egger
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical codes, including Floquet codes, can capture time-dependent phenomena in quantum error correction circuits that are absent from static stabilizer or subsystem codes, such as detecting regions and error propagation. They are also capable of preserving more logical qubits than corresponding schemes in which the same syndrome-extraction measurements are performed without being distributed over time. However, evaluating the performance of dynamical codes is more complicated than for static codes because error detection depends on when an error occurs within the measurement schedule. In this work, we introduce a mapping from the measurement sequence of a Floquet code to a static spacetime subsystem code and show that calculating the distance of a Floquet code can be reduced to calculating the distance of the corresponding static subsystem code. Crucially, our mapping preserves code distance, a property that is not guaranteed for general spacetime code mappings. This reduction converts the dynamical distance problem into a static subsystem code problem, substantially simplifying the analysis of Floquet measurement schedules and facilitating the evaluation of fault tolerance for new measurement schemes.
tldr: The paper maps Floquet-code measurement schedules to static spacetime subsystem codes to compute code distance while preserving distance.
motivation: Dynamical Floquet codes are promising for quantum error correction but harder to analyze than static codes because error detection depends on error timing within the measurement schedule.
method: The authors introduce a mapping from a Floquet code's measurement sequence to a static spacetime subsystem code and prove that this mapping preserves code distance.
result: The reduction converts the dynamical distance problem into a static subsystem-code distance problem, simplifying analysis of Floquet measurement schedules and fault tolerance.
conclusion: This provides a practical theoretical tool for evaluating new dynamical code schemes and their fault tolerance by leveraging static subsystem-code techniques.

title: High-Dimensional Single-Photon Frequency Conversion For Orbital Angular Momentum Comb State
authors: Sheng-Qiang Jia, Hao Sheng, Zhiming Qing, Li Fan, Jianping Ding, Jia-Min Xu, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The orbital angular momentum (OAM) degree of freedom provides an important resource for constructing high-dimensional optical quantum information systems. However, the generation of high-dimensional single-photon OAM comb state and its high-fidelity frequency conversion remain challenging due to limited spatial modulation resolution, imperfect mode matching, and finite nonlinear conversion efficiency. Here, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a scalable scheme for the generation and frequency conversion of high-dimensional single-photon OAM comb state. We prepared a single-photon OAM comb state with a dimension of up to 128, achieving a fidelity of 0.787 between the reconstructed and target states and an effective dimension of 100. Furthermore, using the sum-frequency generation, we demonstrated the frequency upconversion of single-photon high-dimensional OAM comb state from the communication band to a visible wavelength of 520 nm, while verifying the preservation of both the OAM mode distribution and phase information through density matrix reconstruction. Our work established a versatile platform for the generation, manipulation, and characterization of high-dimensional OAM comb states, with potential applications in cross-band quantum information transfer, high-capacity quantum communication, and high-dimensional quantum networks.
tldr: The paper experimentally generates and frequency-converts high-dimensional single-photon orbital angular momentum comb states for cross-band quantum information transfer.
motivation: High-dimensional OAM states are promising for high-capacity quantum communication, but generating and faithfully frequency-converting such single-photon states remains challenging due to spatial modulation limits and imperfect mode matching.
method: The authors prepare a single-photon OAM comb state with dimension up to 128 and use sum-frequency generation to upconvert it from the communication band to 520 nm, reconstructing the density matrix to verify preservation of OAM and phase information.

title: When Malus' Law Meets The Wigner-Bell Inequality: Violation By Nonseparable Classical Light
authors: Xiao-Feng Qian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bell-type inequalities are commonly associated with quantum nonlocality, yet their mathematical structure also reflects more general constraints on the joint probability distributions assigned to measurements performed in different contexts. Here we examine this distinction through the Wigner--Bell inequality using a classical optical field with two nonseparable degrees of freedom. Starting from a subsystem response-factorization assumption, we derive a Wigner-type probability bound requiring the pairwise measurement statistics to be compatible with a single nonnegative global joint distribution. For a classically nonseparable optical field, the corresponding joint probabilities are represented directly by normalized joint intensities and obey Malus' law. We show that these Malus-law probabilities violate the Wigner--Bell bound over a finite range of analyzer settings. The violation does not imply spatial nonlocality or a failure of classical electrodynamics. Rather, it demonstrates the incompatibility of context-dependent optical projection statistics with the global probability assignment underlying the Wigner construction. We further derive an extended Wigner-Bell bound for general imperfect correlations and propose an interferometric experiment for reconstructing the required joint probabilities from intensity measurements. These results provide a transparent optical realization of the probabilistic structure behind Bell-type inequalities and help distinguish consequences of Hilbert-space structure, nonseparability, and measurement context from those specifically associated with quantum nonlocality.

motivation: Bell-type inequalities are usually tied to quantum nonlocality, but their probabilistic structure may also constrain classical context-dependent measurement statistics. The work aims to separate consequences of Hilbert-space structure, nonseparability, and measurement context from genuine quantum nonlocality.

conclusion: The violation is interpreted as incompatibility between context-dependent optical projection statistics and the global probability assignment underlying the Wigner construction, not as spatial nonlocality or a failure of classical electrodynamics.

title: Extracting Operational Entanglement From A Noise-Protected Many-Body System
authors: Bhavay Tyagi, Eric R. Bittner, Kevin E. Bassler
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can noisy dynamics generate entanglement that stays useful at long times? Under collective dephasing, a twelve-spin kicked Ising ring evolves from a uniform product state toward an entangled stationary state that is maximally mixed in the sector fixed by the ring's rotations and reflections. Gates and measurements within each half herald a spin pair that teleports an unknown qubit with a mean fidelity of 90.5\%. Simulations show that stronger noise correlations extend the time over which the ring yields pairs that beat the classical teleportation limit.

result: The heralded protocol achieves a mean teleportation fidelity of 90.5%, and stronger noise correlations extend the time window in which the extracted pairs beat the classical teleportation limit.
conclusion: The work shows that noise-protected many-body dynamics can be a resource for operational entanglement and teleportation, with collective dephasing playing a constructive role.

title: Reproducible Distributions Of Energy-relaxation Times In Superconducting Qubits From Broadband Swap Spectroscopy
authors: Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Maximilien F. Debbas, Ana Vald\'es-Curiel, Ming-Han Chou, Haifeng Qiao, Shahriar Aghaeimeibodi, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, Loren J. Swenson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The distribution of the qubit energy-relaxation time (T1) in a superconducting quantum processor affects its logical error rates. However, reports on qubit fabrication quality focus on the median or best-case T1 from measurements that are not reproducible due to resonant coupling to two-level system (TLS) defects whose frequencies fluctuate in time. Here, we sweep the frequency f01 of a flux-tunable qubit over several GHz with SWAP spectroscopy, quoting the quality factor Q = 2 pi f01 T1 to make T1 comparable across frequencies. We show that the cumulative distribution of Q pooled over the sweep is reproducible across four thermal cycles spanning 326 days, up to the reshuffling of strongly coupled TLSs. In contrast to repeated measurements at a single frequency, the medians of the broadband Q distributions spread by an order of magnitude less over 3 days. The distance between the cumulative distributions of repeats comes close to its sampling floor only for the broadband sweeps. The broadband Q distribution further resolves small coherence differences between identically designed qubits on two dies of the same wafer. These results establish the broadband Q distribution as a reproducible metric for qubit fabrication quality.

method: The authors sweep a flux-tunable qubit's frequency over several GHz using SWAP spectroscopy and pool the resulting Q=2πf01T1 values into cumulative distributions across multiple thermal cycles and devices.

title: Quditology: Harnessing Many Levels For Quantum Information Processing
authors: Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.
tldr: This review surveys experimental progress in preparing, controlling, and measuring high-dimensional qudits across multiple quantum computing platforms for quantum information processing.
motivation: Binary qubits face decoherence and scalability limits, so using higher-dimensional qudits may extract more processing power from a given hardware size and naturally encode high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom.

result: The paper highlights early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation, and error suppression, showing qudits transitioning from conceptual constructs to viable quantum technology building blocks.
conclusion: Qudits offer a promising route to enhanced quantum information processing, though scalable implementation still faces key challenges and requires further experimental and theoretical development.

title: Dimensional Crossover To A Slow Disordered Spin Bath Below The Mean Spin Spacing

abstract: ArXiv:2611.33699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How thin must a layer of spins be to act as a two-dimensional bath? title: Constructively Embedding Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Todd A. Brun Yucheng He
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Implementing quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) requires more than favorable algebraic parameters: the interactions among data qubits and ancillas must also fit physical hardware. Surface codes map naturally onto two-dimensional arrays, but many quantum LDPC codes have Tanner graphs with nonlocal connections. We develop a constructive pipeline that maps a QECC's Tanner graph to the targeted hardware lattice in three stages (continuous embedding, grid assignment, and path routing). Continuous embeddings reveal the geometric structure of the code, including differences between stabilizer generator sets of the same code. The discrete stages produce explicit routed layouts that we can characterize and compare using proxy metrics for footprint, communication overhead, and congestion for syndrome extraction. We examine three continuous embedding methods: multidimensional scaling (distance-based), spectral embedding (Laplacian-based), and spring layout (force-based) for the first stage. Experiments across tested codes show how routing geometry, dimension, and scale selection affect the resulting costs. In ablation studies on the radius-2 (R2) HaPPY code, graph-aware methods for continuous embedding and the choice of path-routing algorithm matter more than the grid assignment under our chosen weights in the cost function. Changing the continuous embedding reveals a trade-off: MDS incurs greater communication overhead than spectral embedding over most tested scales, while spring layout can reduce communication overhead at intermediate scales but increases congestion and is less stable across scales.

result: Experiments show that graph-aware continuous embedding and routing choices strongly affect costs; in the R2 HaPPY code, MDS generally incurs higher communication overhead than spectral embedding, while spring layout can reduce overhead at intermediate scales but increases congestion.

title: A Bright Source Of High-dimensional Spatially Entangled Photon Pairs Based On Beam-like Type-II Spdc

abstract: ArXiv:2611.33852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bright sources of high-dimensional spatially entangled photon pairs are increasingly required for the rapid advancement of quantum technologies. title: A Scalable Dense Silicon Qubit Architecture With Logical Operations
authors: Tetsuo Kodera Masahiro Tadokoro
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below [MATH] per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm [MATH] 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.

title: How Many Autonomous Encoded Qubits Force An Isotropic Noise Response?

With one-bit readouts and no quantum memory or reference, switching encodings cuts the worst-case cost for the Pauli test by a factor of [MATH], up to logarithms. title: Amatlas: A 2d Array Architecture For Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination
authors: Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Seita Tsuboi, Hidetsugu Irie, Junichiro Kadomoto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.
tldr: Amatlas is a 2D processing-element array architecture that runs Union-Find surface-code decoding without any central controller or array-wide synchronization, implemented on FPGA and benchmarked up to code distance 25.
motivation: Real-time surface-code decoding at large code distances is a bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum computing; existing distributed Union-Find decoders require a central controller synchronizing all PEs each stage and map poorly onto planar hardware.
method: One processing element is assigned per stabilizer on the 2D qubit lattice, with all measurement-round states stored in local PE memory so every graph link connects adjacent PEs; each PE advances every clock cycle, with the clock as the only global signal, and the design is realized in RTL and mapped to a VCU129 FPGA.
result: Under circuit-level noise the implementation fits a VCU129 FPGA up to distance 25, with 462 ns average decoding time per round at 0.1% physical error rate, achieving a 0.72% threshold versus 0.78% for prior Union-Find decoding under the same noise model.
conclusion: Removing global coordination yields a scalable, planar-friendly decoder architecture at the cost of a modest threshold reduction, showing a viable path toward hardware real-time decoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Chiral Domain-Wall Modes In Topological Adaptive Quantum Dynamics
authors: Asadullah Bhuiyan, Haining Pan, Chao-Ming Jian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum dynamical systems driven by both unitary evolution and measurements open a new landscape of nonequilibrium phases of matter. The role of topology in enriching this landscape remains less understood than that of entanglement and symmetry. A particularly interesting question concerns protected dynamical modes localized on spacetime domain walls between topologically distinct dynamical phases. These dynamical topological domain-wall modes (DTDMs) are well understood only for [MATH]D walls in [MATH]D fermionic dynamics. In this work, we study [MATH]D topological domain walls in [MATH]D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, modeled by topological adaptive circuits that steer the two sides of each wall toward a Chern insulator and a trivial insulator through measurements and feedforward corrections. Although the circuits target no particular wall state, each wall hosts [MATH]D chiral DTDMs. At long times in each quantum trajectory, they exhibit logarithmic scaling of entanglement and charge variance and algebraically decaying density correlations, surprisingly consistent with the ground state of a [MATH]D chiral free-fermion conformal field theory. This contrasts with purely [MATH]D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, which exhibits only area-law entanglement at finite measurement rates. We also show that the chiral DTDMs exhibit slow purification dynamics. When the system starts from a maximally mixed state, the DTDMs' entropy decays algebraically, accompanied by a vanishing Lyapunov gap, whereas each domain purifies on an [MATH] timescale. Finally, we propose a physical picture for the long-time behavior of the DTDMs by treating the adaptive circuit model as a quantum cooling algorithm. Our results show that topological phases of adaptive dynamics can protect chiral modes on spacetime domain walls against repeated wavefunction collapse and Born-rule randomness.
tldr: The paper studies topological adaptive free-fermion circuits that host protected chiral dynamical modes on spacetime domain walls between distinct measurement-induced dynamical phases.
motivation: Topology in measurement-driven quantum dynamics is less understood than entanglement and symmetry, and protected dynamical domain-wall modes had been characterized mainly in lower-dimensional settings.
method: The authors use charge-conserving free-fermion adaptive circuits with measurements and feedforward corrections to steer opposite sides of each wall toward a Chern-insulator-like and trivial-insulator-like dynamical phase.
result: Each domain wall hosts chiral dynamical topological domain-wall modes exhibiting logarithmic entanglement and charge-variance scaling, algebraic density correlations, and slow purification with algebraic entropy decay and vanishing Lyapunov gap.
conclusion: Topological phases of adaptive quantum dynamics can protect chiral domain-wall modes against repeated wavefunction collapse and Born-rule randomness, with a physical interpretation as a quantum cooling algorithm.

title: Structure Theorem For Quantum Limit Cycle Attractors: A Geometric Path-integral Approach
authors: Nana Siddhartha
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show a Structure Theorem for an arbitrary separable quantum system (\(\dim\leq\aleph_0\)) that is coupled, through a symmetric bidirectional phase interface, to a self-sustaining phase-oscillator environment. Under the assumptions of \(U(1)\) covariance, instantaneous Lindblad bounded positivity, and the existence of an entrainable periodic attractor, the reduced generator is forced into a universal operator structure consisting of a state-dependent coherent recoil together with single-quantum feedback. Positivity further imposes a sharp dimensional dichotomy: purely dissipative gain saturation is forbidden in finite dimensions by trace-norm contraction, so coherent feedback is mandatory for qubits and qudits, whereas unbounded ladder algebras permit purely dissipative saturation. Expanding the general feedback functionals to leading order in the coupling recovers a canonical polynomial master equation that remains completely positive and trace-preserving in every dimension and combines additively with ordinary linear Lindblad channels. An accompanying Inverse Coupling Theorem shows that an autonomous periodic orbit can be sustained only when the interaction manifold has non-trivial fundamental group \(\pi_1()=\), thereby isolating the sinusoidal \(U(1)\)-covariant phase coupling as the generic mechanism. The resulting implementation is realized explicitly for a single qubit, a bipartite two-qubit system, and a bosonic Fock space.
tldr: The paper proves a structure theorem for quantum limit-cycle attractors in open quantum systems coupled to a phase-oscillator environment, deriving a universal Lindblad-type generator with coherent recoil and single-quantum feedback.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize the operator structure required for a separable quantum system to sustain a periodic attractor under Lindblad dynamics and U(1)-covariant phase coupling.
method: They assume U(1) covariance, instantaneous Lindblad bounded positivity, and an entrainable periodic attractor, then use geometric/path-integral reasoning and an inverse coupling theorem to constrain the reduced generator.
result: The reduced generator is forced into a universal form combining state-dependent coherent recoil with single-quantum feedback, with a dimensional dichotomy: finite-dimensional systems require coherent feedback, while infinite-dimensional ladder algebras allow purely dissipative saturation.
conclusion: The work isolates sinusoidal U(1)-covariant phase coupling as a generic mechanism for autonomous quantum periodic orbits and provides explicit implementations for qubits, two-qubit systems, and bosonic Fock spaces.

Expanding the feedback functionals to leading order yields a canonical polynomial master equation that is completely positive and trace-preserving in any dimension and combines additively with standard linear Lindblad channels. An Inverse Coupling Theorem shows that an autonomous periodic orbit requires the interaction manifold to have non-trivial fundamental group π₁(ℳ)=ℤ, singling out sinusoidal U(1)-covariant phase coupling as the generic mechanism. The framework is explicitly implemented for a single qubit, a bipartite two-qubit system, and a bosonic Fock space.

title: The Asymptotic Spectrum Of Tensors Is Connected
authors: Jeroen Zuiddam P\'eter Vrana
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove path-connectedness of the asymptotic spectrum of complex tensors of every fixed order [MATH]: every spectral point is connected by a path to every "one leg versus the rest" flattening rank. In particular, the asymptotic spectrum evaluated at any fixed tensor is a closed interval, answering a question of Strassen. This was previously known only on specific families of tensors (Strassen, FOCS 1986, Crelle 1987-1991; Wigderson and Zuiddam, Bull. AMS 2026) or for specific families of spectral points (Christandl, Vrana and Zuiddam, STOC 2018; Sakabe, Doan and Walter, FOCS 2026; Alman, Li and Pratt, FOCS 2026). To obtain our path-connectedness theorem we develop a general method for "interpolating" between spectral points, which applies to Strassen semirings that are appropriately decomposable (in the sense of an information-theoretic "method of types" on the semiring) and whose spectral points satisfy a cover property (inspired by slice rank). This covers tensors and asymptotic rank (with "types" given by decomposition into symmetric group irreps), as well as other objects and asymptotic problems, like graphs and Shannon capacity, where it matches the interpolation of Vrana (2019). Using our interpolation methods we furthermore obtain new results and simpler proofs of previous results regarding the asymptotic spectrum of rectangular matrix multiplication, polynomial multiplication and non-crossing (laminar) quantum functionals.
tldr: The paper proves that the asymptotic spectrum of complex tensors of fixed order is path-connected, so the spectrum evaluated at any tensor is a closed interval.
motivation: Strassen's asymptotic spectrum provides fundamental limits for tensor rank and related asymptotic problems, but its global connectivity structure was largely open, with prior results only for special tensor families or spectral points.
method: The authors develop an interpolation method between spectral points for appropriately decomposable Strassen semirings, using an information-theoretic method of types and a slice-rank-inspired cover property.
result: They establish path-connectedness of the asymptotic tensor spectrum, answer Strassen's question, and obtain new or simplified proofs for rectangular matrix multiplication, polynomial multiplication, and laminar quantum functionals.
conclusion: The work settles a structural question in asymptotic tensor theory and provides a general interpolation framework applicable to tensors, graphs, Shannon capacity, and related asymptotic spectra.

title: Theory Of Anomalous Diffusion And Superdiffusion In Integrable Spin Chains
authors: Jitendra Kethepalli, Andrew Urilyon, Jacopo de Nardis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrable systems can exhibit diffusive or Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) scaling in two-point correlations even when their current full counting statistics (FCS) differ from those usually associated with these universality classes. We explain this separation using a multispecies particle gas that preserves the scattering structure of integrable spin chains. For anisotropy [MATH], large particles are advected by a mobile bath. The resulting FCS has a Gaussian-mixture form and approaches the M-Wright distribution at late times, with finite-time rounding due to mobile species. At the isotropic point [MATH], all particles are mobile, and the charge transfer by large particles is discrete. A self-consistent Poisson distribution describes the FCS, with a nearly Gaussian bulk and model-dependent, non-Gaussian tails. By contrast, two-point correlations follow from the statistics of a large tracer particle. For [MATH], it undergoes Brownian motion, yielding Gaussian spreading. At [MATH], we provide evidence from fluctuating hydrodynamics for the emergence of the KPZ Pr\"ahofer--Spohn scaling function in dynamical correlations and trace it to the finite coupling of the largest particles to a continuum of slower ones, with long-ranged velocity fluctuations. Our framework shows how universal dynamical two-point correlations coexist with distinct model-dependent current statistics.
tldr: The paper explains how integrable spin chains can show universal diffusive or KPZ two-point correlations while their current full counting statistics remain model-dependent.
motivation: Integrable systems often exhibit anomalous transport and universal scaling, but the relationship between two-point correlation scaling and current full counting statistics is not fully understood.
method: The authors model the dynamics using a multispecies particle gas that preserves the scattering structure of integrable spin chains, analyzing full counting statistics and tracer-particle correlations, with fluctuating hydrodynamics at the isotropic point.
result: For anisotropic chains, large particles are advected by a mobile bath, giving Gaussian-mixture full counting statistics approaching an M-Wright distribution; at the isotropic point, charge transfer becomes discrete with Poissonian statistics, while two-point correlations cross over from Brownian Gaussian spreading to KPZ scaling.
conclusion: Universal dynamical two-point correlations can coexist with distinct model-dependent current statistics, clarifying the separation between correlation scaling and full counting statistics in integrable spin chains.

title: On-Demand Tailoring Of High-Dimensional Orbital Angular Momentum States Via A Phase-Only Hologram
authors: Hao Sheng, Zi-Shuo Wang, Sheng-Qiang Jia, Zi-Mo Cheng, Li Fan, Jianping Ding, Jia-Min Xu, Zhi-Cheng Ren, Xi-Lin Wang, Hui-Tian Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic orbital angular momentum (OAM) provides a naturally discrete and unbounded Hilbert space for high-dimensional encoding and has emerged as a powerful degree of freedom for advanced information processing. On-demand tailoring of both the amplitude and phase profiles of high-dimensional OAM states is essential for numerous applications, particularly in quantum information science. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate an efficient method for achieving such on-demand tailoring using a purely phase-only modulation scheme. The measured fidelity remains above 80% even for a 128-dimensional state, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Compared with previous techniques, our method achieves significantly higher generation efficiency, and this advantage becomes more pronounced as the dimensionality increases. Moreover, our approach substantially reduces experimental complexity while maintaining precise control, thereby offering a practical and scalable solution for high-dimensional OAM state engineering in both classical and quantum information processing.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a phase-only hologram method for tailoring high-dimensional photonic orbital angular momentum (OAM) states with fidelity above 80% up to 128 dimensions.
motivation: High-dimensional OAM states are promising for quantum and classical information processing, but on-demand control of both amplitude and phase profiles remains experimentally challenging and inefficient at high dimensions.
method: The authors propose and implement a purely phase-only modulation scheme using a phase-only hologram to shape high-dimensional OAM states, and characterize performance via fidelity and generation efficiency.
result: The method achieves measured fidelity above 80% for a 128-dimensional OAM state and shows higher generation efficiency than previous techniques, with the advantage growing with dimensionality.
conclusion: This provides a practical, scalable route to high-dimensional OAM state engineering, though its direct relevance to the researcher's core quantum-information-theoretic interests is limited.

title: Estimating The Trotter Error Via Phase Analysis
authors: Benjamin D'anjou Maxime Dion
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Good Trotter error estimates are crucial to correctly assess the resources required to perform an approximate time evolution with a target accuracy. General bounds for finite-size quantum systems are found to be very loose in practice, and it is therefore highly desirable to improve on them. In this work, we analyze the Trotter error in terms of the spectrum of a phase operator that we construct from the Hamiltonian. In the limit of a small Trotter step size, we obtain an estimate of the Trotter error written in terms of a sum of nested commutators between terms of the Hamiltonian. The structure of this estimate allows us to naturally explain the looseness of general bounds. We show that even for a finite step size, our estimate typically remains more accurate than general bounds. Moreover, we argue that it becomes an upper bound for the Trotter error per step in the limit of a large number of steps, reflecting the destructive interference of the errors across steps. Our results provide useful practical heuristics for resource optimization in quantum simulations.
tldr: The paper derives improved Trotter error estimates for Hamiltonian simulation using a phase-operator spectrum and nested commutators.
motivation: General Trotter error bounds for finite-size quantum systems are often too loose for accurate resource estimation in quantum simulation.
method: The authors construct a phase operator from the Hamiltonian and analyze its spectrum to estimate Trotter error in the small-step limit via nested commutators, with extensions to finite step size.
result: Their estimate explains the looseness of general bounds, remains more accurate for finite steps, and becomes an upper bound per step in the many-step limit due to destructive interference.
conclusion: The results offer practical heuristics for resource optimization in quantum simulation, though they are algorithmic rather than information-theoretic.

title: Infrared-absorption Magnetometry In A Diamond Nanocavity: Demonstration And Limits At The Nanoscale
authors: Nicholas J. Sorensen, Elham Zohari, Chris Coutts, Sean Mcnaney, Matteo Feder, Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi, Sigurd Fl{\aa}gan, Vinaya K. Kavatamane, Christoph Simon, Paul E. Barclay
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diamond quantum sensors promise both high spatial resolution and high sensitivity; however, conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout can be difficult to integrate efficiently. Infrared absorption by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provides a promising alternative, although the sensitivity of compact absorption-based sensors is limited by the short optical interaction length between the probe field and the NV ensemble. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate, for the first time, singlet-absorption magnetometry using spin-dense diamond nanocavities. By probing cavity modes near the 1042 nm NV singlet transition, we observe spin-dependent cavity transmission and perform cavity-enhanced magnetic field sensing. We further develop and experimentally validate a model that accurately predicts the spin-dependent cavity response, describes the optimal operating conditions, and identifies the practical limitations of different optically detected magnetic resonance modalities. Together, these results establish cavity-enhanced singlet absorption as a scalable readout mechanism for integrated diamond quantum sensors and provide a practical framework for engineering next-generation nanophotonic diamond quantum magnetometers.
tldr: The paper demonstrates cavity-enhanced infrared-absorption magnetometry using nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond nanocavities, achieving spin-dependent cavity transmission readout and validating a model of the sensing response.
motivation: Conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout for diamond NV sensors is difficult to integrate efficiently, and compact absorption-based sensors suffer from short optical interaction lengths. The authors aim to overcome this by using spin-dense diamond nanocavities to enhance the light-matter interaction.
method: They probe cavity modes near the 1042 nm NV singlet transition, measure spin-dependent cavity transmission, and perform cavity-enhanced magnetic field sensing. They also develop and experimentally validate a model predicting the spin-dependent cavity response and optimal operating conditions.
result: The authors observe spin-dependent cavity transmission and demonstrate singlet-absorption magnetometry with enhanced sensitivity. Their model accurately describes the cavity response and identifies practical limitations of different optically detected magnetic resonance modalities.
conclusion: Cavity-enhanced singlet absorption is established as a scalable readout mechanism for integrated diamond quantum sensors, providing a framework for engineering next-generation nanophotonic diamond magnetometers.

title: On The Hardness Of Optimal Cnot Circuits
authors: Andreas Pavlogiannis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note revisits the computational problem of optimal CNOT synthesis: given an invertible binary matrix [MATH] over the field of two elements and a budget [MATH], decide if [MATH] can be implemented with [MATH] CNOT gates. The [MATH]-completeness of this problem was recently published independently by Acuaviva, Acuaviva, and Acuaviva (arXiv:2608.03825) and by Li and Guan (arXiv:2609.04160). This note gives a new proof, with three features. First, [MATH]-completeness holds even over linear oracles, i.e., matrices of the form [MATH], which are the standard reversible embedding of a linear function [MATH]. These are involutions, and seemingly simpler than the families of the two previous works, which both have order four. Second, hardness persists when SWAP gates are free and qubits may be permuted (and this holds under any connected topology). Third, the exposition is arguably simpler to follow. Along the way, it gives a proof of the XOR-circuit lower bound of Boyar, Matthews, and Peralta [J. Cryptology 26 (2013)] that is, perhaps, simpler than existing ones.
tldr: A note giving a new, simplified proof that deciding whether a binary invertible matrix can be synthesized with a given budget of CNOT gates is NP-complete, even for linear (involution) oracles and with free SWAPs under any connected topology.
motivation: Optimal CNOT synthesis is central to reversible and quantum circuit compilation, and two recent independent works established NP-completeness for order-four gate families; a cleaner proof covering seemingly simpler instances was missing.
method: Reduction-based complexity proof establishing NP-completeness over linear oracles of the form I + uv^T (involutions), extended to settings where SWAP gates are free and qubits may be arbitrarily permuted on any connected topology; the argument also yields a simplified derivation of the Boyar-Matthews-Peralta XOR-circuit lower bound.
result: NP-completeness holds even for the restricted involution family and under free routing/permutation on connected architectures, substantially strengthening prior hardness results, with a more accessible exposition and a simpler XOR lower-bound proof.
conclusion: Optimal CNOT circuit synthesis is intractable in general even under favorable architectural assumptions, implying that practical compilers must rely on heuristics or approximations; the note also offers pedagogical value for lower-bound techniques.

title: Reducing T Gates In Product Formulas With Agent Loops
authors: Luis Mantilla Calder\'on, J\'er\^ome F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Kohei Nakaji, Taylor L. Patti, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum chemistry calculations on a fault-tolerant quantum computer usually require many [MATH] gates. This cost depends on the simulation method and how precisely its rotations are implemented. In this paper, we used Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a large language model (LLM), in a coding-agent loop to optimize the structure and rotation-synthesis precision of product formulas (PFs) for quantum phase estimation (QPE). Each of five independent searches optimized a shared protocol across 115 HamLib molecular Hamiltonians spanning 4--16 qubits over 100 code mutations. The searches started from a calibrated, nested second-order PF with uniform synthesis precision. We minimized [MATH], the estimated total [MATH]-gate cost including QPE queries and repeated attempts for [MATH] success probability, while requiring chemical accuracy for every training Hamiltonian. We name the best protocol found error-limited optimized Trotter evolution (ELOTE). It achieves chemical accuracy for its training data and achieved median and geometric-mean [MATH] reductions of [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. ELOTE combines contributions to the same Pauli string, uses a first-order PF, and varies synthesis precision with coefficient magnitude, Pauli support, and diagonal character. We also tested ELOTE on 76 larger Hamiltonians with 18--22 qubits, which met chemical accuracy in every case. For ten reaction energies, we further optimized a shared [MATH]-ELOTE protocol. It reduced geometric-mean [MATH] by [MATH] relative to ELOTE while preserving chemical accuracy for every signed reaction difference. These classically verified results show cost savings from shared protocols across molecules and reactions, and motivate similar searches in which energy measurements from quantum computers guide explorations in a coding-agent loop.
tldr: The paper uses an LLM coding-agent loop to optimize product-formula structure and rotation-synthesis precision, reducing estimated T-gate costs for quantum phase estimation on molecular Hamiltonians.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum chemistry simulations require many T gates, and reducing T-count is important for practical resource estimates.
method: Five independent LLM-driven code searches optimized a shared product-formula protocol across 115 HamLib molecular Hamiltonians, minimizing estimated total T-gate cost while preserving chemical accuracy.
result: The best protocol, ELOTE, achieved median and geometric-mean T-count reductions of about 72% and 70%, respectively, and maintained chemical accuracy on larger 18-22 qubit Hamiltonians and reaction-energy tests.
conclusion: Shared optimized product-formula protocols can yield substantial T-gate savings across molecules and reactions, motivating further LLM-agent-guided searches informed by quantum-computer energy measurements.

title: Quantum Copy Complexity Of Testing Monotonicity And Other Properties
authors: Preksha Naik
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the sample complexity of testing monotonicity of Boolean functions when the tester is given only copies of the quantum function state [MATH]. We give a tester with sample complexity [MATH], improving on the previous [MATH] upper bound of [CNS26]. We also prove the first nontrivial lower bounds for monotonicity testing from quantum function states, matching our upper bounds over a broad range of [MATH]. Our upper bounds use two approaches. The first approach refines the Fourier-based tester of [CNS26] by handling high-influence functions separately, adapting an idea from [KMS18]. The second approach uses the classical path tester of [KMS18] by constructing a quantum observable whose expectation equals the path tester's violation probability. To prove the lower bounds, we place independent functions in mutually incomparable regions of the Boolean hypercube, building on the classical constructions of [BB16, CWX17]. We introduce a new argument for the quantum setting that replaces a fixed number of copies with a Poisson-distributed number of copies, allowing the contributions from different regions to be analyzed independently. This same framework also allows us to prove an [MATH] lower bound for testing union-closedness and [MATH]-monotonicity from quantum function states.
tldr: The paper determines the quantum copy-complexity of testing monotonicity, union-closedness, and k-monotonicity of Boolean functions when the tester only receives copies of the quantum function state.
motivation: Classical property testing sample complexity is well understood, but the quantum analogue where the input is a quantum state encoding the function is new and was only recently upper-bounded; tight lower bounds were missing.
method: Two testers are given: a refined Fourier-based tester that treats high-influence functions separately, and a path-tester simulation built from a quantum observable whose expectation reproduces the classical violation probability. Lower bounds place independent functions in incomparable hypercube regions and replace fixed copy counts with Poisson-distributed copies so regions decouple.
result: Improved upper bounds over the previous CNS26 result and the first nontrivial lower bounds for monotonicity testing from quantum function states, matching over a broad parameter range; the framework also yields lower bounds for union-closedness and k-monotonicity testing.
conclusion: Quantum copy complexity of property testing can be characterized in several natural cases, but the topic sits in quantum query/complexity theory rather than in the information-theoretic or thermodynamic directions of interest.

title: Why $(4x(1-x))^{3/4}$ Approximates The Binary Entropy So Well: A Proof Of Tops{\o}e's Convexity Conjecture
authors: Jeroen van de Graaf

Topsoe (2001) proved the sharp bounds [MATH], i.e. [MATH], and conjectured that the effective exponent [MATH] is convex. We prove this conjecture. In the variable [MATH], [MATH] extends to a Pick function on [MATH] with an explicit positive density on the cut, so that [MATH] with [MATH] and [MATH] a moment sequence. Pinelis's monotonicity theorem, Topsoe's power-type bounds and the optimality of their exponents follow as corollaries, together with a classification of all exponents [MATH] for which [MATH] bounds [MATH]. The proof is by hand except for one inequality in one real variable on a bounded interval, certified by interval arithmetic. As an application we give sharp, certified constants for the approximation [MATH]: [MATH] on [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves Topsoe's convexity conjecture for the effective exponent in sharp bounds approximating the binary entropy.
motivation: Topsoe established sharp power-type bounds for the binary entropy and conjectured that the effective exponent is convex; this work resolves that conjecture.
method: The proof uses a variable transformation, extends the relevant function to a Pick function on a cut domain with explicit positive density, expresses coefficients via a moment sequence, invokes Pinelis's monotonicity theorem, and certifies one remaining inequality by interval arithmetic.
result: The convexity conjecture is proven, Pinelis-type monotonicity and Topsoe's power bounds follow as corollaries, all exponents yielding valid bounds are classified, and sharp certified constants are given for a specific approximation.
conclusion: The work provides a complete mathematical resolution of a classical binary-entropy approximation conjecture and supplies certified numerical constants, but it has no direct quantum-information extension.

title: Nitrogen-Vacancy Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy Of $^{15}$n Spins In Potassium Nitrite Solution
authors: Sehrish Iqbal, Jitender Kumar, Suvechhya Lamichhane, Rupak Timalsina, Sy-Hwang Liou, Abdelghani Laraoui
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nitrogen is essential in agricultural fertilizers, yet its nanoscale interfacial dynamics remain largely unexplored. Although quadrupolar broadening complicates [MATH]N nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) detection, [MATH]N (I=1/2) provides well-defined nuclear-spin signatures but remains challenging to detect at the nanoscale due to its low natural abundance and small gyromagnetic ratio. Here, we use a microfluidic quantum sensing platform based on shallow nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond to detect [MATH]N NMR from KNO[MATH] solution at room temperature and in a low magnetic field regime. Within femtoliter-scale sensing volumes, we measure a magnetic-field variance of up to ~442 nT[MATH], ~43 times greater than the expected statistical polarization. The [MATH]N spin correlation decays within ~500 [MATH], mainly limited by the NV spin lattice relaxation time and not by the molecular diffusion of the KNO[MATH] molecules. This is consistent with the formation of a KNO[MATH] adsorption layer on the diamond surface, supported by surface characterization.
tldr: A shallow NV-center microfluidic quantum sensing platform is used to detect 15N NMR from KNO2 solution at room temperature and low magnetic field.
motivation: 15N offers well-defined nuclear-spin signatures, but nanoscale detection is challenging due to low natural abundance and small gyromagnetic ratio; nitrogen interfacial dynamics remain largely unexplored.
method: Shallow nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond are coupled to a microfluidic KNO2 solution, and magnetic-field variance and spin-correlation decay are measured in femtoliter-scale sensing volumes.
result: The authors observe a magnetic-field variance up to ~442 nT^2, about 43 times larger than expected statistical polarization, and a 15N correlation decay within ~500 time units, limited mainly by NV spin-lattice relaxation rather than molecular diffusion.
conclusion: The observations are consistent with formation of a KNO2 adsorption layer on the diamond surface, demonstrating NV-based nanoscale NMR of 15N in solution.

title: A Realistic End-to-End Runtime Crossover Estimation For Quantum-Enhanced Training Of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
authors: Maximilian Alexander Wolf, Alona Sakhnenko, Florian Geissler, Andrea Matic, Jeanette Miriam Lorenz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is one promising application domain for Quantum Computing (QC) speedups, but asymptotic complexity considerations often mask the actual engineering costs of actual end-to-end workflows. For the use case of training a linearized Neural Network with a Quantum Linear Solver, a provably favorable quantum scaling has been suggested. We present realistic resource estimates for this problem, accounting for data access, computation, and readout. Our analysis examines three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios, under distinct sparsity-scaling assumptions, thereby enabling progressively more realistic resource estimates. We identify crossover regimes relative to classical methods and find that crossover points emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements. This work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML algorithms under realistic hardware constraints and help identifying the bottlenecks that must be overcome to approach industrial quantum utility.
tldr: The paper estimates realistic end-to-end runtime crossovers for quantum-enhanced training of large-scale machine learning models using a quantum linear solver.
motivation: Asymptotic quantum speedups for machine learning can obscure practical engineering costs, so the authors aim to quantify when quantum advantages might actually appear under realistic data access, computation, and readout constraints.
method: They perform resource estimates for training a linearized neural network with a quantum linear solver across three benchmarking scenarios with different sparsity-scaling assumptions.
result: Crossover points relative to classical methods emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements.
conclusion: The work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML under realistic hardware constraints and highlights bottlenecks that must be overcome for industrial quantum utility.

title: Bounding The Security Of The Falcon Signature Scheme In The Quantum Random Oracle Model
authors: Carl A. Miller Kelsey A. Jackson
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.
tldr: The paper provides a complete security proof for the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model, reducing its security to the RISIS and NTRU problems.
motivation: FALCON is a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme, but a 2024 oversight left its security proof incomplete in the quantum random oracle model; this work fills that gap.
method: The authors use known quantum reprogramming results to construct a reduction from FALCON security to the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem in the QROM.
result: They obtain the first complete QROM security proof for FALCON and propose parameter sets meeting NIST security levels under their reduction.
conclusion: The work strengthens the theoretical foundation of FALCON by extending its security analysis to the quantum random oracle model, though it remains a post-quantum cryptography contribution rather than a core quantum information result.

title: Four Classes Of Few-Weight Linear Codes Over $u\mathbb{F}_q+u^2\mathbb{F}_q+u^3\mathbb{F}_q$ From Simplicial Complexes
