authors: Lan Deng (hubei Key Laboratory Of Applied Mathematics, Faculty Of Mathematics And Statistics, Hubei University, Wuhan, China, School Of Mathematics And Statistics, Hanjiang Normal University, Shiyan, China), Zhao Hu (hubei Provincial Engineering Research Center Of Intelligent Connected Vehicle Network Security, School Of Cyber Science And Technology, Hubei University, Wuhan, China), Nian Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we construct linear codes over the commutative non-unital ring [MATH], where [MATH], using simplicial complexes in [MATH] and their complements. For codes defined by two arbitrary nonempty simplicial complexes, we determine the lengths and [MATH]-dimensions. When each complex has a single maximal element with nonempty proper support, we use an [MATH]-linear Gray map and exponential sums to determine the parameters and Lee weight distributions of four classes of codes. These classes have two, at most five, at most four, and at most eight nonzero Lee weights, respectively. Puncturing the Gray images yields projective codes with dual minimum distance three. Using the Griesmer bound, we obtain families of distance-optimal projective codes, including a binary family whose lengths exceed the bound by three. The Gray images are Euclidean self-orthogonal for [MATH] and for [MATH] under an additional condition, and Hermitian self-orthogonal for [MATH]. We also give sufficient conditions for minimality of both the Gray images and the projective codes.
tldr: The paper constructs four classes of few-weight linear codes over a non-unital ring using simplicial complexes and analyzes their Gray images, Lee weight distributions, projective puncturings, and self-orthogonality.
motivation: Few-weight linear codes are interesting for their algebraic structure and applications, and simplicial complexes provide a combinatorial construction method. The authors aim to extend such constructions to a specific non-unital ring setting and derive codes with controlled weight distributions.
method: They define linear codes over uF_q + u^2F_q + u^3F_q from arbitrary nonempty simplicial complexes and complements, determine lengths and dimensions, and use an F_q-linear Gray map plus exponential sums to compute parameters and Lee weight enumerators for four classes under a single-maximal-element condition.
result: The four code classes have two, at most five, at most four, and at most eight nonzero Lee weights. Puncturing their Gray images gives projective codes with dual minimum distance three, including Griesmer-bound-optimal families and a binary family exceeding the bound by three; self-orthogonality and minimality conditions are also derived.
conclusion: The work provides new combinatorial constructions of few-weight linear codes over a mixed ring alphabet with detailed weight and optimality analyses. It is primarily a classical coding-theory contribution with no direct quantum information, thermodynamic, network, or hybrid-system application.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms For Tsp And More
authors: Masayuki Miyamoto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on [MATH] cities in [MATH] time. To date, no [MATH]-time classical algorithm is known for any [MATH]. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time [MATH], which is still the best known quantum time bound. In this work, we improve the running time to [MATH]. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.
tldr: The paper improves the best-known quantum running time for the traveling salesman problem by combining the Ambainis et al. Grover-plus-dynamic-programming framework with recent extremal set-system techniques, and derives matching quantum space-time tradeoffs and extensions to related problems.
motivation: TSP is a canonical NP-hard problem whose best quantum bound (Ambainis et al., SODA 2019) has remained unchallenged, while new classical set-system-based space-time tradeoffs suggest room for quantum improvement.
method: The optimal tour is decomposed into four consecutive subpaths of differing sizes; set-system-based dynamic programming computes partial optimal values with small success probability, and amplitude amplification boosts the success probability to give the improved runtime.
result: An improved quantum time bound for TSP over the previous best, a new quantum space-time tradeoff improving Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant, and the same upper bounds for several related problems.
conclusion: Set-system frameworks originally developed for classical space-time tradeoffs translate productively into quantum algorithm design, yielding state-of-the-art quantum bounds for TSP and related optimization problems.

title: Qpat: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework For Quantum-Assisted Training And Classical Inference
authors: Yixiong Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.
tldr: QPAT uses a quantum circuit Born machine as a generative prior to improve classical model training while keeping inference fully classical.
motivation: The authors aim to leverage quantum inductive biases from QML without suffering NISQ-era bottlenecks such as barren plateaus, data-loading issues, and quantum inference latency.
method: A QCBM is trained as a learnable prior and coupled to classical backbones via decoupled fitness-based scoring and stochastic Drop-Prior mechanisms to distill structural knowledge into classical weights.
result: Across six benchmarks in time-series, vision, and NLP, QPAT reportedly improves predictive performance and seed stability over purely classical backbones, with ablations ruling out simple random or classically learned priors.
conclusion: The framework offers a practical hybrid route to QML benefits with classical inference, but its contribution is primarily applied machine learning rather than quantum information theory.

title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm For The Generalised Geography Game
authors: Shibdas Roy Mriganka Sandilya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Generalized Geography Game ([MATH]) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a directed graph, where players alternately move a token along edges without revisiting previously visited vertices. In the existing literature, determining whether an arbitrary position in a graph is a winning position for either player is a well-known [MATH]-complete decision problem. Certain formulations of [MATH] have been shown to fall outside the [MATH]-complete complexity class. While [MATH]-complete problems are believed to take exponential time for classical computation, quantum computation offers new possibilities. In this work, we present a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time ([MATH]) algorithm for solving the [MATH] problem. The proposed algorithm runs in time [MATH], which is polynomial in the input size [MATH], and achieves bounded error with [MATH]. This result demonstrates the potential of quantum algorithms to efficiently solve combinatorial game problems that are traditionally considered computationally hard in the classical setting.
tldr: The authors claim a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for the PSPACE-complete Generalized Geography game on directed graphs.
motivation: Generalized Geography is PSPACE-complete and believed to require exponential time classically, so the authors explore whether quantum computation can offer an efficient alternative.
method: A quantum algorithm is proposed that runs in time polynomial in the input size n and reportedly achieves bounded error, though the abstract gives no detail on the underlying quantum subroutine, oracle model, or complexity-theoretic assumptions.
result: The algorithm is claimed to solve the game in polynomial time with bounded error, ostensibly placing a PSPACE-complete problem in BQP.
conclusion: The paper asserts that quantum algorithms can efficiently solve traditionally hard combinatorial game problems, a claim that would overturn standard complexity-theoretic beliefs and thus requires much stronger justification than presented.

title: Northstar: Efficient Verifiable Negacyclic Polynomial Arithmetic With Applications To Encrypted Lattice-based Multi-Asset Erc-20 And Verifiable Fhe
authors: Yeoh Wei Zhu, Shaltiel Eloul, Yash Satsangi, Rob Otter
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice-based cryptography can be used to construct a variety of post-quantum cryptographic schemes, ranging from standard cryptographic primitives such as digital signatures and encryption, to fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). However, the verification of correct lattice computations remains relatively expensive, particularly for computationally intensive FHE operations and for resource-constrained environments such as on-chain verification via smart contracts. We propose Northstar, an efficient technique for proving negacyclic arithmetic natively. When integrated with existing STARK proving frameworks, Northstar achieves the best overall performance across prover time, verifier time, and proof size compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches for verifiable FHE constructions. Furthermore, Northstar is used to construct the first verifiable encrypted multi-asset (~ 1000 assets) variant of ERC-20 that is efficiently verifiable by a smart contract, and is practically deployable in the current blockchain ecosystem.
tldr: Northstar introduces an efficient proof technique for negacyclic polynomial arithmetic to enable verifiable FHE and encrypted lattice-based multi-asset ERC-20 tokens.
motivation: Verifying lattice-based computations, especially FHE operations and on-chain smart contracts, remains expensive, limiting practical deployment.
method: The paper proposes Northstar, a native negacyclic arithmetic proving technique integrated with STARK frameworks to reduce prover/verifier costs and proof size.
result: Northstar outperforms prior verifiable FHE approaches across prover time, verifier time, and proof size, and enables the first efficiently smart-contract-verifiable encrypted multi-asset ERC-20 variant.
conclusion: The work advances practical verifiable post-quantum cryptography and blockchain-deployable FHE verification, but is not directly aligned with quantum information theory research interests.

title: How Many Keys Must A Quantum Computer Break To Take Over A Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient For Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks
authors: Seyyed Mohammad Hassan Halataei
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockchains that run on proof of stake, among them Ethereum and Solana, are secured by a vote: a transaction becomes irreversible once computers holding two thirds of the deposited money have signed it. Each signature is made with a secret key whose public counterpart is permanently visible, and a large quantum computer could compute the secret from the public key. We ask a simple question: how many such keys would it have to break to take over the vote? We call the answer the quantum Nakamoto coefficient and measure it on live data from fifteen networks, collected on 15 November 2026. For fourteen of them, 2 to 18 keys are enough to break the network's security guarantee and 7 to 77 to control it outright; at one key every 12 minutes, the pace implied by recent resource estimates, a single quantum computer would defeat the guarantee of any of these networks in less than four hours and take full control in less than sixteen hours. Ethereum is far more robust, but a 2025 change that lets operators merge their deposits into fewer keys has cut the number of keys at its first threshold from about 465,000 to 7,682, a factor of 60. We derive a simple formula for this effect, and another for the small rotating committee on which wallets rely, and confirm both on the data. For fourteen of the fifteen networks, the first large quantum computer would be less than a day away from total control. Their validator signatures should therefore be migrated to post-quantum schemes before such a machine exists, since once it does, the time to respond is measured in hours.
tldr: The paper defines a 'quantum Nakamoto coefficient' measuring how many validator signing keys a quantum adversary must break to compromise the security guarantee or seize control of fifteen proof-of-stake blockchains.
motivation: Proof-of-stake blockchains rely on ECDSA-style signatures whose public keys are permanently visible, so a future large-scale quantum computer could forge validator votes; stakeholders need quantitative estimates of how vulnerable each network is.
method: Using live staking and validator data from fifteen networks collected on 15 November 2026, the author counts the minimum number of distinct keys needed to cross the two-thirds signing thresholds, and derives simple analytic formulas for key-merging effects and rotating wallet committees.
result: For fourteen of fifteen networks, 2-18 broken keys suffice to break the security guarantee and 7-77 to take full control, implying total compromise within under a day at one key per 12 minutes; Ethereum's first-threshold key count fell from ~465,000 to 7,682 after a 2025 consolidation change.
conclusion: The author urges migration of validator signatures to post-quantum schemes before fault-tolerant quantum computers exist, since response times after their arrival would be measured in hours.

title: A Non-Commutative Binomial Theorem, Extensions, And Applications
authors: Raghu Meka Ravi Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a matrix trace inequality analogous to the binomial theorem for reals: for Hermitian matrices [MATH] and [MATH], and a nonnegative even integer [MATH] (and any nonnegative integer [MATH] when [MATH] are positive semi-definite), \[ \bigl((A + B)^k\bigr) \le \sum_{\ell=0}^k {\ell} \bigl(A^\ell B^{k-\ell}\bigr). \] The above natural inequality implies the classical Golden--Thompson inequality [MATH]. It also proves an extension, which can be used to show other new inequalities as well as give short proofs of inequalities such as the Schatten-[MATH] two-point inequality for [MATH] and Hanner's inequality for [MATH]. The main proof was discovered by Gemini Carbon within an agentic system.
tldr: The paper proves a matrix trace inequality analogous to the binomial theorem for Hermitian matrices, from which the Golden–Thompson inequality and other norm inequalities (Schatten-p two-point, Hanner's) follow.
motivation: The authors aim to establish a natural non-commutative analogue of the binomial expansion at the level of matrix traces, and to unify/derive several classical matrix inequalities as corollaries.
method: Pure matrix analysis: an inequality bounding the trace of (A+B)^k by a sum of terms of the form Tr(A^l B^{k-l}), valid for Hermitian matrices with even k (and PSD matrices for any k), proved by the authors via an agentic AI system (Gemini Carbon).
result: The inequality implies the Golden–Thompson inequality and yields short proofs of the Schatten-p two-point inequality and Hanner's inequality, plus further new inequalities.
conclusion: The work provides a compact unifying inequality in matrix analysis; its bearing on quantum information is only indirect, as these are general-purpose mathematical tools rather than information-theoretic results.

title: Exact Minimum Distances Of Primitive Narrow-Sense Bch Codes: At And Beyond The Bose Distance
authors: Run Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the exact minimum distances of two families of primitive narrow-sense BCH codes of length [MATH], where [MATH] is a prime power and [MATH]. For [MATH], codes with designed distance [MATH] have minimum distance and Bose distance both equal to their designed distance. Furthermore, for integers [MATH] satisfying [MATH], codes with designed distance [MATH] have Bose distance equal to their designed distance and minimum distance [MATH]. Consequently, the gap between the minimum distance and the Bose distance in this family is exactly [MATH] and grows without bound as [MATH] increases, with fixed [MATH].The proofs proceed by constructing good zero-sets from quadratic forms for the first family, and by combining upper bounds provided by the first family with lower bounds derived from the divisibility of codeword weights in punctured generalized Reed--Muller codes for the second. We also derive explicit dimension formulas by counting cyclotomic cosets.
tldr: The paper exactly determines the minimum distances of two families of primitive narrow-sense BCH codes, showing the gap between minimum distance and Bose distance grows without bound.
motivation: The Bose distance (from the BCH bound) is only a lower bound on the true minimum distance; for many BCH families the exact minimum distance and the size of the gap to the Bose distance remain open.
method: Good zero-sets are constructed from quadratic forms to handle the first family, while the second combines upper bounds from the first family with lower bounds derived from divisibility of codeword weights in punctured generalized Reed-Muller codes; explicit dimension formulas come from counting cyclotomic cosets.
result: For one family the minimum distance equals the designed/Bose distance; for the other, the Bose distance equals the designed distance while the minimum distance is strictly smaller, giving an unbounded gap as the code length grows.
conclusion: The work settles exact minimum distances and dimensions for these BCH families and demonstrates that the Bose-distance bound can be arbitrarily loose.

title: Evaluating Post-Quantum And Hybrid Signatures For Blockchains: Performance, Storage And Ledger Growth
authors: Essam Ghadafi Anthony Mikhaiel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 [MATH]s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.
tldr: An empirical benchmark of 13 classical and post-quantum signature configurations (ECDSA, ML-DSA, Falcon, SLH-DSA, and hybrids) in a simulated blockchain, projecting signing/verification cost, throughput, and ledger growth onto five public chains.
motivation: Quantum computing threatens ECDSA-based blockchains, so migration to post-quantum signatures is expected, but the practical costs — larger transactions, slower verification, faster ledger growth — are poorly quantified beyond the security analysis.
method: A common simulated blockchain framework is used to measure signing and verification times, transaction throughput, and signature/public-key sizes for 13 configurations, with measured overheads extrapolated to Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain, and TRON.
result: Lattice-based verification is cheap (Falcon-512 at 30.1 us vs ECDSA 32.8 us), but storage overhead is large: Falcon-512 would inflate ledger sizes by 79-229%; hybrids add modest extra storage but ECDSA+Falcon-512 roughly doubles Falcon-512 verification cost, and Bitcoin/Solana transaction-size limits impede migration.
conclusion: Storage overhead, not verification cost, is likely the dominant obstacle to post-quantum migration of blockchains; the work is an applied engineering benchmark rather than an information-theoretic contribution.

title: The Functional Batch Conjecture And Its Extension To All Finite Fields
authors: Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy Isaac Barouch Essayag (yohananov)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the code whose servers store all [MATH] nonzero linear combinations of [MATH] information symbols over [MATH] is a functional batch code with list size [MATH]: every list of [MATH] requested nonzero linear combinations, repetitions allowed, can be recovered from pairwise disjoint sets of at most two servers. This holds for every finite field and every [MATH], and the list size cannot be increased, even if recovery sets of any size are allowed. For [MATH] the statement is the functional batch conjecture for the binary simplex code, in its stronger form with recovery sets of size at most two, and it follows from the conjecture of Balister, Gyri and Schelp on perfect matchings of [MATH] with prescribed differences, which was proved by the second author in a separate paper. We also determine the minimum length of a functional batch code with [MATH] information symbols over [MATH]: it is [MATH] for the list size [MATH], for every [MATH], and, for odd [MATH], it is [MATH] for the list size [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves a functional batch conjecture for a code storing all nonzero linear combinations of information symbols over any finite field, showing list-size bounds with recovery sets of at most two servers, and determines minimal lengths of such codes.
motivation: Batch codes address the problem of distributing encoded data across servers so that any small set of requests can be served by disjoint recovery sets; the functional variant concerns requests for linear combinations rather than individual symbols.
method: Combinatorial and algebraic proof over arbitrary finite fields, connecting the binary case to the Balister–Győri–Schelp conjecture on perfect matchings with prescribed differences, plus constructions and bounds for minimal length.
result: List size two suffices and is optimal even when recovery sets may be arbitrarily large; for odd characteristics minimal lengths are determined for list sizes two and three.
conclusion: The results settle the functional batch conjecture in strong form and generalize it from the binary simplex code to all finite fields.

title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis Of Information Hiding In Semantic Communication
authors: Shijun Xiang Yanhao Huo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic communication shifts the transmission goal from the accurate recovery of syntactic symbols to the reliable conveyance of semantic content, yet a systematic information-theoretic characterization of information hiding at the semantic layer is still missing. Building on the semantic information theory of Niu-Zhang and the classical information hiding theory of Moulin-O'Sullivan, this paper establishes an information-theoretic framework for information hiding under semantic communication. The classical hiding model is extended to a two-layer structure (semantic host, syntactic host, syntactic composite signal, syntactic received, semantic received) bridged by synonymous mappings f_s, f_x and the inverse mapping f_y^{-1}, subject to four distortion constraints: syntactic transparency, semantic fidelity, syntactic perturbation, and semantic destruction. The capacity is cast as a Stackelberg game with the hider moving first and the payoff J(Q,A) = I(U~; Y~ | K) - I(U~; S~ | K), yielding the single-letter maximin C^s = max_Q min_A J(Q,A), whose achievability and converse follow from random coding and joint typicality decoding. Relative to the classical capacity, comparison payoffs built from the up/down semantic mutual information give the endpoint sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) with the classical value C in the same interval, while closing semantic tolerance yields C^s_no-tol <= C_cl under a fair comparison. These results clarify that semantic hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding. Binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples confirm the degeneration under one-to-one mappings and the capacity loss under coarsening.
tldr: The paper develops an information-theoretic framework for information hiding (steganography) at the semantic layer of semantic communication, deriving single-letter maximin hiding capacities via a Stackelberg game formulation.
motivation: Semantic communication changes the transmission goal from exact symbol recovery to semantic content conveyance, but no systematic information-theoretic characterization of semantic-layer information hiding existed; the authors extend Moulin-O'Sullivan classical hiding theory using Niu-Zhang semantic information theory.
method: A two-layer hiding model (semantic host, syntactic host, composite signal, syntactic and semantic received signals) bridged by synonymous mappings and four distortion constraints is proposed, with capacity cast as a Stackelberg maximin game J(Q,A) = I(U~;Y~|K) - I(U~;S~|K), solved via random coding and joint typicality arguments.
result: The semantic capacity satisfies the sandwich C^s_end(0,1) <= C^s <= C^s_end(1,0) containing the classical capacity C, and under vanishing semantic tolerance C^s_no-tol <= C_cl; binary, ternary, and Gaussian examples show degeneration to classical results for one-to-one mappings and capacity loss under coarsening.
conclusion: Semantic-layer hiding is not unconditionally superior to classical hiding; the framework quantifies exactly when semantic tolerance helps or hurts hiding capacity.

title: Optimal \texorpdfstring{$(1,1)$}{(1,1)}-Criss-Cross Deletion-Correcting Codes With Linear-Time Encoder And Decoder
authors: Zhiqiang Li, Yubo Sun, Gennian Ge
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a [MATH]-ary [MATH] array subject to a [MATH]-criss-cross deletion, which removes one row and one column. We first derive a sphere-packing type lower bound on the redundancy of codes correcting such deletions. For every [MATH] and [MATH], the redundancy is greater than [MATH]. For fixed [MATH], it is at least [MATH] as [MATH]. We then present two code constructions. The first construction achieves redundancy [MATH] by selecting a largest syndrome class. It matches the lower bound up to a vanishing term and admits [MATH]-time decoding. The second construction has redundancy [MATH] and admits [MATH]-time algorithms for both encoding and decoding. For fixed [MATH], these running times are linear in the number of array entries.
tldr: The paper studies q-ary arrays corrupted by a (1,1)-criss-cross deletion (removal of one row and one column), deriving sphere-packing lower bounds on redundancy and constructing deletion-correcting codes with linear-time encoding and decoding.
motivation: Criss-cross deletions model synchronized row/column loss in array-based storage and two-dimensional data structures, and prior work lacked tight redundancy bounds and efficient code constructions for the single-row/single-column case.
method: The authors derive a sphere-packing-type lower bound on redundancy for q-ary M×N arrays, then give two constructions: one based on selecting the largest syndrome class under a suitable parity-check map, and one with an explicit structured encoder achieving linear-time encoding and decoding.
result: Redundancy is shown to exceed a given threshold for all parameters and to grow at least logarithmically in the array dimensions for fixed q; the first construction attains redundancy matching the bound up to a vanishing term with near-linear decoding, while the second achieves slightly larger redundancy with linear-time encoding and decoding.
conclusion: Optimal-order redundancy for criss-cross deletion correction is achievable with computationally efficient codes, closing the gap between sphere-packing bounds and explicit constructions for this two-dimensional deletion model.

title: A Perturbative Two-Eigenvalue Faber-Krahn Problem For The Gaussian Short-Time Fourier Transform
authors: Yifan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that, for every fixed s\in (0,\infty), the set of area s maximizing the weighted sum of the first two eigenvalues of the associated Toeplitz operators on the Fock space must be a disc, up to translations and sets of measure zero. To do so, we first prove the existence of maximizer sets. Then we show that every maximizer set must be a perturbation of a disc when the weight is sufficiently small. Finally, we use the vector-valued version of the analytic implicit function theorem and the inverse function theorem to conclude that the perturbation must vanish when the weight tends to zero.
tldr: The paper proves a perturbative two-eigenvalue Faber-Krahn-type result for Toeplitz operators on the Fock space, showing that area-constrained maximizers of a weighted sum of the first two eigenvalues are discs up to translations and measure-zero sets.
motivation: The work is motivated by spectral shape-optimization problems of Faber-Krahn type in the setting of Gaussian short-time Fourier transforms and Fock-space Toeplitz operators.
method: The authors prove existence of maximizers, show that any maximizer is a perturbation of a disc for sufficiently small weight, and then use vector-valued analytic implicit and inverse function theorems to show the perturbation vanishes as the weight tends to zero.
result: For every fixed positive area parameter, the optimal set for the weighted sum of the first two eigenvalues is a disc up to translations and measure-zero modifications.
conclusion: This establishes a perturbative two-eigenvalue Faber-Krahn theorem for the Gaussian short-time Fourier transform, contributing to mathematical spectral optimization rather than quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Symmetry-Aware Residual Learning Of Few-Body Molecular Wave Functions
authors: Meital Bojan, Mikhail Maslov, Jing-Lun Li, Alex M. Bronstein, Mikhail Lemeshko
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultracold polar molecules are a highly controllable platform for engineering quantum matter, but modeling their few-body properties remains computationally challenging. Their anisotropic long-range interactions and rich internal structure lead to high-dimensional eigenvalue problems for which conventional grid-based solvers are largely restricted to two-molecule systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics-informed neural variational method that exploits known physical structure of the molecular wave function. Our key idea is to factor the wave function into analytic and neural components. The analytic component encodes rotational symmetry and asymptotic decay, while the neural residual learns the remaining intermediate-range behavior. This decomposition reduces the effective dimensionality of the problem without relying on ad hoc approximations or problem-specific discretization grids. We benchmark our method against high-accuracy two-molecule solvers and recover both ground and excited bound states with mean relative errors below 0.01%. We further demonstrate the method's applicability to three-body systems by computing field-linked trimer ground-state energies in percent-level agreement with an independent grid-based calculation. This provides a systematic route to larger molecular systems and opens opportunities to study correlations and dynamics in interacting quantum matter.
tldr: The paper introduces a symmetry-aware neural variational method for computing few-body molecular wave functions of ultracold polar molecules.
motivation: Ultracold polar molecules are a controllable platform for quantum matter, but their anisotropic long-range interactions create high-dimensional eigenvalue problems that are difficult for conventional grid-based solvers beyond two-molecule systems.
method: The wave function is factored into an analytic component encoding rotational symmetry and asymptotic decay and a neural residual component learned variationally, reducing effective dimensionality without ad hoc grids.
result: The method matches high-accuracy two-molecule solvers with mean relative errors below 0.01% and computes three-body field-linked trimer ground-state energies in percent-level agreement with an independent grid-based calculation.
conclusion: This provides a systematic computational route to larger molecular systems and may enable studies of correlations and dynamics in interacting quantum matter.

title: Fuel As Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links After Total Key Compromise
authors: Leon Birkel, Mohammad Hamad, Sebastian Steinhorst
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.
tldr: The paper proposes OrbitLock, an orbit-position-gated authentication protocol for inter-satellite laser links that remains secure even after total key compromise.
motivation: Optical inter-satellite links rely solely on keys, so total key compromise leaves no secret for re-authentication; existing rekeying and post-compromise protocols do not solve this without an authenticated starting point.
method: The authors formalize a position-gated adversary and prove a tight lower bound on the propellant cost for an impostor satellite to block and retransmit a laser beam while not in free fall, then combine this orbit gate with ML-KEM in a history-chained protocol.
result: For satellites on a shared circular orbit, a CubeSat-class impostor requires continuous thrust and runs out of propellant in about two days under a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol uses under 0.02% of the link capacity.
conclusion: OrbitLock enables link authentication without pre-shared crosslink keys and can retroactively authenticate past keys after total compromise, but it is a classical/post-quantum satellite network security protocol rather than a quantum information result.

title: Numerical Studies Of Ground State Atomic Parity Violation Measurements In Cesium
authors: Chunya Wang, Matthew Summers, Jonah A. Quirk, Diego Garcia, Carol E. Tanner, D. S. Elliott
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report results of numerical simulations of an ongoing measurement designed to measure the electric dipole (E1) transition moment between hyperfine components of the ground state of atomic cesium. This E1 moment is non-zero solely due to nuclear weak interactions between the nucleons, leading to a nuclear anapole moment of the cesium nucleus. Through these simulations, we explore the effect on the microwave spectrum of a static transverse magnetic field, a spatial offset of the atomic beam from the axis of the radio-frequency (rf) cavity, the angular tilt of the rf cavity, and the ac Stark shift by the Raman-coupling beams used to generate the initial superposition state between ground state components. The results of these simulations help place limits on the experimental parameters, and help guide the future experimental procedures.
tldr: Numerical simulations of an ongoing cesium atomic-beam experiment aimed at measuring ground-state atomic parity violation via the nuclear anapole moment, studying systematic effects on the microwave hyperfine spectrum.
motivation: Precision measurement of the parity-violating E1 transition moment between ground-state hyperfine levels of cesium probes nuclear weak interactions and the nuclear anapole moment, testing the Standard Model in atomic systems.
method: Numerical simulation of the experiment, modeling the influence of static transverse magnetic fields, atomic-beam offset from the rf cavity axis, rf cavity tilt, and ac Stark shifts from Raman-coupling beams on the microwave spectrum.
result: Quantifies the sensitivity of the measured hyperfine microwave spectrum to each investigated systematic effect, thereby bounding tolerable ranges for the experimental parameters.
conclusion: The simulations constrain experimental parameters and will guide future procedures for the parity-violation measurement; the work is precision atomic/nuclear physics rather than quantum information science.

title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity In The Rom
authors: Miranda Christ, Oliver Korten, Tal Malkin, Noam Mazor, Shyamal Patel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector [MATH] into a commitment whose size is independent of [MATH], such that a verifier can open any bit [MATH] using [MATH] hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations. We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity [MATH], where [MATH] is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.
tldr: The paper proves that hash-based vector commitments with sublogarithmic verifier query complexity are impossible in the random oracle model, showing high-arity Merkle trees are essentially optimal.
motivation: Merkle trees have been the most efficient hash-based vector commitments for decades, and verifier runtime is a bottleneck for SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries, leaving open whether sublogarithmic verifier complexity is achievable.
method: A black-box lower bound is established in the random oracle model via a new 'disjoint product lemma', a computational analogue of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer inequality, yielding an omega(log n / log log n)-style query lower bound for deterministic verifiers.
result: Any deterministic vector commitment built from a random oracle with input length lambda requires verifier query complexity matching the high-arity Merkle tree bound up to constant factors, ruling out sublogarithmic verification even from collision-resistant hash functions.
conclusion: Merkle trees are optimal among black-box hash-based vector commitments, and the disjoint product lemma is offered as a tool for further random-oracle lower bounds and separations.

title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis Of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys
authors: Yongkang Xiao, Jing Chen, Min Shi, Kun He, Mei Wang, Ruiying Du
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern cryptographic protocols such as WPA2-PSK, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Bluetooth Classic (BC) tolerate low-entropy keys for user-friendliness, backward compatibility, or resource-constrained deployment, yet existing symbolic protocol verifiers rely on the perfect-encryption assumption and therefore cannot reason about brute-force attackers. Prior work addresses this gap only through protocol-specific, manually encoded reveal rules, which neither generalize across protocols nor systematically explore compound-key decomposition. We introduce the first protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic methodology for low-entropy keys, built on three abstractions: the message-derivation fact MDerive, which captures brute-force prerequisites independently of concrete function symbols; a three-tier breaking-oracle design (value-breaking, relationship-breaking, message-derivation) that composes with the standard Dolev-Yao attacker; and a graded bit-level attacker model that bounds the key length an attacker is allowed to exhaust. We realize the methodology as EntropyVerif, a syntax-sugar extension of Tamarin that requires no kernel modification. Using EntropyVerif we automatically rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks, and uncover a new attack on BC which we call the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack: by repeatedly downgrading one side of a BC session and recombining the recovered key fragments, an attacker reduces session-key recovery against devices using the maximum 128-bit key from [MATH] to [MATH], bottoming out at [MATH] for [MATH]---a factor of [MATH] reduction that has been responsibly disclosed to the Bluetooth SIG. Across three real-world protocols and six BC device configurations, our results show that entropy-aware symbolic analysis is both feasible and necessary.
tldr: The paper introduces EntropyVerif, an automated symbolic verification methodology for cryptographic protocols that tolerate low-entropy keys, enabling reasoning about brute-force attackers beyond the perfect-encryption assumption.
motivation: Many real-world protocols such as WPA2-PSK and Bluetooth tolerate low-entropy keys, but existing symbolic verifiers assume perfect encryption and cannot model brute-force key exhaustion, while prior fixes are protocol-specific and manual.
method: The authors propose protocol-agnostic abstractions including the MDerive fact, a three-tier breaking oracle composed with the Dolev-Yao attacker, and a graded bit-level attacker model, implemented as a Tamarin syntax-sugar extension called EntropyVerif.
result: EntropyVerif rediscovers known PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks and uncovers a new Bluetooth Classic Unilateral Multi-Downgrade attack that reduces effective session-key recovery from 128 bits to much lower values across device configurations.
conclusion: Entropy-aware symbolic analysis is shown to be feasible and necessary for protocols with low-entropy keys, but the work is classical cryptographic protocol verification and does not address quantum information theory.

title: Quantization And Codebook Stability Of Euclidean And Kl Lattice Quantizers
authors: Haoxuan Luo, Ryan Gabrys, Farzad Farnoud
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small edits to raw data can cause large changes in the compressed version, which can be costly in applications such as data synchronization and incremental backup. We study quantization stability, the probability that two perturbed distributions map to the same representative, and codebook stability, the probability that the resulting Huffman codebooks are the same. We first quantize the empirical distribution and then construct a Huffman code from the quantized distribution, which can improve codebook stability at the cost of some compression efficiency. We study two quantizers based on a shifted and scaled lattice in the probability simplex: the Euclidean Lattice Quantizer (ELQ) and the KL Quantizer (KLQ). For ELQ, we derive bounds on quantization stability and KL distortion. For KLQ, we show that its quantization cells can be determined by comparisons with adjacent lattice codewords and use the distances to the cell boundaries to derive a quantization stability bound. For a symmetric codebook of positive types, we obtain the exact worst-case KL distortion over the full probability simplex. We also give a heuristic choice [MATH] of the minimum codeword probability and compare it with the minimum coordinate of a Lloyd-optimized codebook. Simulations using canonical Huffman coding compare ELQ and KLQ with an existing compander-based quantizer and show the trade-off between KL distortion, codebook stability, and encoded length under random deletions.
tldr: The paper analyzes quantization stability and Huffman codebook stability for two lattice-based quantizers (Euclidean Lattice Quantizer and KL Quantizer) operating on empirical distributions in the probability simplex.
motivation: Small perturbations of raw data can drastically change compressed outputs, which is problematic for data synchronization and incremental backup, so quantizing the empirical distribution before Huffman coding is proposed to improve codebook stability.
method: Bounds on quantization stability and KL distortion are derived for ELQ, while for KLQ the quantization cells are characterized via comparisons with adjacent lattice codewords, yielding a stability bound from distances to cell boundaries; a symmetric codebook of positive types gives exact worst-case KL distortion.
result: Exact and bounded characterizations of KL distortion and stability are obtained, a heuristic minimum codeword probability is proposed and compared to Lloyd-optimized codebooks, and simulations with canonical Huffman coding quantify the trade-off between KL distortion, codebook stability, and encoded length under random deletions.
conclusion: Lattice-based quantization offers a tunable trade-off between compression efficiency and robustness of codebooks to data perturbation, but the work is entirely classical source-coding theory with no quantum information, thermodynamic, network, or hybrid-platform content.

title: Quantization Concealment Of Angular Momentum: Dynamic Origin Of Spins
authors: Wei Ku Wenjie Long
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since their introduction, spins of elementary particles remain a phenomenological addition to modern quantum theories. While relatively recent studies on Dirac and other linearized equations of motion have revealed the spatial current nature of the spin magnetic moment (instead of the commonly pictured self-rotation), the dynamical origin of this circulating current remains unresolved. Here, we expose a long-overlooked generic shortcoming of wave mechanics ("quantization concealment of angular momentum") that undesirably reduces the canonical angular momentum of bound eigen-modes and renders incomplete the minimal coupling to magnetic fields. Recovering the kinetic orbital angular momentum resolves [MATH]-orbital's counterintuitive "zero" angular momentum and reproduces all planar modes' anomalous Zeeman splitting. Regarding spins as effective remedy to the concealment offers natural explanations to their main puzzles: 1) dynamical origin of spin magnetic moment and 2) frame invariance of spin angular momentum. This implies absence of spin magnetic moment for free particles, a strong prediction verifiable through Stern-Gerlach experiments on electrons.
tldr: The paper argues that a generic shortcoming of wave mechanics, termed quantization concealment of angular momentum, obscures the kinetic orbital angular momentum of bound eigenmodes and provides a dynamical origin for particle spin as an effective remedy.
motivation: The authors aim to resolve long-standing puzzles about the physical origin of spin and the spin magnetic moment, which remain phenomenological additions in quantum theory despite recent insights into the spatial current nature of the magnetic moment.
method: The work analyzes canonical angular momentum in bound eigenmodes and minimal coupling to magnetic fields, recovering the kinetic orbital angular momentum to reproduce anomalous Zeeman splitting and reinterpret spin as an effective construct.
result: Recovering the concealed kinetic orbital angular momentum explains the zero angular momentum of certain orbitals and all planar modes' anomalous Zeeman splitting; spin emerges as an effective remedy, implying free particles lack spin magnetic moments.
conclusion: The paper predicts the absence of spin magnetic moments for free electrons, a claim testable via Stern-Gerlach experiments, and reframes spin as a dynamical consequence of quantization concealment rather than an intrinsic property.

title: From The Deterministic Hook Effect To Stochastic Reliability In Ternary Complex Formation
authors: Deepak K. Agrawal
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ternary binding systems occur in signaling, scaffold-mediated assembly, and targeted protein degradation. A mediator brings two partners into a productive ternary complex, but excess mediator can hold them in separate binary complexes. Consequently, ternary complex formation can increase and then decrease as the mediator dose increases, producing the hook effect. Deterministic dose-response curves describe the average behavior but do not indicate whether individual small compartments reliably form the complex. A minimal reversible binding network was studied using deterministic equations, exact stochastic simulations, and a simple catalytic extension. The deterministic model recovered the hook-shaped response. In stochastic simulations, small volumes often failed to accumulate the required number of complexes, even where the deterministic prediction was favorable. At low mediator doses, failure reflected a shortage of mediator molecules; at high doses, material accumulated in free or binary-bound forms. Larger volumes increased the range of mediator doses supporting reliable formation, while stricter copy-number thresholds narrowed that range. Faster ternary-complex completion or slower breakup improved reliability. In the catalytic model, product formation also depended on how early productive complexes formed. These results show why a favorable average binding response does not necessarily ensure reliable assembly in small reaction volumes.
tldr: The paper studies deterministic versus stochastic reliability of ternary complex formation, explaining why average hook-shaped dose-response behavior can mask failure in small volumes.
motivation: Ternary binding systems are important in signaling and targeted protein degradation, and the hook effect means excess mediator can suppress productive complex formation; the authors ask whether favorable average dose-response curves imply reliable assembly at the single-compartment level.
method: The author analyzes a minimal reversible binding network using deterministic rate equations, exact stochastic simulations, and a simple catalytic extension.
result: Deterministic equations reproduce the hook effect, while stochastic simulations show frequent failure in small volumes even at favorable deterministic doses; reliability improves with larger volumes, faster complex completion, slower breakup, and lower copy-number thresholds.
conclusion: A favorable average binding response does not guarantee reliable ternary complex formation in small reaction volumes, so stochastic effects are essential for assessing assembly reliability.

title: A Coupled Thermomechanical Model With Volterra Memory: Influence Of The Kernel Class On Relaxation Asymptotics
authors: Andrii Siasiev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The aim of this study is to determine how the class and asymptotic behaviour of a Volterra memory kernel influence relaxation in a coupled thermomechanical model. The model describes the mutual interaction between an internal mechanical variable and temperature through temperature-dependent material properties and mechanical dissipation. The analysis combines a Volterra integral formulation, a spectral representation of the memory mechanism, thermodynamic decomposition of the hereditary power, local well-posedness analysis, linearization near equilibrium, and Laplace-transform asymptotic arguments. The spectral representation separates the energy stored in the relaxation modes from irreversible hereditary dissipation and establishes the thermodynamic consistency of the memory contribution. Under minimal assumptions on the constitutive functions and the kernel, local existence and uniqueness of solutions are obtained; for thermodynamically dissipative memory and a non-negative external heat source, positivity of the absolute temperature is preserved. The main result concerns the linearized dynamics near equilibrium: with the thermomechanical coupling kept unchanged, an exponential kernel produces exponential relaxation, whereas a power-law kernel with a long tail produces algebraic relaxation. A numerical comparison performed for the same set of dimensionless thermomechanical parameters illustrates these two asymptotic regimes. The results show that changing the class of the memory kernel alone can change the qualitative long-time relaxation law of the coupled system.
tldr: The paper studies how the class of a Volterra memory kernel controls long-time relaxation in a coupled thermomechanical model.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how hereditary memory affects relaxation asymptotics in thermomechanical systems with temperature-dependent properties and mechanical dissipation.
method: The analysis uses a Volterra integral formulation, spectral representation of memory, thermodynamic decomposition, local well-posedness, linearization near equilibrium, Laplace-transform asymptotics, and numerical comparison.
result: Exponential kernels yield exponential relaxation, while power-law kernels with long tails yield algebraic relaxation, even with thermomechanical coupling fixed.
conclusion: Changing only the memory-kernel class can qualitatively alter the long-time relaxation law of the coupled system.

title: Time-reflection Nonlocal Equations From $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$-symmetric Oscillator Pairs: Physical Origin And Variational Formulation
authors: Ya\u{g}{\i}zhan \c{s}ahin Ilmar Gahramanov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that every second-order differential equation with time reflection describes the [MATH]-symmetric solutions of a local pair of oscillators that is invariant under exchange combined with time reversal. For linear equations the pair is built from springs, balanced gain and loss, and a gyroscopic coupling. We determine when such a pair has a regular first-order Lagrangian, and when the solutions of the equation fix its coefficients. As the main example, we consider a recently studied equation whose solutions do not depend on its velocity coupling. In the corresponding pair this coupling acts only on the conserved total momentum, which vanishes for [MATH]-symmetric solutions, and each of the two conditions that single out the model places the pair at an exceptional point. When the spring and velocity couplings are both nonzero, the pair has no regular first-order Lagrangian, while the equation has one with second derivatives. We also propose an electronic realization and construct a Bateman-type Hamiltonian, from which the velocity coupling is removed by a canonical transformation.
tldr: The paper shows that time-reflection nonlocal equations arise from PT-symmetric solutions of coupled oscillator pairs with balanced gain/loss and gyroscopic coupling, and analyzes their Lagrangian and Hamiltonian structure.
motivation: The authors aim to uncover the physical origin of second-order differential equations with time reflection by relating them to local oscillator pairs invariant under exchange combined with time reversal.
method: They construct linear oscillator pairs with springs, gain/loss, and velocity coupling, determine conditions for a regular first-order Lagrangian, and use canonical transformations to derive a Bateman-type Hamiltonian.
result: PT-symmetric solutions make the velocity coupling act only on the conserved total momentum, which vanishes; certain conditions place the pair at an exceptional point, and nonzero spring and velocity couplings preclude a regular first-order Lagrangian while allowing a second-derivative Lagrangian.
conclusion: The work provides a physical and variational foundation for time-reflection nonlocal equations and proposes an electronic realization, but it lies outside the researcher's prioritized quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems directions.

title: Bistable Waves And Propagation Success On Hexagonal Lattice
authors: Jian Fang, Yifei Li, Yijun Lou, Jian Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by propagation phenomena occurring on media with hexagonal structures, we propose an idealized system of bistable reaction-diffusion equations posed on a hexagonal lattice, and investigate the existence and speed of traveling wave solutions. We establish a sharp criterion for propagation success (nonzero wave speed) and failure (zero wave speed), where the criterion is determined by an angle-dependent periodic threshold function and the ratio of two parameters in the nonlinearity. Moreover, the sign of the wave speeds is governed by the angle and the parameter ratio. Our results imply that the hexagonal structure and bistability significantly affect the propagation dynamics.
tldr: The paper studies bistable reaction-diffusion equations on a hexagonal lattice and derives angle-dependent criteria for traveling-wave propagation success or failure.
motivation: The work is inspired by propagation phenomena in hexagonal media and aims to understand how lattice geometry and bistability affect wave propagation.
method: The authors propose an idealized system of bistable reaction-diffusion equations on a hexagonal lattice and analyze existence and speed of traveling wave solutions.
result: They establish a sharp threshold criterion for nonzero versus zero wave speed, determined by an angle-dependent periodic threshold function and a parameter ratio; the sign of wave speeds also depends on angle and parameter ratio.
conclusion: Hexagonal structure and bistability significantly affect propagation dynamics, yielding angle-dependent propagation criteria.

title: Electrical Grid Stabilisation Through Agent Strategies : A Mean-field Game Approach
authors: Loumi Gatouillat, Guillaume Roux, Dganit Meidan, C\'ecile Appert-Rolland, Cosimo Gorini, Denis Ullmo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose and solve a minimal model based on mean-field game theory to study decentralized power consumption strategies to stabilize power grids. The mean-field Kuramoto description of an electrical network is coupled to agents with anticipatory capacity for decision making in energy consumption. Each agent minimizes an individual cost which includes both a financial part (cost induce by consumption and by power reservation) imposed by a central authority, and a (personal) non-monetary part. This elementary model of active oscillators is exactly solvable in the steady state regime. We show that the synchronized regime of the network can be significantly extended by the game.
tldr: The paper proposes a mean-field game model coupling Kuramoto oscillators to anticipatory agents to study decentralized power-consumption strategies for stabilizing electrical grids.
motivation: Power grids require decentralized control strategies to maintain synchronization under fluctuating consumption, and the authors aim to model strategic agent behavior using mean-field game theory.
method: They couple a mean-field Kuramoto description of an electrical network with agents that minimize individual costs comprising financial and non-monetary terms, and solve the model exactly in the steady-state regime.
result: The synchronized regime of the network can be significantly extended by the game-theoretic anticipatory strategies of the agents.
conclusion: Strategic decentralized consumption decisions can improve grid stability, illustrating the value of mean-field game approaches for power-grid synchronization problems.

title: A Nonequilibrium-capturing Unified Gas-kinetic Scheme Ii: Multi-frequency Radiation Transport
authors: Hongyu Liu, Xiaojian Yang, Xing Ji, Jianxian Qiu, Kun Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional discrete ordinate methods are widely used for thermal radiative transfer, but their fixed number of angular degrees of freedom (DoFs) incurs unnecessary computational cost near equilibrium. We therefore develop a nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme (NCUGKS) for multi-frequency radiation transport. The scheme preserves the mul tiscale capability of UGKS through interface evolution that couples transport and collision. Radiation intensity is expanded in an orthonormal basis of the discrete angular space. The expansion coefficients serve as angular DoFs, with their number adapted independently to local nonequilibrium in each cell, frequency group, and quadrant. At each time step, the coefficients to be evolved are selected using the exponentially decayed contribution from the previous step and the requirements of interface transport. The selected coefficients are advanced by the finite volume scheme and corrected to match the macroscopic radiation energy before higher-degree coefficients are discarded according to the prescribed relative tail tolerance. Therefore, in the optically thick limit, the resulting representation retains only one angular DoF per quadrant. Numerical tests spanning different optical regimes show close agreement with reference solutions, validating its accuracy. Furthermore, in terms of memory and computational efficiency, the proposed method reduces memory by factors from 21.7 to 154.0 and achieves speedups from 24.87 to 257.9 compared with the original discrete ordinate UGKS. NCUGKS thus provides the ability to accurately simulate multiscale ra diative transfer with reduced memory and computational costs. The proposed approach also offers a framework for adapting angular degrees of freedom in other discrete ordinate methods.
tldr: The authors introduce a nonequilibrium-capturing unified gas-kinetic scheme (NCUGKS) for multi-frequency radiative transfer that adaptively reduces angular degrees of freedom in near-equilibrium regions to cut memory and cost.
motivation: Conventional discrete ordinate methods fix the number of angular degrees of freedom, which wastes computation in optically thick (near-equilibrium) regions where few angular modes matter.
method: Radiation intensity is expanded in an orthonormal basis over the discrete angular space; expansion coefficients act as angular DoFs chosen per cell, frequency group, and quadrant based on exponential decay of prior-step contributions and interface transport requirements, then advanced by a finite-volume scheme and corrected to match macroscopic radiation energy, with higher-degree coefficients discarded via a tail tolerance.
result: Numerical tests across optical regimes agree closely with reference solutions, while memory is reduced by factors of 21.7–154.0 and speedups of 24.87–257.9 are achieved versus the original discrete-ordinate UGKS.
conclusion: NCUGKS enables accurate multiscale radiative transfer simulation at much lower memory and computational cost, and offers a general framework for adapting angular degrees of freedom in other discrete-ordinate methods.

title: Deep-learning-enabled Rapid Spatially Multiplexed Wavefront Sensing With A Thin Diffuser
authors: Ming Xue, Shijie Wei, Shulei Zhao, Zhuojia Shi, Tengfei Wu, Xiaopeng Shao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional wavefront sensing typically measures aberrations along a single guide-star direction, limiting the correction of field-dependent aberrations over a wide field of view. Spatial multiplexing with a thin diffuser enables simultaneous measurements across multiple isoplanatic patches, but the computational cost of reconstruction makes it difficult to track changing aberrations. We propose a deep-learning approach that combines recurrent all-pairs field transforms for displacement estimation with Zernike coefficient regression. Experimental results show that the method accurately reconstructs multiple wavefronts from a single speckle pattern and reduces three-channel reconstruction time from 2801.6 ms with conventional digital image correlation (DIC) to 23.1 ms. The reconstructed wavefronts agreed more closely with sequential single-channel references than those obtained by multiplexed DIC, and simulations showed that Zernike regression was more robust to noise than direct gradient integration. These results suggest a path toward dynamic wide-field aberration sensing and high-speed adaptive optics.
tldr: The paper proposes a deep-learning method combining recurrent all-pairs field transforms and Zernike coefficient regression for rapid spatially multiplexed wavefront sensing with a thin diffuser.
motivation: Conventional wavefront sensing measures aberrations along a single guide-star direction, limiting correction of field-dependent aberrations over a wide field of view; spatial multiplexing with a thin diffuser enables simultaneous multi-patch measurement but reconstruction is computationally expensive.
method: The authors use recurrent all-pairs field transforms for displacement estimation and regress Zernike coefficients to reconstruct multiple wavefronts from a single speckle pattern.
result: The method reduces three-channel reconstruction time from 2801.6 ms with conventional digital image correlation to 23.1 ms and yields wavefronts closer to sequential single-channel references, with simulations showing improved noise robustness of Zernike regression over direct gradient integration.
conclusion: The approach suggests a path toward dynamic wide-field aberration sensing and high-speed adaptive optics.

title: Carrier Relaxation Confines The Bogdanov--Takens Degeneracy Of An Optically Injected Semiconductor Laser
authors: A. Mart\'in-Ruiz, E. Chan-L\'opez, Carlos Antonio Mar\'in-Mendoza
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optically injected semiconductor lasers are forced nonlinear oscillators whose locking boundaries are organized by codimension-two points. We ask which property of the carrier balance permits or forbids a Bogdanov--Takens (BT) point in the standard three-dimensional rate equations. Taking the carrier inversion [MATH] as distinguished observable, the rate that enters the spectral conditions is the slope of the gain--loss balance, [MATH], where [MATH] is the damping of the relaxation oscillation and [MATH] the normalized stimulated-emission factor. The two BT conditions become affine in [MATH] and imply the exact sum rule [MATH] between injection amplitude [MATH] and intracavity intensity [MATH]. The product of the two relaxation eigenvalues that survive at a saddle-node is bounded below by [MATH], so that no BT point exists for [MATH], whatever [MATH], the linewidth enhancement factor, the injection strength and the detuning; below this barrier every contact between Hopf and saddle-node curves is a fold--Hopf point. For [MATH] the barrier is completed to an exact existence criterion. We prove that the unfolding of a BT point by injection strength and detuning is transversal if and only if two explicit curves cross transversally in the plane of locked states; for [MATH] this is a simple root of an explicit function, and transversality fails exactly at the existence threshold. Two BT points at [MATH], [MATH] are verified to be generic, and the contacts between Hopf and saddle-node curves are classified into fold--Hopf, BT and nilpotent triple-zero points.
tldr: The paper analyzes the conditions under which an optically injected semiconductor laser can exhibit a Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation in its standard three-dimensional rate equations.
motivation: Optically injected semiconductor lasers are forced nonlinear oscillators whose locking boundaries are organized by codimension-two bifurcations, and the authors ask which carrier-balance properties permit or forbid a Bogdanov–Takens point.
method: Using the carrier inversion as a distinguished observable, the authors derive spectral conditions for Bogdanov–Takens points, obtain an exact sum rule between injection amplitude and intracavity intensity, and establish existence and transversality criteria.
result: They find a lower bound on the product of relaxation eigenvalues at a saddle-node, showing that no Bogdanov–Takens point exists below a threshold and that fold–Hopf points occur instead; above the threshold they give exact criteria and verify generic two-point examples.
conclusion: Carrier relaxation strongly constrains the Bogdanov–Takens degeneracy in optically injected semiconductor lasers, and the Hopf–saddle-node contacts are classified into fold–Hopf, Bogdanov–Takens, and nilpotent triple-zero points.

title: Existence Of Single-resonance Parametric Bound States In The Continuum: System Of Schr\"odinger Equations
authors: Ya Yan Lu Xiuchen Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is an eigenmode of a linear wave system with its eigen-frequency embedded in the radiation continuum of scattering states. At the frequency of a BIC, scattering problems with given incident waves from infinity lose uniqueness. Due to their close connection with strong resonance effects, BICs have found many useful applications in classical and quantum wave systems. Existence theories of BICs have been established for some cases involving the so-called symmetry-protected BICs, Friedrich-Wintgen BICs, and Fabry-Perot BICs. The single-resonance parametric BICs (srp-BICs) are another important class of BICs. Such a BIC emerges from a single resonant state through tuning a real parameter. Using a simple system of two one-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations, we demonstrate the formation of srp-BICs and establish a rigorous existence theory.
tldr: The paper proves existence of single-resonance parametric bound states in the continuum using a simple system of two one-dimensional Schrödinger equations.
motivation: Bound states in the continuum are important wave phenomena with applications in classical and quantum wave systems, but a rigorous existence theory for single-resonance parametric BICs was lacking.
method: The authors analyze a reduced model consisting of two coupled one-dimensional Schrödinger equations and tune a real parameter to demonstrate the emergence of a BIC from a single resonance.
result: They establish a rigorous existence theory for single-resonance parametric BICs in this model system.
conclusion: The work extends BIC existence theory to a new class and provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for single-resonance parametric BICs.

title: Vector Quantized Information Bottleneck Mitigation Of Adversarial Attacks On Modulation Classifiers
authors: Silvija Kokalj-Filipovic Attanasia Garuso
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) signal processing based on machine learning, including Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC), plays a critical role in Next Generation (NextG) intelligent communications but remains highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Prior work explored Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) as a means to improve robustness, but only in continuous spaces and never for RF classifiers. We investigate the impact of discrete-space information bottlenecks on the adversarial robustness of AMC models. Classification accuracy of attacked modulated RF waveforms is evaluated in two frameworks designed to leverage VIB for adversarial robustness: (i) a two-stage framework where VIB is applied in the preprocessing step using a Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQVAE) to suppress adversarial perturbations in the process of input signal reconstruction and (ii) a Vector Quantized Classifier (VQC) that leverages VIB inside the classifier proper. The architectures of VQVAE and VQC are identical up to the bottleneck where the VQVAE adds a decoder while VQC utilizes a classification head. We train both VQVAE and VQC with loss functions that we derive from the VIB information-theoretic model. Both frameworks incorporate vector quantization and KL regularization to enforce discrete bottlenecks that filter out adversarial noise. Evaluations under white-box attacks demonstrate that discrete bottlenecks significantly enhance robustness: VQVAE outperforms its continuous VAE (Variational Autoencoder) counterpart, while VQC achieves strong robustness without requiring signal reconstruction.
tldr: The paper applies vector-quantized discrete information bottlenecks (VQVAE and Vector Quantized Classifier) to harden RF automatic modulation classification models against white-box adversarial attacks.
motivation: ML-based RF signal processing such as automatic modulation classification is deployed in NextG communications but is highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations; prior variational information bottleneck defenses were limited to continuous latent spaces and never tested on RF classifiers.
method: Two frameworks are proposed: a two-stage VQVAE preprocessing scheme that reconstructs inputs through a discrete bottleneck to suppress adversarial noise, and a VQC that embeds the same vector-quantized bottleneck inside the classifier; both are trained with loss functions derived from a variational information bottleneck model with vector quantization and KL regularization.
result: Under white-box attacks, discrete bottlenecks markedly improve robustness: the VQVAE outperforms its continuous VAE counterpart, and the VQC attains strong robustness without needing explicit signal reconstruction.
conclusion: Discrete, vector-quantized information bottlenecks are an effective defense for RF modulation classifiers, suggesting information-theoretic compression can filter adversarial perturbations.

title: Link Invariants From Charge-conserving Yang--Baxter Operators
authors: Laura Rodr\'iguez Sierra C\'esar Galindo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turaev's enhanced Yang--Baxter operators produce invariants of oriented links from solutions of the Yang--Baxter equation.
