If the enhancing endomorphism is diagonal with generic eigenvalues, Turaev's compatibility condition forces the Yang--Baxter operator [MATH] to be charge-conserving, that is, to send each [MATH] into the span of [MATH] and [MATH]. Charge-conserving Yang--Baxter operators were classified by Martin and Rowell. Building on their classification, we determine all enhancements of charge-conserving Yang--Baxter operators with diagonal enhancing endomorphism, and we identify the resulting link invariants. The link invariant associated with such an enhancement is a sum over the colourings of the components of the link by the connected components of [MATH], in which each monochromatic sublink contributes a specialization of the HOMFLY--PT polynomial and different colours interact only through linking numbers. Every such state sum arises in this way.
tldr: The paper classifies enhancements of charge-conserving Yang--Baxter operators with diagonal enhancing endomorphisms and identifies the resulting oriented link invariants as state sums involving HOMFLY--PT specializations and linking numbers.
motivation: Turaev's enhanced Yang--Baxter operators yield link invariants, and generic diagonal enhancements force charge conservation, motivating a complete classification of such enhancements and their invariants.
method: Building on Martin and Rowell's classification of charge-conserving Yang--Baxter operators, the authors determine all compatible diagonal enhancements and analyze the associated link invariants.
result: Every such invariant is a sum over colorings of link components by connected components, where monochromatic sublinks contribute HOMFLY--PT specializations and different colors interact only through linking numbers; conversely, every such state sum arises this way.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of link invariants arising from charge-conserving Yang--Baxter operators with diagonal enhancements, connecting them to HOMFLY--PT polynomials and linking-number interactions.

title: Several Classes Of Few-weight Linear Codes Based On Weil Sums
authors: Lan Deng (hubei Key Laboratory Of Applied Mathematics, Faculty Of Mathematics And Statistics, Hubei University, Wuhan, China, School Of Mathematics And Statistics, Hanjiang Normal University, Shiyan, China), Zhao Hu (key Laboratory Of Intelligent Sensing System And Security), Nian Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear codes over finite fields with few weights are of significant interest due to their applications in areas such as secret sharing schemes, strongly regular graphs, and association schemes. In this paper, we construct several classes of p-ary linear codes based on Weil sums via the defining-set construction of bivariate form, where p is an odd prime. Utilizing the theory of quadratic forms and Weil sums over finite fields, the parameters and weight distributions of the codes are completely determined. As a result, several families of three-weight or four-weight linear codes are obtained from our construction. In addition, it is shown that most of our codes are minimal.
tldr: The paper constructs several classes of p-ary few-weight linear codes using Weil sums and bivariate defining sets, determining their parameters and weight distributions.
motivation: Few-weight linear codes over finite fields are useful in secret sharing, strongly regular graphs, and association schemes, motivating new constructions with explicitly determined weight distributions.
method: The authors use the defining-set construction of bivariate form and apply quadratic form theory and Weil sums over finite fields to compute code parameters and weight enumerators.
result: Several families of three-weight or four-weight linear codes are obtained, and most of the constructed codes are shown to be minimal.
conclusion: The work provides new explicit families of few-weight linear codes with potential applications in classical secret sharing and combinatorial structures, but it does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Functional Factor Graphs And The Functional Sum-Product Algorithm
authors: Giuseppe Thadeu Freitas de Abreu Kuranage Roche Rayan Ranasinghe
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a generalization of factor graphs and the sum-product algorithm (SPA), widely used in the estimation of data, channel state information and sensing parameters, to unknowns that are functions, such as waveforms, time-varying channels and continuous-aperture array currents, which must otherwise be sampled first. In order to mitigate the challenge that functions have no probability density functions (PDFs), the proposed scheme measures densities relative to the prior of each function, not to the flat reference implicit in every PDF. Messages then become likelihood ratios, and the factor-node rule an average over the priors, still exact on trees. For Gaussian models, the proposed functional SPA (FSPA) is Gaussian belief propagation (GaBP) with kernels in place of matrices and a grid-independent convergence condition, whereas scalar GaBP on grid samples provably slows down under refinement, as information hops from sample to sample. Simulations in a multi-user detection setting confirms the latter, and shows that sampling first can also fail for smooth priors.
tldr: The paper generalizes factor graphs and the sum-product algorithm to infer functional unknowns such as waveforms and continuous-aperture currents, with Gaussian belief propagation as a special case.
motivation: Standard factor graphs require unknowns to be sampled into finite-dimensional variables, which can be inefficient or inaccurate for intrinsically functional unknowns and may degrade under grid refinement.
method: The authors formulate functional factor graphs by measuring densities relative to each function's prior rather than a flat reference measure, turning messages into likelihood ratios and the factor-node rule into prior-weighted averages; for Gaussian models this yields kernel-based Gaussian belief propagation.
result: The proposed functional sum-product algorithm remains exact on trees and has a grid-independent convergence condition; simulations in multi-user detection show that scalar Gaussian belief propagation on grid samples slows under refinement and can fail for smooth priors.
conclusion: Functional factor graphs provide a principled inference framework for function-valued unknowns and avoid sampling artifacts, but the work is in classical statistical signal processing rather than quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: New Insights Into The Parameterized Complexity Of Cutwidth
authors: Klara Jacobsen, Klaus Jansen, Lis Pirotton, Bj\"orn Schumacher
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Cutwidth problem asks for a linear ordering of the vertices that minimizes the maximum number of edges crossing between two consecutive positions. The problem is proven to be NP-hard by Gavril [CISS '77], which motivated research in parameterized complexity. A previously claimed FPT result for Cutwidth and Imbalance parameterized by twin cover by Gorzny and Buss [COCOON '19] was later invalidated. Misra and Mittal [Theor. Comput. Sci. '21] clarified this issue, proved that Imbalance is in XP parameterized by twin cover and in FPT parameterized by [MATH]-bounded twin cover, i.e., where the size of the cliques outside the twin cover are bounded by [MATH]. The analogous questions remained open for cutwidth. In this work, we answer one of them by showing that Cutwidth is FPT parameterized by [MATH]-bounded twin cover. Additionally, we present an XP algorithm for Cutwidth parameterized by vertex integrity and prove W[1]-hardness for the parameter treedepth.
tldr: This paper settles open parameterized-complexity questions for the classical Cutwidth problem, showing FPT-ness under k-bounded twin cover, an XP algorithm for vertex integrity, and W[1]-hardness for treedepth.
motivation: Earlier claims of fixed-parameter tractability for Cutwidth and Imbalance under twin cover were shown to be invalid, leaving the cutwidth analogues unresolved; this work closes part of that gap.
method: Parameterized complexity analysis using structural graph parameters (k-bounded twin cover, vertex integrity, treedepth), with FPT algorithms, XP algorithms, and W[1]-hardness reductions.
result: Cutwidth is proven FPT parameterized by k-bounded twin cover, an XP algorithm is given for vertex integrity, and W[1]-hardness is established for treedepth.
conclusion: The results clarify the parameterized landscape of Cutwidth, but the techniques are purely combinatorial and have no bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Computer-assisted Proof Of One-cell Snaking And Lattice Trapping For A Nonlinear Square Lattice
authors: Jiangchao Qian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a computer-assisted proof of lattice trapping in an infinite nonlinear square lattice with interaction potential [MATH] and an antiplane crack far field [MATH]. We construct a connected branch of equilibria whose single-cell segment contains exactly two nondegenerate quadratic folds, with a stability sequence of stable, Morse index one, and stable in the full energy space. The fold loads satisfy [MATH] and [MATH], establishing a strictly positive lattice-trapping width [MATH]. A uniqueness argument establishes exact translation closure and smooth continuation across lattice cells. The proof combines renormalized energy, Schur complement estimates, analytic infinite-tail bounds, interval arithmetic, and exact integer positivity certificates. All finite input data, verification programs, and recorded certificate outputs are provided in the accompanying certificate archive.
tldr: The paper gives a computer-assisted proof of lattice trapping and one-cell snaking for an antiplane crack in an infinite nonlinear square lattice.
motivation: Lattice trapping is a fundamental mechanism by which a crack in a discrete lattice can remain pinned between loads, but rigorous proofs in nonlinear infinite lattices are difficult.
method: The proof combines renormalized energy, Schur complement estimates, analytic infinite-tail bounds, interval arithmetic, and exact integer positivity certificates to construct a connected branch of equilibria with two quadratic folds.
result: The authors establish a strictly positive lattice-trapping width and show a stability sequence of stable, Morse index one, and stable in the full energy space, with exact translation closure and smooth continuation across lattice cells.
conclusion: This provides a rigorous computer-assisted verification of one-cell snaking and lattice trapping in a nonlinear square lattice, with all verification data and certificates archived.

title: A $q$-analogue Of An Inverse Problem Leading To Second-order Linear Functionals
authors: Wathek Chammam
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: R. Sfaxi studied the linear functional [MATH] determined by the equation [MATH]. We replace the derivative by the Hahn operator [MATH] and study the solution [MATH] of [MATH]. For [MATH] we solve the equation explicitly when [MATH] is a Dirac mass, and we deduce that [MATH] is positive-definite whenever [MATH] and [MATH] is positive-definite on [MATH]. We show that [MATH] is [MATH]-semiclassical if and only if [MATH] for two non-zero polynomials [MATH] and [MATH], and we work out the [MATH]-analogues of the Hermite and Laguerre examples. Finally we treat the [MATH]-classical functional [MATH] whose moments are the [MATH]-factorials: here [MATH], and for [MATH] the functional [MATH] is positive-definite if and only if.
tldr: The paper constructs a q-analogue (via the Hahn operator) of an inverse problem for second-order linear functionals, characterizing positivity and q-semiclassicality and deriving q-Hermite and q-Laguerre examples.
motivation: R. Sfaxi previously studied a linear functional defined by a differential equation relating a functional to its derivative; the author aims to generalize this framework by replacing the ordinary derivative with the Hahn finite-difference operator.
method: The equation is solved explicitly for the case where the right-hand side is a Dirac mass, positivity of the resulting functional is analyzed, and a q-semiclassicality criterion is established in terms of two nonzero polynomials, with q-analogues of Hermite and Laguerre examples worked out.
result: The functional is shown to be positive-definite under stated conditions, to be q-semiclassical exactly when the associated polynomial pair satisfies the given relation, and the q-classical functional with q-factorial moments is characterized, including a positivity criterion.
conclusion: The work extends the theory of semiclassical and classical linear functionals to the Hahn-operator setting, providing a q-analogue of known inverse problems and explicit examples.

title: Quantifying Combined Rate- And Noise-induced Transitions In A Multiscale System
authors: Ryan Deeley, Peter Ashwin, Ulrike Feudel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Excitations in multiscale dynamical systems produce persistent but impermanent excursions away from a quiescent state. A novel mechanism for inducing excitations, through a combination of rate-dependent parametric and stochastic forcing, is discussed using the FitzHugh-Nagumo model as an example. In the absence of noise, a quasithreshold separating the state space between supercritical and subcritical behaviour is defined with respect to slow manifolds associated with the metastable excited state. This is formulated in an autonomous system framework, which can be obtained via a compactification of time. Techniques from singular perturbation theory elucidate how canard trajectories shape the geometric structure of the quasithreshold as the system's pullback attractor moves through it. The probability with which weakly stochastically driven sample paths travel through the quasithreshold and undertake (i) solely noise-induced and (ii) combined rate- and noise-induced excitations is estimated numerically for each of the corresponding forcing scenarios, using the adaptive multilevel splitting algorithm. The probability of weak stochastic forcing preventing a rate-induced excitation, which occurs deterministically, is likewise estimated. This quantifies the different rates at which the probability of each transition scenario scales exponentially with the noise strength, in accordance with sample path large deviation principles. It is revealed that a combination of (deterministically subcritical) parametric and stochastic forcing is exponentially more likely to induce excitations than stochastic forcing alone, which is attributed to the pullback attractor and quasithreshold converging towards one another.
tldr: A classical multiscale dynamical-systems study quantifying how combined rate-induced (parametric) and noise-induced excitations occur in the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, using large-deviation scaling of transition probabilities.
motivation: Excitations in multiscale systems produce persistent but impermanent excursions from a quiescent state, and the authors want to characterize a novel excitation mechanism where slow parametric forcing and weak stochastic forcing act together rather than separately.
method: A quasithreshold separating supercritical from subcritical behaviour is defined geometrically relative to slow manifolds of the metastable excited state, formulated in an autonomous framework via time compactification; singular perturbation theory (canard trajectories, pullback attractors) is combined with numerical estimation of transition probabilities using adaptive multilevel splitting.
result: Transition probabilities for noise-only, combined rate-and-noise, and noise-prevented rate-induced scenarios scale exponentially with noise strength following large-deviation principles; combined deterministic-subcritical parametric forcing plus noise is exponentially more likely to induce excitation than noise alone, attributed to convergence of pullback attractor and quasithreshold.
conclusion: Rate- and noise-induced transitions in multiscale systems can be quantified jointly, showing that weak parametric forcing dramatically amplifies stochastic excitation likelihood—a purely classical dynamical-systems result with no quantum information or thermodynamic content.

title: Two-timescale Variational Q-learning For Ergodic Risk-sensitive Control Of Markov Chains
authors: Guodong Pang Nicola G. Sassone
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a variational Q-learning algorithm for the ergodic risk-sensitive control of a discrete-time Markov chain with finite state and action spaces and an unknown transition kernel. The proposed algorithm is a two-timescale stochastic approximation algorithm, where the slow iteration solves for the fixed point of the multiplicative Bellman equation cast in a variational form, while the fast iteration solves the associated optimization problem over the probability simplex that stems from the variational representation. We prove that the iterates converge almost surely to the risk-sensitive Q-function and maximizing transition kernel. The proof adapts the ODE method for two-timescale stochastic approximation, where we analyze the global asymptotic stability of the equilibria of the corresponding fast and slow ODEs as well as bound the trajectory of the fast ODE away from zero. The main challenge lies in proving that, almost surely, the slow iterates are norm-bounded and the fast iterates are bounded below away from zero on the support of the transition kernel. We address this by using a fluid scaling approach for the slow iteration combined with tailored estimates for the fast iteration to control a certain fluid-scaled relative entropy error that arises in the ODE approximation. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithm and compare it with the existing risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithms.
tldr: The paper develops a two-timescale variational Q-learning algorithm for ergodic risk-sensitive control of finite-state Markov chains with unknown transition kernels.
motivation: Risk-sensitive control is important for decision-making under uncertainty, but existing Q-learning methods for ergodic risk-sensitive objectives can be challenging to analyze and implement efficiently.
method: The authors formulate the multiplicative Bellman equation variationally and solve it with a two-timescale stochastic approximation scheme: a slow Q-learning update and a fast simplex-constrained optimization update. Convergence is proved using ODE methods, global asymptotic stability, fluid scaling, and relative-entropy error control.
result: The iterates are shown to converge almost surely to the risk-sensitive Q-function and maximizing transition kernel, and numerical experiments compare performance with existing risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithms.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous convergence framework for variational risk-sensitive Q-learning, but it is a classical stochastic-control and reinforcement-learning contribution with no direct quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, or hybrid-systems component.

title: A Fast Tangential Rational Krylov Subspace Method With Randomized Sketching For Large Lyapunov Matrix Equations
authors: Fei Xue Tianqi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a tangential rational Krylov subspace method augmented with randomized sketching for solving continuous-time Lyapunov equations [MATH], where [MATH] is large and sparse and [MATH] has a rank much higher than one. Numerical solutions require high-dimensional rational Krylov subspaces (e.g., of dimensions up to [MATH]), leading to substantial computational cost and long runtime. Building on the adaptive strategies of [SIAM\,J.\,Matrix\,Anal.\,Appl., 35\,(2014), pp.\,476--498], which expand the subspace using the most relevant directions, we introduce several enhancements: selective orthogonalization of basis vectors and fast residual-norm estimation enabled by randomized sketching, and the option to use either adaptive distinct poles or a small set of repeated poles. We derive a new computable error bound for the approximate solutions and show that sketching does not degrade the convergence rate relative to the standard (non-sketched) algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved robustness and efficiency, with reduced runtimes and often higher accuracy than the standard tangential method.
tldr: The paper proposes a fast tangential rational Krylov subspace method with randomized sketching for solving large continuous-time Lyapunov matrix equations.
motivation: Large sparse Lyapunov equations with high-rank right-hand sides require high-dimensional rational Krylov subspaces, making standard methods computationally expensive.
method: The authors enhance an adaptive tangential rational Krylov method using selective orthogonalization and randomized sketching for fast residual-norm estimation, with choices of adaptive distinct poles or repeated poles, and derive a computable error bound.
result: Numerical experiments show improved robustness and efficiency, reduced runtime, and often higher accuracy than the standard tangential method, while sketching preserves the convergence rate.
conclusion: The proposed method provides an efficient numerical linear algebra approach for large Lyapunov equations, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Physics-Informed Learning For Multiplayer Differential Games
authors: Takuma Adams, Andrew C. Cullen, Tansu Alpcan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in [MATH]-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit [MATH]-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
tldr: The paper proposes a physics-informed neural network policy-iteration scheme with vanishing-viscosity annealing to approximate viscosity solutions of coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman systems for N-player adversarial differential games.
motivation: Computing per-player feedback strategies in multi-player differential games is hard because the coupled HJB system is high-dimensional and generally admits no classical solutions.
method: Viscosity solutions are approximated with PINNs inside a policy iteration loop with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule, with regret bounded via computable residuals.
result: The authors prove an explicit epsilon-Nash guarantee, finite-time attainment of the stopping criterion, and a computable value-function approximation error bound for two-player zero-sum games, validated on pursuit-evasion experiments.
conclusion: The framework provides certified approximate equilibria for high-dimensional differential games, but is a control-theory / scientific-machine-learning contribution with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Certified Outage Bounds For RIS-Assisted Noma With Source-Side Thermal Energy Harvesting
authors: Victor Rabiet
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian useful-gain and mean-interference approximations can cause opposite power-sizing errors in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We extend a source-side thermal energy harvesting model with Poisson interference and certify two-sided outage bounds. In a tested environment, the combined required signal-to-noise ratio error has opposite signs at 20 and 24 elements per user. Under another power convention, mean or moment-matched Gamma-distributed interference can predict false feasibility with exact useful gain. In the Gamma case, the Gaussian gain approximation can mask this false feasibility. Propagated Chernoff bounds give sufficient designs. Results concern the specified model and tested regimes.
tldr: The paper derives certified two-sided outage bounds for RIS-assisted NOMA systems with source-side thermal energy harvesting and Poisson interference, focusing on approximation errors in power sizing.
motivation: Gaussian useful-gain and mean-interference approximations can cause opposite power-sizing errors in RIS-assisted NOMA, so reliable outage certification is needed for system design.
method: It extends a source-side thermal energy harvesting model with Poisson interference and uses propagated Chernoff bounds to obtain sufficient design conditions and two-sided outage bounds under Gaussian and Gamma interference models.
result: In tested regimes, the combined required SNR error changes sign between 20 and 24 RIS elements per user, and Gamma-distributed interference can predict false feasibility that Gaussian gain approximations may mask.
conclusion: The proposed certified bounds provide sufficient designs for the specified model and tested regimes, highlighting the limitations of standard Gaussian approximations in RIS-assisted NOMA.

title: Syringe Reuse In Hcv Transmission Among People Who Inject Drugs: Behavioral Thresholds And Optimal Control
authors: Mohammad Zaman, Emel Khan, Ishfaq Ahmad, Hiromi Seno
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) transmission among people who inject drugs (PWID) is driven largely by syringe sharing and reuse, yet existing models rarely treat reuse as a behavior that individuals adopt and abandon. In this work, we develop and analyze a four-compartment epidemic model that explicitly incorporates syringe reuse as a distinct behavioral process, introducing a high-risk susceptible subgroup that acquires infection through both direct contact and syringe-mediated transmission. We establish the well-posedness and biological feasibility of the model, derive the basic reproduction number, and analyze the existence and stability of the disease-free and endemic equilibria along with closed-form behavioral threshold conditions for syringe-reuse adoption and cessation. Global sensitivity and scenario analyses reveal that while transmission and recovery parameters dominate epidemic potential, behavioral parameters governing the adoption and cessation of syringe reuse play a crucial role in disease persistence and control thresholds. The model's projected infection dynamics are broadly consistent with observed U.S. HCV incidence trends. We further formulate an optimal control problem targeting reuse initiation and cessation, and show through cost-effectiveness analysis that combined behavioral interventions outperform single-component strategies in reducing both infection and high-risk behavior. These results indicate that behavioral prevention aimed at syringe reuse is a necessary component of sustained HCV control among PWID.
tldr: A four-compartment epidemic model treats syringe reuse as an adoptable/abandonable behavior and derives behavioral thresholds plus optimal control strategies for HCV transmission among people who inject drugs.
motivation: Existing HCV transmission models for people who inject drugs rarely model syringe sharing/reuse as a dynamic behavioral process that individuals adopt and abandon, limiting understanding of behavioral prevention levers.
method: The authors build a compartmental epidemic model with a high-risk susceptible subgroup infected via direct contact and syringe-mediated transmission, derive the basic reproduction number, analyze equilibrium stability, obtain closed-form behavioral thresholds, and formulate an optimal control problem with cost-effectiveness analysis.
result: Transmission and recovery parameters dominate epidemic potential, but behavioral adoption/cessation parameters critically govern persistence and control thresholds; combined behavioral interventions outperform single-component strategies.
conclusion: Behavioral prevention targeting syringe reuse is argued to be a necessary component of sustained HCV control among PWID.

title: Statistical Analysis Of Crossing Beam Speckle Fields
authors: Ian D. Min-Roberts, Wojciech Rozmus, Pierre A. Michel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on the statistical analysis of single beam speckles, this paper develops a statistical description of speckle fields formed by crossing laser beams. A formal definition of individual speckles and their domains allows us to quantify the effective size and abundance of speckles. For two crossing beams, the effective speckle size is derived from the local curvature of the intensity field, and the expected speckle abundance is found asymptotically with the Kac-Rice formula. Monte Carlo simulations of speckle abundance show excellent agreement with the theoretical abundance formula. The two beam speckle analysis is then applied to a symmetric quad beam configuration motivated by polarization smoothing and demonstrates that increasing the separation between beams reduces expected stimulated Brillouin scattering reflectivity from saturated speckles. The statistical model is then extended to an arbitrary number of beams using a coordinate free formulation to obtain the spectral density of laser driven electron density fluctuations.
tldr: The paper develops a statistical description of speckle fields formed by crossing laser beams and applies it to beam-smoothing configurations and laser-plasma instabilities.
motivation: Speckle statistics for single beams are well studied, but crossing-beam configurations relevant to polarization smoothing and stimulated Brillouin scattering require a quantitative model of speckle size, abundance, and induced density fluctuations.
method: The authors define individual speckles and derive effective speckle size from local intensity curvature, compute expected speckle abundance asymptotically via the Kac-Rice formula, validate with Monte Carlo simulations, and extend the analysis to arbitrary beam number using a coordinate-free formulation.
result: The theoretical speckle abundance agrees well with simulations; for a symmetric quad-beam configuration, increasing beam separation reduces expected stimulated Brillouin scattering reflectivity from saturated speckles.
conclusion: The work provides a statistical framework for crossing-beam speckle fields and connects it to laser-plasma instability metrics, but it is outside the listed quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems research directions.

title: The Phases Of Hierarchy
authors: Gerard Mccaul
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a dynamical phase theory of hierarchy, in which depth decides whether a population of size [MATH] that revises its own environment can correct it without overcorrecting. The statistics that let a large majority detect a small bias - the basis of the Condorcet jury theorem - also make its response grow as [MATH]. Fed back into the environment it is judging, this sharpening destabilises the matched state through a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain, which we obtain analytically for a class of models we term adaptive normal forms. We show that this instability can be attenuated by hierarchical layering, requiring a depth scaling logarithmically with [MATH]. This recovers known logarithmic bounds in organisational economics directly from dynamic stability conditions. Hierarchical depth carries its own costs however, and by analysing the signal chain transmission up the hierarchy we show that beyond a finite depth no correction reaches the top before its deadline, and that below it the cost of arrival grows exponentially with depth. A hierarchy that is too flat therefore oscillates and one that is too deep cannot be steered in time, leaving a bounded window of depth between an unstable flat phase and a frozen inertial phase. We further show that these results can be generalised by treating each layer as a real-space renormalisation step, classifying aggregation rules by how they transmit bias. This establishes a connection between these dynamic results to attention in Transformers, where a residual update is diffusion on the token graph and depth plays the role of scale. Finally we show these phase boundaries are observable in finite sampling, and propose measurements which may characterise the proposed phases in real adaptive systems.
tldr: A dynamical-systems theory of hierarchical organization is developed, showing that a bounded window of hierarchy depth separates an unstable flat phase from a frozen inertial phase, with links to renormalization and Transformer attention.
motivation: The paper aims to explain why hierarchies have a characteristic depth, deriving known logarithmic scaling bounds in organizational economics from dynamical stability conditions rather than from static information arguments.
method: Adaptive normal forms are introduced to model a population revising its environment; a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain is derived analytically, layers are treated as real-space renormalization steps, and signal-chain transmission up the hierarchy is analyzed.
result: Depth must scale logarithmically with population size to suppress instability, but beyond a finite depth no correction arrives before its deadline and below it arrival cost grows exponentially with depth, yielding a bounded stability window observable in finite sampling.
conclusion: The framework connects hierarchical depth, aggregation rules, and depth-as-scale attention in Transformers, and proposes measurements to characterize the predicted phases in real adaptive systems.

title: Equilibrium Finiteness And Saari's Conjecture For The Planar Circular Restricted N-body Problem
authors: Qinglong Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish two results for planar Newtonian centers in uniform rotation. First, the associated quadratic-plus-Newtonian amended potential has finitely many equilibria for every finite configuration of at least two distinct centers with positive masses. Second, every collision-free planar test-particle motion with constant amended potential, equivalently constant rotating-frame speed, is stationary in the rotating frame. When the centers are primary bodies in a circular relative equilibrium, this proves the amended-potential form of Saari's conjecture for the restricted \(N\)-body problem.
tldr: The paper proves equilibrium finiteness and a Saari-conjecture result for planar circular restricted N-body problems using amended potentials.
motivation: The work addresses mathematical questions about equilibria and stationary motions in Newtonian N-body systems under uniform rotation.
method: The author studies quadratic-plus-Newtonian amended potentials for planar Newtonian centers and analyzes collision-free test-particle motions with constant amended potential.
result: The amended potential has finitely many equilibria for finite configurations of at least two positive-mass centers, and constant amended-potential collision-free motions are stationary in the rotating frame.
conclusion: This establishes the amended-potential form of Saari's conjecture for the restricted N-body problem when the centers form a circular relative equilibrium.

title: The Traveling Salesman Problem With Non-convex Polygonal Neighborhoods: A Hybrid Iterated Local Search--Block Coordinate Descent Approach
authors: Paula C. R. Ertel Ernesto G. Birgin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Traveling Salesman Problem with Neighborhoods (TSPN) generalizes the classical TSP by requiring a tour to visit a set of regions in the Euclidean plane rather than fixed point coordinates. It has applications in last-mile delivery, surveillance, and remote sensing in precision agriculture. In this paper, we address the Euclidean TSPN with arbitrary, non-convex polygonal neighborhoods---a highly complex setting due to the joint continuous and combinatorial optimization challenges. To solve the continuous subproblem of determining optimal visit points for a given visiting sequence, we propose a Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) method based on solving fast one-dimensional geometric subproblems. Computational experiments demonstrate that BCD computes optimal visit points for a fixed sequence in almost all instances in which optimality is certified, more than six orders of magnitude faster than a commercial solver solving the equivalent Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Programming (MIQCP) formulation. This efficiency enables an effective hybrid Iterated Local Search metaheuristic (ILS-BCD) that thoroughly explores the combinatorial search space at low computational cost. Extensive computational tests on 235 benchmark instances derived from the Generalized TSP (GTSP), with up to 100 neighborhoods, show that ILS-BCD matched or improved upon the best-known GTSP tours in all cases, obtaining strictly shorter tours in 234 instances. On the 80 instances for which optimality is proven, ILS-BCD attains the optimal tour length in all of them, within a relative difference below 0.001%. On 60 larger instances, with as many as 6,325 neighborhoods, ILS-BCD remains competitive up to about 220.
tldr: The paper develops a hybrid iterated local search and block coordinate descent method for the Euclidean traveling salesman problem with non-convex polygonal neighborhoods.
motivation: TSPN generalizes the traveling salesman problem to visiting regions rather than points and is useful in delivery, surveillance, and precision agriculture, but non-convex polygonal neighborhoods make the problem computationally challenging.
method: The authors propose a block coordinate descent algorithm to optimize visit points for a fixed visiting sequence by solving fast one-dimensional geometric subproblems, and embed it in a hybrid iterated local search metaheuristic.
result: The BCD routine finds optimal visit points much faster than a commercial MIQCP solver, and ILS-BCD matches or improves best-known GTSP tours on all 235 benchmark instances, proving optimal on 80 instances.
conclusion: The hybrid ILS-BCD approach is highly effective for TSPN with arbitrary non-convex polygonal neighborhoods and scales to instances with thousands of neighborhoods.

title: Stochastic Optimization With Network Distribution Dynamics Via Local Jacobian Approximation
authors: Yuchen Cai, Zhiyu He, Michael Muehlebach, Florian D\"orfler
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network systems feature complex interactions among agents, whereby local decisions can influence the state distributions observed by other agents through coupled network dynamics. Such endogenous distribution shifts across large-scale networks pose significant challenges and call for distributed and adaptive decision-making pipelines. To address these challenges and collectively optimize a steady-state performance objective, we propose a distributed network-aware decision-response (D-NAD) gradient algorithm. This algorithm enables each agent to approximate network-response sensitivity using only local information (i.e., the Jacobians of local dynamics and objectives) and neighborhood communication. We establish a non-asymptotic closed-loop convergence guarantee and quantify the impact of the Jacobian approximation errors therein. Numerical experiments on a semi-synthetic networked electric-vehicle price--demand problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: The paper proposes a distributed network-aware decision-response gradient algorithm that lets agents approximate network-response sensitivity using only local Jacobians and neighborhood communication to optimize a steady-state performance objective under endogenous distribution shifts.
motivation: In large-scale network systems, local decisions shift the state distributions observed by other agents through coupled dynamics, creating endogenous distribution shifts that complicate distributed, adaptive decision-making.
method: Each agent approximates the sensitivity of the network response using local Jacobians of its own dynamics and objective plus neighbor communication, yielding a distributed gradient algorithm (D-NAD) for which a non-asymptotic closed-loop convergence guarantee is derived and the effect of Jacobian approximation error is quantified.
result: The authors establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees including error bounds from local Jacobian approximations, and numerical experiments on a semi-synthetic networked electric-vehicle price-demand problem demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness.
conclusion: Local Jacobian approximation with neighborhood communication suffices for distributed optimization in networked systems with endogenous distribution dynamics, though the work is purely classical optimization and unrelated to quantum information science.

title: The Squared Antipode Of A Twisted Function Algebra Is Locally Unipotent
authors: Shlomo Gelaki Pavel Etingof
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a proalgebraic group over an algebraically closed field [MATH] of characteristic zero, and let [MATH] be a dimension-preserving tensor functor, possibly nonsymmetric. We prove that a tensor automorphism [MATH] of [MATH] is locally unipotent if and only if its trace on [MATH] equals [MATH] for every [MATH]. Applied to the Drinfeld element of a dual twisted function algebra [MATH], this proves our conjecture from 2000 that the square of the antipode in [MATH] is locally unipotent (arXiv:0002128). Without the trace assumption, we show that for any [MATH] the eigenvalues of [MATH] on [MATH] determine, modulo roots of unity, its eigenvalues on [MATH] for every Schur functor [MATH]. The proof combines the Koszul identity, polynomial growth of symmetric powers, Fourier inversion, and congruences for Newton sums.
tldr: The paper proves that the squared antipode of a twisted function algebra is locally unipotent, confirming a 2000 conjecture via tensor-category and algebraic-group methods.
motivation: It aims to resolve a conjecture about local unipotence of the squared antipode in dual twisted function algebras and to characterize when tensor automorphisms are locally unipotent via trace conditions.
method: The proof combines the Koszul identity, polynomial growth of symmetric powers, Fourier inversion, and congruences for Newton sums in the setting of proalgebraic groups and dimension-preserving tensor functors.
result: A tensor automorphism is locally unipotent iff its trace equals the dimension on every object, and applied to the Drinfeld element this establishes local unipotence of the squared antipode.
conclusion: The work confirms the conjecture and provides eigenvalue relations for Schur functors without the trace assumption, but it is a pure algebraic result with no direct quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, or hybrid-systems contribution.

title: Pacl: Patch-based Admissibility And Conservative Limiting Framework For Bound-preserving Compact Single-step Dg Methods For Hyperbolic Conservation Laws
authors: Zheng Sun Yue Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a Patch-based Admissibility and Conservative Limiting (PACL) framework for compact single-step discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretizations of hyperbolic conservation laws. The key idea is to establish admissibility of weighted averages over overlapping cell patches after a complete high-order time step. Continuous patch weights cancel interior numerical flux contributions, yielding admissibility estimates for weighted patch averages under suitable time-step conditions. A conservative patch correction uses these averages as reference states to obtain admissible physical cell averages, and a subsequent cellwise scaling enforces whole-cell or nodal admissibility in the original DG space. The framework requires neither a strong-stability-preserving decomposition nor auxiliary first-order discretizations, and all limiting is performed at the end of each time step. For scalar conservation laws, we prove a patchwise weak maximum principle for compact Runge--Kutta DG (cRKDG), ADER-DG with converged or fixed-Picard predictors, and Lax--Wendroff DG. We also prove that, under the stated local mesh and scaling assumptions, a single application of the scalar limiter preserves approximation order at active bounds, including flat extrema. For the compressible Euler equations, we establish patch admissibility for cRKDG and fixed-Picard ADER-DG under time-step conditions that maintain positive predictor density while allowing nonpositive predictor pressure. The analysis covers both exact spatial integration and compatible quadrature. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order accuracy and bound preservation, including problems with near-vacuum states and strong shocks.
tldr: The paper introduces PACL, a patch-based limiting framework for bound-preserving compact single-step discontinuous Galerkin methods for hyperbolic conservation laws.
motivation: High-order DG discretizations of hyperbolic conservation laws can produce unphysical oscillations and violate bounds; existing limiters often require SSP decompositions or auxiliary first-order schemes.
method: The framework proves admissibility of weighted averages over overlapping cell patches after a full high-order time step, then applies a conservative patch correction and cellwise scaling to enforce admissibility without SSP decomposition or first-order auxiliary discretizations.
result: For scalar laws, patchwise weak maximum principles are proven for cRKDG, ADER-DG, and Lax-Wendroff DG, and order preservation at active bounds is established; for Euler equations, patch admissibility is proven under time-step conditions allowing nonpositive predictor pressure.
conclusion: PACL provides a conservative, single-step limiting framework that preserves high-order accuracy and enforces bounds for compact DG methods, demonstrated numerically on near-vacuum and strong-shock problems.

title: Proof Of A Cardinality Conjecture For The Correction Terms In The Quantum $K$-theoretic Divisor Axiom
authors: Mizuki Takahashi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a conjecture due to Kato and Sagaki (arXiv:2604.04476) concerning the cardinality of sets of directed paths in the quantum Bruhat graph that occur in the quantum [MATH]-theoretic divisor axiom for the full flag manifolds in the quasi-minuscule case. We prove that the cadinality is equal to one or even, and its signed sum vanishes in the latter case. Consequently, the cancellation-free divisor axiom obtained by Kato and Sagaki under this conjecture holds unconditionally. The proof uses Schremmer's results on affine Bruhat order and Demazure products, together with a theorem that we prove for arbitrary Coxeter groups.
tldr: The paper proves a cardinality conjecture about correction terms in the quantum K-theoretic divisor axiom for full flag manifolds in the quasi-minuscule case.
motivation: Kato and Sagaki conjectured a combinatorial property needed to make their cancellation-free divisor axiom unconditional.
method: The proof uses Schremmer's results on affine Bruhat order and Demazure products, plus a theorem proved for arbitrary Coxeter groups.
result: The cardinality of the relevant directed-path sets is shown to be one or even, and the signed sum vanishes in the even case.
conclusion: This establishes the Kato-Sagaki cancellation-free divisor axiom unconditionally in the quasi-minuscule case.

title: Sharpness Of The Kadec'-type Theorem For The Union Of Intervals
authors: Oleg Asipchuk Thibaud Alemany
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we establish the sharpness of a Kadec'-type theorem for finite unions of intervals admitting the integers as an orthonormal spectrum by constructing an explicit counterexample.
tldr: The paper proves sharpness of a Kadec'-type theorem for finite unions of intervals that admit the integers as an orthonormal Fourier spectrum, via an explicit counterexample.
motivation: Kadec'-type results characterize which sets support Riesz bases or orthonormal exponential systems; the sharpness of the union-of-intervals extension was left open.
method: Pure mathematical analysis: construction of an explicit counterexample demonstrating that the hypotheses of the Kadec'-type theorem for unions of intervals cannot be relaxed.
result: An explicit counterexample shows the theorem's condition on unions of intervals is sharp, i.e. the constant or hypothesis cannot be improved.
conclusion: The Kadec'-type theorem for unions of intervals with integer orthonormal spectrum is optimal; the boundary of the admissible class is identified.

title: Two 3-Dimensional Coefficient Inverse Problems For Wave-like Equations With A Single Location Of The Point Source
authors: Michael V. Klibanov, Jingzhi Li, Tian Niu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper two long standing open questions are addressed for the first time. Those questions are about Lipschitz stability estimates and uniqueness theorems for two Coefficient Inverse Problems (CIPs) for 3-Dimensional wave-like Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with formally determined input data. We assume that a certain associated PDE is written in finite differences with respect to time t. The unknown coefficients depend on all three spatial variables. The key novelty here is that the input data for these CIPs are generated by only a single location of the point source at the moment of time {t = 0}. In the first CIP (CIP1) the unknown coefficient is the potential of a wave-like PDE. The second CIP (CIP2) is concerned with a far more challenging case when the unknown coefficient is involved in the principal part of the hyperbolic operator. In addition to Lipschitz stability and uniqueness results, numerical methods are developed for both CIPs. Their convergence analysis establishes the global convergence property of both numerical techniques. The latter is unlike the local convergence of conventional numerical procedures for CIPs. The method for CIP1 is tested computationally. Its extensive numerical testing for complicated media structures consistently demonstrates a very accurate performance of this method for noisy input data. The authors declare that artificial intelligence was not used for any part of this work.
tldr: The paper proves Lipschitz stability and uniqueness results for two 3D coefficient inverse problems for wave-like PDEs using input data from a single point source, and develops globally convergent numerical methods.
motivation: Long-standing open questions about stability estimates and uniqueness for formally determined coefficient inverse problems for hyperbolic PDEs with a single point source location had remained unresolved.
method: The PDE is discretized in time by finite differences, and the authors derive Lipschitz stability estimates and uniqueness theorems for both a potential-coefficient problem (CIP1) and a principal-part-coefficient problem (CIP2), accompanied by numerical schemes with global convergence analysis.
result: Both CIPs admit Lipschitz stability and uniqueness guarantees, and the numerical method for CIP1 shows accurate reconstruction for complicated media under noisy data with global (not merely local) convergence.
conclusion: The work provides the first stability and uniqueness results for these single-source 3D hyperbolic inverse problems and offers practically accurate, globally convergent computational methods.

title: Formalization, Transparency, And Collusion In Open-Source Game Theory
authors: Colomban Duclaux, Riccardo Formenti, Pepijn Cobben, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, Zhijing Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperation among AI agents will undermine alignment protocols when it takes the form of collusion. Under these protocols, agents often have some information about one another, and how much they have may determine whether they collude. Open-source game theory studies the extreme case, in which each program reads its opponent's source code and acts based on what it can prove about it. We develop formal foundations for this theory: we specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem concerning DupocBot and CupodBot through a transposition argument, and mechanize the framework in Lean 4; to our knowledge, this is the first mechanization of resource-bounded open-source game theory. We then extend the framework to the more realistic setting of partial transparency, where each program receives only partial information about its opponent. In Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, where mutual cooperation models collusion, greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics. This suggests that controlling how much agents can know about one another matters for alignment protocols.
tldr: The paper formalizes open-source game theory for AI agents, mechanizes it in Lean 4, and studies how partial transparency affects cooperation and collusion in Prisoner's Dilemma settings.
motivation: The authors aim to understand when information-sharing AI agents may collude and thereby undermine alignment protocols, focusing on the extreme case where agents can read each other's source code.
method: They specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem about DupocBot and CupodBot via a transposition argument, mechanize the framework in Lean 4, and extend it to partial transparency with Prisoner's Dilemma experiments.
result: Greater transparency is found to increase both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics, suggesting transparency control matters for alignment.
conclusion: The work provides a formal and mechanized foundation for resource-bounded open-source game theory and highlights transparency as a design lever for managing collusion among AI agents.

title: Approximate Counting And The Provability Of Combinatorial Principles
authors: Oliver Korten, Jiatu Li, Igor C. Oliveira, Hanlin Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding which axioms suffice for the provability of known results in algorithms and complexity and whether they can settle longstanding conjectures in these areas is a fundamental direction at the intersection of logic and computer science. Motivated by this research program and its applications, we investigate bounded arithmetic theories designed to serve as a logical foundation for *probabilistic reasoning*, the relation between these theories, and whether they can prove more theorems than their underlying base theory for *deterministic reasoning*. In more detail, for nearly twenty years, Je\'abek's theory [MATH] [Je07a] has provided a standard framework for the formalization of results from theoretical computer science relying on probabilistic techniques. In a recent work, [CLOW26] introduced a (possibly weaker) theory called [MATH]. This theory is able to capture a large set of probabilistic arguments using four simple axioms for *approximate counting*. Both theories extend Cook's theory [MATH] [Coo75] for deterministic polynomial-time reasoning. Our main result establishes that, in the relativized setting, [MATH] does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle ([MATH]). Consequently, [MATH] is not conservative over [MATH] with respect to relativized [MATH] sentences. Moreover, we establish that the unprovability of [MATH] is part of a more general phenomenon: for a large class of finite combinatorial principles, the existence of an *infinite model* of the negation of the principle *characterizes* its unprovability in [MATH]. This result, which is analogous to a theorem of Riis [Rii94], implies that [MATH] and [MATH] prove exactly the same finite combinatorial principles of this form.
tldr: Bounded arithmetic theories for probabilistic reasoning are compared, showing that Jeřábek's theory does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle in the relativized setting, and characterizing unprovability of a broad class of finite combinatorial principles via infinite models.
motivation: Understanding which axioms suffice to prove results in algorithms and complexity, and whether probabilistic-reasoning theories can prove more than their deterministic base theories, is a fundamental logic/CS question.
method: Proof-theoretic analysis of bounded arithmetic theories (Jeřábek's theory and the newer approximate-counting theory CLOW26) over Cook's theory PV, using relativized separations and model-theoretic characterizations analogous to Riis's theorem.
result: The new approximate-counting theory does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle in the relativized setting, hence is not conservative over Jeřábek's theory for relativized sentences; more generally, existence of an infinite model of a principle's negation characterizes its unprovability.
conclusion: The two probabilistic-reasoning theories prove exactly the same finite combinatorial principles of the studied form, clarifying the logical strength of approximate counting axioms.

title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework For Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification With Quantitative Rtl Analysis
authors: Md Ajoad Hasan, Dipayan Saha, Upoma Das, Sujan Kumar Saha, Mark Tehranipoor, Farimah Farahmandi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.
tldr: SecID is an LLM-guided multi-agent framework for identifying threat-specific secondary security assets in RTL hardware designs.
motivation: Pre-silicon hardware security verification requires identifying internal security-critical signals whose exploitation depends on specific threat mechanisms, but these secondary assets are difficult to find manually due to complex data- and control-flow dependencies.
method: The framework combines deterministic RTL analysis, bounded dynamic evaluation, and LLM reasoning to make asset decisions supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms.
result: SecID is demonstrated on seven open-source SoC and IP designs and validated with comparisons to prior work, fault simulation, formal analysis, ablations, threshold-sensitivity studies, and repeatability analysis.
conclusion: The work provides a scalable path toward hardware-security verification by identifying highly threat-relevant secondary assets for a given primary asset, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Non-manipulability And Approachability Beyond Two-Player Games
authors: Natalie Collina, Elijah Journey Fullerton, Jingyi Liu, S. Matthew Weinberg
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of guaranteeing non-manipulability and low regret for [MATH] independent learners in an [MATH]-player repeated general game with one optimizer. Non-manipulability is a property which guarantees that learning agents can prevent a strategic opponent from exploiting their learning dynamics for its own benefit, while no-regret provides guarantees to a learner with respect to a fixed static benchmark. This problem is well understood in games with a single learner and a single optimizer, where the intersection of non-manipulable and no-regret algorithms is exactly the class of all no-swap regret algorithms. But having multiple independent learners introduces a fundamental constraint: without shared randomness, the learners' joint mixed actions must remain product distributions and individual no-swap regret guarantees need not provide a guarantee of non-manipulability. Our core contributions are as follows. We introduce a set of [MATH] algorithms that [MATH] learners can play which individually guarantee sublinear swap regret and, when played in conjunction with each other, jointly guarantee non-manipulability against an optimizer. These algorithms require the computation of a Nash equilibrium at every timestep, and we show that this computational cost is inherent in general games. We construct a reduction from computing Nash in [MATH]-player games to finding [MATH] jointly non-manipulable no-external regret algorithms. Therefore, polynomial time algorithms which guarantee multi-learner non-manipulability in conjunction with no-external regret do not exist unless PPAD [MATH] FBPP. In order to construct these algorithms, we develop new techniques for Blackwell approachability beyond [MATH]-player games. We provide a general characterization for sets which are approachable by [MATH] players without correlated randomness.
tldr: The paper studies how to guarantee non-manipulability and sublinear swap regret for multiple independent learners facing a single strategic optimizer in repeated general N-player games, showing that computing Nash equilibria at every step is computationally inherent.
motivation: Non-manipulability and no-regret guarantees are well understood for two-player (one learner, one optimizer) settings, but with multiple independent learners lacking shared randomness the joint mixed actions must remain product distributions, breaking the known equivalence with no-swap regret algorithms.
method: The authors construct a family of algorithms each individually achieving sublinear swap regret while jointly guaranteeing non-manipulability, develop new techniques extending Blackwell approachability beyond two-player games, and build a reduction from computing Nash equilibria in N-player games to finding jointly non-manipulable no-external-regret algorithms.
result: They obtain polynomial-time impossibility results (no such algorithms exist unless PPAD ⊆ FBPP), give a general characterization of sets approachable by N players without correlated randomness, and establish that per-timestep Nash computation is necessary in general games.
conclusion: The work characterizes the computational and informational limits of multi-learner non-manipulability, extending approachability theory to multi-player settings and clarifying what guarantees are achievable without shared randomness.

title: Tropical And Maximum Colorful Matchings In Vertex-colored Graphs
authors: Johanne Cohen, Yannis Manoussakis, Hong Phong Pham, Zsolt Tuza
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A subgraph of a vertex-colored graph istropical if it contains every color. We study matchings by the number of colors they cover. A matching is maximum colorful if no matching covers more colors. When a tropical matching exists, the maximum colorful matchings are exactly the tropical matchings. We give polynomial-time algorithms for two problems: a maximum matching that covers the most colors, and a tropical matching with the fewest edges. Both algorithms rest on a counterpart of Berge's theorem: a matching is optimal if and only if it admits no tropical augmentation, or no tropical reduction. These are chains of alternating paths linked by relays, and each one is found by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph. The same tools give a maximum colorful matching with the fewest edges, and show that all maximum matchings that are maximum colorful are connected by flips. Finally, the sets of colors that a matching can cover form a matroid. The greedy algorithm then computes a matching of maximum color weight. This paper extends the conference version and the PhD thesis of one of the authors.
tldr: The paper presents polynomial-time algorithms for finding maximum colorful matchings and minimum-edge tropical matchings in vertex-colored graphs, via a colorful analogue of Berge's augmenting-path theorem.
motivation: Matchings that cover many colors generalize standard matchings and arise in combinatorial optimization; the authors aim to characterize and compute color-covering optima efficiently.
method: They prove a counterpart of Berge's theorem using 'tropical augmentations' and 'tropical reductions' — chains of alternating paths joined by relays — each computable by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph, and show the coverable color sets form a matroid.
result: Polynomial-time algorithms are obtained for maximum matching covering the most colors, tropical matching with fewest edges, maximum colorful matching with fewest edges; all maximum-colorful maximum matchings are connected by flips, and a greedy algorithm solves max color-weight matching.
conclusion: The work extends a conference version and a PhD thesis, providing a matroidal and algorithmic theory of color-covering matchings in vertex-colored graphs.

title: Semantic Tanner-Graph Decoding For Ldpc Codes
authors: Wenjing Wei, Chentao Yue, Branka Vucetic, Yonghui Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional low-density parity-check (LDPC) belief propagation (BP) decoding operates on a Tanner graph, with no factor describing the source structure. This paper proposes a semantic Tanner graph for LDPC-coded text transmission and develops semantic-factor-aided BP (SF-BP) decoding. The source text is tokenized into discrete tokens, which are then mapped to binary messages for channel coding. For each token, the proposed graph introduces a semantic factor connected to the corresponding information-bit variable nodes forming the token. A fine-tuned language model assigns this factor a posterior distribution over all possible token symbols in the alphabet at each token position. During SF-BP decoding, semantic-factor and LDPC parity-check messages are combined at their shared variable nodes for message passing. Simulation results show that SF-BP significantly improves the block error rate (BLER) and Sentence-BERT similarity (BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) compared with conventional BP. For example, SF-BP reduces BLER from approximately 1 to 6.51 x 10^-6 and increases Sentence-BERT similarity from 0.21 to 1 - 1.26 x 10^-6 for the (1248, 1040) LDPC code at 4 dB.
tldr: The paper proposes a semantic Tanner graph and semantic-factor-aided belief propagation decoding for LDPC-coded text transmission, using a fine-tuned language model to provide token-level posterior information during decoding.
motivation: Conventional LDPC BP decoding ignores source structure, so the authors aim to exploit semantic dependencies in text to improve decoding performance.
method: Text is tokenized and mapped to binary messages; for each token, a semantic factor connected to its information-bit variable nodes is assigned a posterior distribution by a fine-tuned language model, and these semantic messages are combined with LDPC parity-check messages in SF-BP decoding.
result: Simulations show SF-BP improves BLER and Sentence-BERT similarity over conventional BP, e.g., reducing BLER from about 1 to 6.51e-6 and increasing similarity from 0.21 to nearly 1 for a (1248,1040) LDPC code at 4 dB.
conclusion: Semantic-factor-aided BP decoding can substantially improve LDPC-coded text transmission performance by incorporating source semantics into the Tanner graph.

title: Direct Cognition Problem: A Semantic Skeleton Of Mathematics And Its Growth
authors: Nikolai N. Evdokimov Vasilii A. Gromov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a finite semantic skeleton from three axioms of classical propositional logic without specifying a target theorem. During growth, the constructor records which proofs share an intermediate lemma. When choosing the final anchors, it also counts inferences that use a premise the lemma can supply by substitution. The primary skeleton contains ten anchors whose certificates expand to the axioms through 27 shared inference steps. It shortens all 30 previously unseen proof structures in an external catalogue of typed combinators, saving 90 of 412 steps. One anchor recurs in all five runs of the constructor. In a post hoc test, this anchor alone shortens 26 of the 30 proofs. It also shortens 331 of 475 previously unseen proofs of familiar theorems in a second corpus.
tldr: The paper constructs a finite semantic skeleton from propositional-logic axioms that compresses and reuses proof structures in external corpora of typed combinators and familiar theorems.
motivation: The authors aim to automatically discover compact, reusable proof anchors without targeting a specific theorem, thereby capturing structural regularities in mathematical proofs.
method: They grow a semantic skeleton from three classical propositional-logic axioms, track shared intermediate lemmas and substitution-based premise use, and select final anchors that certify back to the axioms via shared inference steps.
result: The skeleton contains ten anchors, shortens all 30 unseen proofs in one combinator catalogue by 90 of 412 steps, and one recurring anchor alone shortens 26 of those proofs and 331 of 475 proofs in a second corpus.
conclusion: The approach suggests that small axiom-derived semantic skeletons can provide broadly reusable proof-shortening lemmas across mathematical domains.

title: A Complete Axiomatisation Of Distribution-Based Branching Bisimilarity For Non-Deterministic And Probabilistic Choice
authors: Rob J. van Glabbeek, Jan Friso Groote, Erik P. de Vink
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a notion of branching bisimilarity for non-deterministic probabilistic processes. In order to characterise the corresponding notion of rooted branching probabilistic bisimilarity, an equational theory is proposed for a basic, recursion-free process language with non-deterministic as well as probabilistic choice. The proof of completeness of the axiomatisation builds on the completeness of strong probabilistic bisimilarity on the one hand and on the notion of a concrete process, i.e. a process that does not display (partially) inert {\tau}-moves, on the other hand. The approach is first presented for the non-deterministic fragment of the calculus and next generalised to incorporate probabilistic choice, too.
tldr: The paper gives a complete equational axiomatisation of rooted branching bisimilarity for a recursion-free process calculus combining non-deterministic and probabilistic choice.
motivation: Branching bisimilarity is well understood for non-deterministic processes, but a satisfactory behavioural equivalence and complete axiomatisation for processes mixing non-deterministic with probabilistic choice was missing.
method: An equational theory is proposed for a basic recursion-free process language; completeness is proven by reducing to the known completeness of strong probabilistic bisimilarity and by eliminating partially inert tau-moves via the notion of a concrete process, first for the non-deterministic fragment and then extended to probabilistic choice.
result: A sound and complete axiomatisation characterising rooted branching probabilistic bisimilarity is obtained for the full language with both non-deterministic and probabilistic choice.
conclusion: The work extends the classical branching-bisimulation framework of process algebra to probabilistic settings, providing a foundational equivalence theory for concurrent probabilistic systems.

title: Poisoning Attacks To Local Differential Privacy Protocols For Dynamic Graphs
authors: Shang Liu, Yuhan Bao, Hongbin Zhao, Yanmei Zhang, Guan Yuan, Yang Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the increasing adoption of privacy-preserving techniques in dynamic graph analysis, local differential privacy (LDP) has become a fundamental paradigm for protecting user data in decentralized environments. However, despite its strong privacy guarantees, LDP-based dynamic graph protocols remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks through malicious data injection. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against privacy-preserving dynamic graphs under the LDP framework. Considering the temporal evolution of dynamic graphs, we identify key challenges in attack design and evaluation, including how to schedule attack resources across time and how to measure cumulative attack impact. To address these challenges, we introduce an absolute gain metric to quantify the overall deviation of graph statistical metrics before and after attacks across time. Based on this metric, we further propose a unified poisoning attack framework for dynamic graphs, which consists of target node selection, dynamic fake node scale scheduling, and fake edge injection. Within this framework, we design a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that dynamically schedules attack resources to maximize attack effectiveness, along with two baseline strategies, equal-scale attack (ESA) and random-scale attack (RSA), for comparison. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed attacks can significantly degrade the accuracy of graph metric estimation for target nodes.
tldr: The paper presents the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against local differential privacy (LDP) protocols for dynamic graphs, proposing a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that schedules adversarial resources over time to maximally corrupt graph metric estimation.
motivation: LDP has become a standard paradigm for privacy-preserving dynamic graph analysis, yet its robustness against malicious data injection remains unexamined, leaving a security gap in decentralized privacy-preserving systems.
method: The authors introduce an absolute-gain metric to quantify cumulative attack impact over time, then build a unified poisoning framework comprising target node selection, dynamic fake-node scale scheduling, and fake-edge injection; TEA schedules attack resources dynamically and is compared against equal-scale (ESA) and random-scale (RSA) baselines.
result: Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic dynamic graph datasets show that the proposed attacks significantly degrade the accuracy of graph statistical metric estimation for target nodes.
conclusion: LDP-based dynamic graph protocols are vulnerable to temporally scheduled poisoning attacks, highlighting the need for robustness-aware defenses in privacy-preserving dynamic graph analysis.

title: From Models To Services: Systematizing Security Assurance For Model-as-a-Service
authors: Jianming Zhou, Yang Luo, Guangpu Chen, Zhaoyu Chen, Yifeng Gao, Qingni Shen, Zhonghai Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are mainly delivered as cloud services, in which the assets of different principals are coupled within a single service pipeline, while the related security research is scattered across several fields with differing threat models. This paper systematizes this research from a service perspective. We decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, use them to code 120 studies, and evaluate 50 defenses under a unified set of criteria. The results show that 44.2% of the studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers. Finally, we propose a research agenda by comparison with current standards and regulations.
tldr: This paper systematizes security research for Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) LLM cloud deployments by decomposing the service into a five-layer stack with five trust boundaries and coding 120 studies against six adversary classes and six security goals.
motivation: Large language models are predominantly delivered as cloud services where multiple principals' assets are coupled in one pipeline, yet the security literature is fragmented across fields with inconsistent threat models, making a unified service-level view necessary.
method: The authors build a taxonomy consisting of a five-layer MaaS stack, five trust boundaries, six adversary classes, and six security goals, then use it to code 120 studies and evaluate 50 defenses under unified criteria, comparing findings against current standards and regulations.
result: They find that 44.2% of studies focus on behavioral integrity while service integrity, availability/cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%; defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and no cryptographic or hardware mechanism protecting against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers.
conclusion: The paper proposes a research agenda to rebalance MaaS security toward under-studied goals and calls for mechanisms that customers can deploy independently of providers, informed by comparisons with existing standards and regulations.

title: Karhunen-Lo\`{e}ve Expansion Of Time-Rescaled Brownian Bridge And Inference Of Unit Distribution
authors: Leonardo Chhabra, Anindya Goswami, Nikhil Thekkedath Haridas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Karhunen-Lo\`{e}ve (KL) basis of the time-rescaled Brownian bridge (TRBB) with time rescales of the form [MATH].
