For testing unit distributions, we construct a new statistic based on the projection of empirical process onto the KL basis functions of the TRBB and derive its asymptotic distribution. Moreover, using this statistic, we develop a goodness-of-fit test for uniformity and study its power against a specific non-uniform alternative. Numerical experiments indicate that, in the settings considered, the proposed test can have higher power than classical alternatives such as the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cram\'{e}r-von Mises tests. Furthermore, we propose a two-parameter family of TRBBs and derive the closed-form KL expansion for this new deterministically time-changed process. The family includes a diverse class of monotone rate time rescales, both increasing and decreasing, while retaining a tractable eigenstructure. Finally, an analysis with real data reveals greater flexibility of the proposed parametric family for modelling monotone densities on [MATH].
tldr: The paper derives Karhunen-Loève expansions for time-rescaled Brownian bridges and uses them to construct a goodness-of-fit test for uniformity.
motivation: The authors aim to develop a new projection-based statistic for testing unit distributions and to model monotone densities via a flexible two-parameter family of time-rescaled Brownian bridges.
method: They project the empirical process onto KL basis functions of the time-rescaled Brownian bridge, derive the asymptotic distribution of the resulting statistic, and construct a uniformity test; they also derive closed-form KL expansions for a new parametric family.
result: Numerical experiments show the proposed test can have higher power than Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises tests in the considered settings, and real-data analysis demonstrates greater modeling flexibility.
conclusion: The work provides new theoretical and practical tools for goodness-of-fit testing and density modeling using time-rescaled Brownian bridges, but it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Error Estimates For A Structure-preserving Finite-element Scheme Of Quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan Systems
authors: Aaron Brunk, Ansgar J\"ungel, Maria Luk\'a\v{c}ov\'a-Medvid'ov\'a
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A conforming finite-element scheme for quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems in a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions is presented. The system consists of the Navier-Stokes equations, together with a quasi-incompressibility constraint, coupled with the cross-diffusion Maxwell--Stefan equations. The numerical scheme preserves the partial masses and the quasi-incompressibility constraint and dissipates the discrete energy. First-order error estimates in space and time are shown for a diffusion-augmented mobility matrix by using the relative energy method and suitable projection error estimates. Numerical experiments in two space dimensions illustrate the convergence of the scheme and indicate second-order convergence in space in the [MATH] norm.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes a structure-preserving finite-element scheme for quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems with first-order error estimates.
motivation: The authors aim to numerically solve coupled fluid-flow and cross-diffusion systems while preserving key physical structures such as partial masses, the quasi-incompressibility constraint, and discrete energy dissipation.
method: A conforming finite-element discretization is proposed for the coupled Navier-Stokes and Maxwell-Stefan equations under periodic boundary conditions, with error analysis based on the relative energy method and projection estimates.
result: The scheme is proven to preserve partial masses and quasi-incompressibility and to dissipate discrete energy, and first-order convergence in space and time is shown for a diffusion-augmented mobility matrix; numerical experiments indicate up to second-order spatial convergence in one norm.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorously analyzed structure-preserving numerical method for a class of coupled fluid and multicomponent diffusion systems, with convergence supported by theory and two-dimensional experiments.

title: FokasNets: Completing Missing Boundary Data In Physics-Informed Neural Networks And Operators Via The Global Relation
authors: Kyriakos C. Georgiou, Khemraj Shukla, Athanassios S. Fokas, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.
tldr: FokasNets integrates the Fokas method's Global Relation with physics-informed neural networks and operators to improve boundary-data completion and PDE solution accuracy.
motivation: Standard physics-informed neural networks often struggle with mixed boundary conditions and accurate boundary/interior solutions, especially for operator learning tasks.
method: The authors lift neural network representations to impose Dirichlet boundary conditions by construction and use the Global Relation as an additional training solve to infer missing boundary data, developing Fokas-PINNs and Fokas Operator Networks with theoretical error, stability, and universal approximation analysis.
result: Numerical experiments on manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks show significant accuracy improvements over standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets, with operator-learning improvements reaching multiple orders of magnitude and faster convergence to fixed error thresholds.
conclusion: FokasNets provide a theoretically grounded and empirically effective framework for solving mixed-boundary PDE problems and learning solution operators, but the work is entirely in numerical analysis and scientific machine learning, not quantum information science.

title: The Kalton--Peck Space Disproves Rubio De Francia's Conjecture
authors: Rishad Shahmurov Veli Shakhmurov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the classical complex Kalton--Peck space [MATH] is not isomorphic to [MATH] for any UMD Banach space [MATH], Hilbert space [MATH], and [MATH]. Since [MATH] is UMD, this disproves Rubio de Francia's conjecture on intermediate UMD spaces. The proof combines the logarithmic block identity, a shift-commutator estimate on the interpolation strip, a unified obstruction in terms of reciprocal Hilbert norms, and Hahn--Banach with elementary convexity. It allows arbitrary compatible placements. We also realize [MATH] as a quotient of a closed subspace of an intermediate UMD space for every fixed interpolation parameter less than one.
tldr: The paper proves that the Kalton–Peck space is not isomorphic to any UMD Banach space, Hilbert space, or related intermediate space, thereby disproving Rubio de Francia's conjecture on intermediate UMD spaces.
motivation: Rubio de Francia conjectured that certain intermediate spaces arising in interpolation of UMD spaces remain UMD, and the Kalton–Peck space provides a natural test case for this conjecture.
method: The proof combines a logarithmic block identity, a shift-commutator estimate on the interpolation strip, a unified obstruction in terms of reciprocal Hilbert norms, and Hahn–Banach arguments with elementary convexity.
result: The authors show that the complex Kalton–Peck space is not isomorphic to any UMD Banach space or Hilbert space, disproving the conjecture, and also realize it as a quotient of a closed subspace of an intermediate UMD space for every interpolation parameter less than one.
conclusion: The work settles a long-standing conjecture in Banach space interpolation theory and clarifies the limitations of UMD-space stability under complex interpolation.

title: Node Differential Privacy Via Node-Stable Graph Projections
authors: Ishaq Aden-Ali, Adam Sealfon, Adam Smith, Thomas Steinke, Jonathan Ullman
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree [MATH] unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree [MATH], and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when [MATH] is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal [MATH]-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree [MATH] yet is [MATH]-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.
tldr: The paper introduces node-stable graph projections and Lipschitz extensions for designing accurate node-differentially private algorithms on graph-structured data.
motivation: Node differential privacy is challenging because realistic graphs have heterogeneous degrees, and exploiting low-degree structure while preserving worst-case privacy requires new algorithmic tools.
method: The authors construct a randomized nearly linear-time node-stable graph projection that clips degrees while limiting the effect of changing one node, and a deterministic Lipschitz extension for bounded edge weights.
result: These tools yield node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on edge-associated records, improving accuracy and computational efficiency over prior projection methods.
conclusion: The work advances practical differentially private graph analysis but is unrelated to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: BridgeHammer: Dnn Backdoor Attack Via CPU-iGPU Shared-memory Rowhammer
authors: Yufei Wang, Saion K. Roy, Yunsi Fei
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heterogeneous systems-on-chips (SoCs) share physical memory between CPUs and integrated GPUs (iGPUs), creating a path for CPU-side memory corruption to compromise the integrity of deep learning models used for iGPU inference. Implanting a backdoor that causes targeted misclassifications on trigger-bearing inputs while retaining accuracy on normal inputs requires carefully selected weight changes. However, realizing these changes presents two challenges: where to induce faults, since vulnerable DRAM locations may not contain the targeted weights, and when to intervene, since memory placement and fault injection must align with different stages of the model deployment lifecycle that involve two distinct computation domains. We present BridgeHammer, a Rowhammer-based backdoor attack that addresses these challenges by coordinating targeted weight placement before zero-copy binding for the iGPU and fault injection before inference. The iGPU then uses the corrupted model for subsequent inferences. We evaluate BridgeHammer on a heterogeneous Intel CPU-iGPU platform using OpenVINO, targeting ResNet-20, VGG-16, and ResNet-50 at both INT8 and FP32 precision. Across all six configurations, BridgeHammer achieves an 88.9% attack success rate (ASR) and 86.3% clean accuracy on average, with reliable target-page placement and bit-flip reproduction. These results demonstrate a new integrity vulnerability on heterogeneous CPU-iGPU SoCs, motivating cross-domain memory integrity protections.
tldr: BridgeHammer is a Rowhammer-based backdoor attack that exploits CPU-iGPU shared memory to corrupt DNN weights and induce targeted misclassifications during iGPU inference.
motivation: Heterogeneous SoCs share physical memory between CPUs and integrated GPUs, creating a cross-domain integrity risk for DNN models deployed on iGPUs. The authors aim to show that carefully timed and placed Rowhammer faults can implant a functional backdoor without substantially degrading clean accuracy.
method: The attack coordinates targeted weight placement before zero-copy binding for the iGPU and injects Rowhammer bit flips before inference, so the iGPU subsequently uses the corrupted model. It is evaluated on an Intel CPU-iGPU platform with OpenVINO using ResNet-20, VGG-16, and ResNet-50 at INT8 and FP32 precision.
result: Across six configurations, BridgeHammer achieves an average 88.9% attack success rate and 86.3% clean accuracy, with reliable target-page placement and bit-flip reproduction.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a new integrity vulnerability in heterogeneous CPU-iGPU SoCs and motivates cross-domain memory integrity protections for DNN inference.

title: On The Index Of Positivity Of Linear Functionals: A Complement To The Hermite Case And New Examples
authors: Wathek Chammam
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the Dirac functional [MATH] is the only normalized linear functional on the space of real polynomials whose index of positivity is infinite. This complements the recent study of the Hermite case by R. Sfaxi and F. Marcell\'an [Bull. Malays. Math. Sci. Soc. 48 (2025) 138]: the index of the Hermite functional [MATH] is finite, and so are those of [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH], for which the value [MATH] was stated there. The key observation is that real Cauchy powers act on log-moments by scaling. This yields explicit upper bounds for the index in terms of the first four moments. In particular [MATH] is not even positive for any integer [MATH], and [MATH]. We identify the point of the original argument that needs to be modified, a free integration constant in the construction of the weights of [MATH], and we give the adjusted statements. Finally, we compute the positivity sets exactly for two new families: the real powers of [MATH], which are Jacobi functionals on [MATH], and the real powers of [MATH], which are generalized Gegenbauer functionals containing the Chebyshev functional [MATH]. For the latter, [MATH]. These examples show that our bounds are sharp and that every value in [MATH] is the index of some functional.
tldr: The paper proves that the Dirac functional is the only normalized linear functional on real polynomials with infinite index of positivity, and computes exact positivity sets for new families of Jacobi and generalized Gegenbauer functionals.
motivation: Motivated by a recent study of the Hermite functional's finite index of positivity (Sfaxi & Marcellán), the author aims to characterize which functionals have infinite index and to correct an error (a free integration constant) in the original argument.
method: The key technique is observing that real Cauchy powers act on log-moments by scaling, yielding explicit upper bounds on the index in terms of the first four moments, combined with a corrected weight-construction argument.
result: Dirac is shown to be the unique normalized functional with infinite index; explicit moment-based bounds are derived, and exact positivity sets are computed for real powers of two functionals (Jacobi-type on [0,1] and generalized Gegenbauer-type containing Chebyshev).
conclusion: The examples demonstrate the bounds are sharp and that every integer value can be realized as the index of some functional, extending and correcting the prior Hermite-case analysis.

title: Horseshoe-Type Shrinkage From Ratio-Generated Priors
authors: Radhika Kulkarni, Anirban Dasgupta, Brani Vidakovic
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a class of horseshoe-type shrinkage priors generated by ratios of independent numerator and denominator random variables. Large denominator values produce concentration near zero, small denominator values generate heavy tails, and the numerator determines scale and geometry and may also influence tail behavior. We establish general origin and tail asymptotics, including power and logarithmic singularities. Under a Gaussian likelihood and regularly varying prior tails, the posterior mean approaches the observation for large signals, with risk approaching that of the unshrunk observation. The denominator also induces a latent shrinkage factor. For a Cauchy denominator, this factor has exactly the [MATH] distribution, whatever the numerator. With a Gaussian numerator and appropriate scale calibration, it recovers the classical horseshoe shrinkage coefficient, whereas non-Gaussian numerators can change the effective posterior shrinkage, even in its asymptotic rate. The Cauchy/Cauchy prior illustrates the theory, with a logarithmic singularity at the origin in one dimension, power singularities in higher dimensions, and logarithmically modified Cauchy-order tails. Its posterior mean shrinks smoothly, whereas its spatial median behaves nearly as a threshold rule. We also compare the Cauchy/Cauchy posterior mean with fifteen established shrinkage procedures on the four standard Donoho-Johnstone test functions, finding competitive, though not uniformly superior, wavelet-denoising performance. The ratio construction generalizes several published shrinkage priors and offers a flexible framework for sparse estimation, with natural applications to wavelet shrinkage, variable selection, and structured multivariate shrinkage.
tldr: The paper introduces a class of horseshoe-type shrinkage priors built from ratios of independent numerator and denominator random variables, and analyzes their asymptotics and posterior behavior for sparse estimation and wavelet denoising.
motivation: Existing horseshoe and related global-local shrinkage priors are constructed in ad hoc ways; the authors seek a unifying generative framework that explains origin/tail behavior, latent shrinkage factors, and asymptotic risk.
method: Ratio-of-random-variables construction with general origin and tail asymptotics (power and logarithmic singularities), analysis under Gaussian likelihood and regularly varying tails, plus a Cauchy/Cauchy case study and comparison with fifteen shrinkage procedures on Donoho-Johnstone test functions.
result: Posterior mean approaches the observation for large signals under regularly varying prior tails; the latent shrinkage factor has a universal distribution for a Cauchy denominator; Cauchy/Cauchy shows logarithmic origin singularity in 1D, power singularities in higher dimensions, and competitive but not uniformly superior wavelet-denoising performance.
conclusion: The ratio construction generalizes several published shrinkage priors and provides a flexible framework for sparse estimation, variable selection, and structured multivariate shrinkage.

title: Linear Images Of Graphs Of Vector-valued Affine Fractal Interpolation Functions
authors: Robert Ma{\l}ysz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the Hausdorff and box dimensions of every linear image of the graph of a vector-valued affine fractal interpolation function with positive vertical factors. The same formula holds for signed factors under a rank condition on the active branches. Outside an explicit finite union of hyperplanes in the space of vertical factors it holds simultaneously for all choices of interpolation knots and all linear images. The dimension is determined by the branch contractions, the rank of the projected deviations from the endpoint line, and the affine dimension of the projected knots. The proof gives uniform entropy estimates over bounded slopes for tilted projections of homogeneous triangular systems. Permutations of words with prescribed symbol frequencies then transfer the dimension estimates to unequal branch contractions. For the homogeneous systems covered by the entropy estimate, we also compute the exact dimensions of Bernoulli measures and their tilted projections. Examples with exceptional factors exhibit distinct Hausdorff and box dimensions.
tldr: The paper computes Hausdorff and box dimensions of linear images of graphs of vector-valued affine fractal interpolation functions, including Bernoulli measure dimensions for homogeneous triangular systems.
motivation: Fractal interpolation functions generate self-affine graphs whose dimensions under projections are not fully understood, particularly for vector-valued (multidimensional) settings and signed vertical factors.
method: Dimension formulas are derived via uniform entropy estimates over bounded slopes for tilted projections of homogeneous triangular systems, then extended to unequal branch contractions via word permutations with prescribed symbol frequencies.
result: Dimensions are shown to depend on branch contractions, the rank of projected deviations from the endpoint line, and the affine dimension of the projected knots; the formula holds simultaneously for all knots and linear images outside an explicit finite union of hyperplanes.
conclusion: Exceptional parameter choices can yield distinct Hausdorff and box dimensions, and exact Bernoulli measure dimensions are obtained for the homogeneous systems covered by the entropy estimate.

title: Singular Rational S-functions Of Second-order ODEs: Structure, Degree Bounds And A Kovacic-type Search
authors: L. A. C. P. Da Mota L. G. S. Duarte
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a rational second-order ODE [MATH], the [MATH]-function method reduces the search for a first integral to finding a rational solution [MATH] of the Riccati-type equation [MATH] along the total-derivative field [MATH]. The standard ansatz [MATH], with [MATH], misses every [MATH] with poles outside [MATH]. Such singular solutions cannot be avoided: for point transforms of linear equations without hyperexponential solutions we describe every quasi-regular [MATH] explicitly, and for a generic transformation none exists. We then determine the structure of singular solutions. Outside [MATH] every pole is simple, with residue [MATH], and is not a Darboux surface; along non-characteristic factors of [MATH] the leading polar coefficient is free Cauchy data; and the only unknown denominator is a squarefree polynomial [MATH], which enters a linear equation. A Newton-polygon analysis at infinity gives the polynomial part up to a correction of bounded weight. The weighted degree of [MATH] is determined exactly when the excess is zero and the top Riccati equation has no algebraic solution, and is bounded by residues of the top field otherwise, conditionally on the vanishing of that correction. The dependence of [MATH] on [MATH] is obtained, without a degree bound, from the rational solutions of a linear differential system. These results give a certified search procedure, implemented twice, which finds the singular [MATH] of nine non-Liouvillian pull-backs of the Airy and Bessel equations. In one regime it is a decision procedure; for instance, it proves that [MATH] has no rational [MATH].
tldr: A pure-mathematics paper developing the structure, degree bounds, and a certified Kovacic-type search procedure for singular rational S-functions of rational second-order ODEs.
motivation: The standard S-function ansatz for finding first integrals of rational second-order ODEs misses all solutions with poles outside the total-derivative field, so a systematic theory of these singular solutions is needed.
method: The authors characterize quasi-regular S-functions for point transforms of linear equations, analyze pole structure and residues, perform a Newton-polygon analysis at infinity, and derive degree bounds, implementing a certified search procedure twice.
result: They obtain exact degree determination when the excess is zero and the top Riccati equation has no algebraic solution, bounds otherwise, and the procedure finds singular S-functions for nine non-Liouvillian pull-backs of the Airy and Bessel equations, proving in one case that no rational S-function exists.
conclusion: The work yields a rigorous, sometimes decision-grade algorithm for first-integral search in differential algebra/symbolic computation, with no connection to quantum information science.

title: Norm Of The Generalized Hilbert Matrix Operator Between Some Spaces Of Analytic Functions
authors: Shanli Ye Shaoyang Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the generalized Hilbert operator \[ \mathcal H_bf(z)=\int_0^1{(1-tz)^{b+1}}f(t)\,dt, \qquad b>0, \] on several spaces of analytic functions in the unit disk. For logarithmically weighted Korenblum spaces, we obtain an exact supremum representation and a lower estimate for the norm of the mapping from [MATH] to [MATH]. We then establish two-sided estimates and characterize the boundedness range of [MATH] on the [MATH]-Bloch spaces [MATH]. We also derive norm bounds for the mapping from [MATH] into the endpoint Zygmund-type space [MATH]. Furthermore, we give a norm representation for [MATH] and identify a norm-attaining function. In particular, for [MATH], the norm is expressed explicitly in terms of a Beta function. Finally, we obtain an exact supremum representation of the norm of [MATH] on [MATH], together with explicit norm estimates. Our results extend those of Hao et al. [J. Geom. Anal. 35 (2025), Paper No. 184] for the classical Hilbert matrix operator ([MATH]) to the generalized case [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies norm estimates and boundedness of a generalized Hilbert matrix operator acting on spaces of analytic functions in the unit disk.
motivation: The classical Hilbert matrix operator is well studied on analytic function spaces, and this work extends recent results by analyzing a generalized version with parameter b > 0.
method: The authors derive supremum representations, lower estimates, two-sided bounds, and explicit Beta-function expressions for the operator norm on logarithmically weighted Korenblum spaces, Q-Bloch spaces, Zygmund-type spaces, and related analytic function spaces.
result: They characterize the boundedness range on Q-Bloch spaces, obtain norm bounds into endpoint Zygmund-type spaces, identify a norm-attaining function, and give explicit norm expressions in special cases.
conclusion: The results extend known norm estimates for the classical Hilbert matrix operator to the generalized setting and provide explicit norm representations on several analytic function spaces.

title: A Stackelberg Strategy For The Semi-linear Heat Equation With Boundary Controls
authors: Jose Antoinio Villa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work continues the results presented in where a hierarchical control problem is solved. Our first goal is the case of both controls acting on the boundary. The follower control solves a null controllability problem, and the leader minimizes a [MATH] cost functional. Additionally, we solve the case where one control acts on the boundary and the other on an open subset of the domain. More precisely, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a leader-follower couple and give some techniques to solve the problem.
tldr: This paper studies a Stackelberg (leader-follower) hierarchical control problem for the semi-linear heat equation, considering cases where controls act on the boundary or on an interior open subset.
motivation: The work extends prior results on hierarchical control by treating both boundary-boundary and boundary-interior control configurations for a semi-linear parabolic PDE.
method: The follower solves a null controllability problem while the leader minimizes a cost functional; existence and uniqueness of a leader-follower pair are proven, with techniques proposed for solving the resulting problem.
result: Existence and uniqueness of the leader-follower couple are established for both control configurations, along with methods to solve the associated optimization/controllability problems.
conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous PDE-control framework for Stackelberg games in semi-linear heat equations, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Universal Stabilization With Six Records
authors: Senhan Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter shows that a single feedback controller needs only six retained observation records to handle the largest universally stabilizable uncertainty range for the scalar discrete-time benchmark model of Xie and Guo, when uncertainty is measured by the radius of a generalized Lipschitz ball. Existing constructions can require arbitrarily many records along bounded trajectories. Our controller retains at most six genuine state-response pairs and five auxiliary real scalars. Each update requires a uniformly bounded number of elementary operations. No knowledge of the plant, its generalized Lipschitz constants, or the disturbance bound is required.
tldr: A single feedback controller using only six retained observation records achieves the maximal universally stabilizable uncertainty range for the scalar discrete-time benchmark of Xie and Guo.
motivation: Existing constructions for universal stabilization of unknown scalar plants can require arbitrarily many records along bounded trajectories, so a bounded-memory construction with a uniformly bounded per-update cost is desirable.
method: The author designs a feedback controller that keeps at most six genuine state-response pairs plus five auxiliary real scalars, with each update using a uniformly bounded number of elementary operations and no prior knowledge of the plant, its generalized Lipschitz constants, or the disturbance bound.
result: The six-record controller matches the largest uncertainty range (in the radius of a generalized Lipschitz ball) that is universally stabilizable for the benchmark model, improving on constructions needing unbounded record counts.
conclusion: Six records are sufficient for universal stabilization in this scalar benchmark, showing that bounded memory and bounded computation suffice for the full stabilizable uncertainty range.

title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing Of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches In LLM-Generated Plc Code
authors: S M Zia Ur Rashid, Sazidul Islam Hira, Suman Rath
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define and build , a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character [MATH]-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.
tldr: The paper introduces a label-free static verifier that detects mismatches between imported Python packages/symbols and the declared industrial protocol or PLC vendor target in LLM-generated control code.
motivation: Existing code-grounding checks only verify that imported packages or symbols exist, not that they are appropriate for the declared industrial target, so real but wrong-vendor libraries slip through unnoticed.
method: The authors build a version-pinned graph of documented protocol bindings and statically audit 883 generated scripts against declared vendor/protocol targets, also testing n-gram and AST-based machine-versus-human classification under disjoint partitions.
result: About 20.4% of scripts show import-level mismatches (14.2% when requiring a reachable protocol call), 96.6% of mismatching scripts still import existing packages, and character n-grams achieve macro-F1 1.000 on human-vs-machine classification, partly exploitable via a trailing newline.
conclusion: Vendor-protocol consistency is a worthwhile static audit target for LLM-generated PLC code, whereas provenance/authorship classification on repository-labelled corpora is not reliable detection.

title: Beyond The Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis Of Transferability In Adversarial Malware Detection
authors: Veysel Alevcan, Mohammad Furqan Ali, Teresa Sousa, Lu\'is Miguel Campos, Christoforos Ntantogian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models are already being deployed at scale for malware detection. Therefore there is a pressing need to rigorously study adversarial robustness. To that end, we introduce the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE): a platform for automated security stress-testing. We performed transfer attacks, via EMBER2018, against a Random Forest target. Counterintuitively, we found single-step FGSM to have the highest attack success rate (ASR) of 52.9% compared to iterative PGD with 45.2% (p < 0.002). Compared to iterative attacks which tend to overfit surrogate networks creating brittle perturbations, FGSM created more transferable examples. We benchmarked our attacks using ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and resilience index. Through these metrics, proposed in concordance with emerging standards in AI governance, we expose shortcomings as our transferability scores peak at ~0.8 with constrained perturbations. We highlight the practical security implications of these findings and demonstrate AAIE for automated adversarial auditing.
tldr: The paper introduces the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE) platform and studies the transferability of adversarial attacks against a Random Forest malware detector trained on EMBER2018, finding single-step FGSM transfers better than iterative PGD.
motivation: ML-based malware detection is deployed at scale, so its adversarial robustness against transfer attacks from surrogate models must be rigorously characterized and audited.
method: The authors build an automated adversarial security stress-testing platform (AAIE) and run FGSM and PGD transfer attacks on EMBER2018 against a Random Forest target, scoring them with ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and a resilience index aligned with AI-governance standards.
result: Counterintuitively, single-step FGSM achieved a higher attack success rate (52.9%) than iterative PGD (45.2%, p < 0.002), and transferability scores peaked near 0.8 under constrained perturbations, since iterative attacks overfit surrogate networks and produce brittle perturbations.
conclusion: Single-step perturbations can be more transferable than iterative ones, and the proposed metrics and AAIE platform offer practical tooling for automated adversarial auditing of malware classifiers.

title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning For TEE-based Edge Ai Protection
authors: Daniela M. Vela Hernandez, Samuel Hildebrand, Sean Oesch, Brian Weber, Shayan Monadjemi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.
tldr: Onnx2TEE is an automated pipeline that partitions ONNX neural network graphs across rich Trusted Execution Environments on edge hardware to protect model weights while limiting TEE resource overhead.
motivation: Edge-deployed AI models are valuable intellectual property exposed to hostile environments, but running whole large models inside resource-constrained TEEs is impractical, so selective protection of parameter-dense components is needed.
method: The authors build a model-independent, graph-aware segmentation scheme that splits non-sequential feed-forward ONNX computation graphs between trusted and untrusted regions, minimizing boundary communication while preserving data dependencies.
result: Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin with Arm TrustZone, the pipeline concentrates model parameters into a few segments and shows trusted-app memory usage depends on both compute and intermediate tensor sizes.
conclusion: Graph-aware partitioning enables practical, selective TEE protection of edge AI models, though it targets classical systems security rather than quantum information science.

title: RegionAlign: Manipulating Parameter Layouts For Localized Fault Injection On LLMs And VLMs
authors: Xiaomeng Wang, Peter Horvath, Zhengyu Zhao, Martha Larson, Zhuoran Liu, Lejla Batina
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical fault injection can flip stored weight bits, degrading LLMs and VLMs. Existing work largely overlooks how supply-chain manipulation affects fault vulnerability. We introduce RegionAlign, which allows a malicious provider to manipulate only the parameter layout before deployment, using bit-sensitivity search and channel permutations to concentrate vulnerable bits in one memory region while preserving weight values and clean performance. Under matched budgets, software experiments show greater degradation from search-selected in-region flips with RegionAlign than with original or random layouts. EMFI feasibility study confirms weight corruption. RegionAlign reveals a stealthy supply-chain threat that layout manipulation weakens physical fault resilience.
tldr: RegionAlign is a supply-chain threat that manipulates LLM/VLM parameter layouts to concentrate bit-flip-vulnerable weights in a single memory region without changing weight values or clean performance.
motivation: The paper addresses how malicious providers can exploit parameter layout before deployment to increase susceptibility to physical fault injection, a threat overlooked in prior fault-injection work.
method: It uses bit-sensitivity search and channel permutations to rearrange parameters so vulnerable bits are co-located, then evaluates degradation from search-selected in-region bit flips under matched budgets and studies EMFI feasibility.
result: Experiments show greater model degradation from RegionAlign layouts than from original or random layouts under matched flip budgets, and EMFI confirms weight corruption is feasible.
conclusion: Layout manipulation is a stealthy supply-chain attack that can weaken physical fault resilience of LLMs and VLMs, motivating layout-aware security defenses.

title: Precept: Security Self-Improvement Of Coding Agents Via Evolving Principles
authors: Keyan Guo, Rupam Patir, Haipeng Cai, Hongxin Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
tldr: PRECEPT gives AI coding agents a self-evolving library of secure-coding principles so that security lessons learned from their own failures persist across sessions and transfer to new code.
motivation: Coding agents often fix a vulnerability when shown a failing test but reintroduce the same vulnerability class in later sessions, and neither persistent context nor generic human-oriented secure-coding principles close this gap.
method: The authors measure vulnerability retention across 14 task sequences with Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code, then build PRECEPT, an evolving principle library seeded from authoritative secure-coding guidance and revised against the agent's own failures, keeping a revision only if fresh executions show improved security without degrading functional success.
result: PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code on unseen task families, versus 81.9% for the strongest unaided agent and 87.7% for the strongest baseline, with gains continuing across evolution steps.
conclusion: Security self-improvement is identified as a distinct missing capability for coding agents, and evolving self-tailored principles provide an effective mechanism for achieving it.

title: Higher-Dimensional Automata In Geometric Logic
authors: Kenan Oggad
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does the topos of a higher-dimensional automaton know about its infinite behaviour that its language does not? We write partial HDAs with an infinite run as models of a geometric theory over an intuitionistic metatheory with no choice. The topos of a machine is that of sheaves on its prefixes. The label word of a prefix records the shape and acceptance bit of each cell with the ipomset of each step. Under unique choice these words give a geometric morphism to the label topos of sheaves on label words, which thus records the shapes and acceptance bits that the B\"uchi language forgets. Machines sharing their B\"uchi language and their frames can differ over the label topos. The bouquet of two squares shares its frame and its B\"uchi language with the interleaved square; each accepted run of either reads the two events in parallel forever. Only the interleaved square has runs through cells of shape a, and the geometric sequent excluding such runs separates the two over the label topos. Over alphabets with decidable equality, finite rigid machines are unambiguous exactly when their label maps are inclusions of locales, and their equivalence over the label topos is decided whenever either is unambiguous. Equivalences of frames over the label topos transport points with their labels, and the invariants of fibres and of the language of points follow from this transport. On finite partial HDAs over alphabets with decidable equality, Muller and B\"uchi acceptance coincide exactly under a weak form of excluded middle.
tldr: A topos-theoretic study of higher-dimensional automata (HDAs) that characterizes what the topos of a machine knows about infinite behaviour beyond its Büchi language.
motivation: The authors ask what extra semantic information the topos of a higher-dimensional automaton captures relative to its recognized language, and how much of that information is lost by standard language equivalence.
method: Partial HDAs with infinite runs are modelled as models of a geometric theory over an intuitionistic metatheory without choice; the topos of a machine is the topos of sheaves on its prefixes, and label words yield a geometric morphism to the label topos.
result: Machines with the same Büchi language and frames can differ over the label topos (e.g. the bouquet of two squares vs. the interleaved square), the difference being witnessed by a geometric sequent; unambiguity of finite rigid machines corresponds to label maps being inclusions of locales, and equivalence over the label topos is decidable in that case.
conclusion: The topos of an HDA encodes structural information (shapes, acceptance bits, parallelism) invisible to the Büchi language, and equivalences of frames transport labelled points, yielding fibre and point-language invariants; over finite partial HDAs, Muller and Büchi acceptance coincide under a weak form of excluded middle.

title: Computing Feasible Ef1 Allocations Under Generalized Assignment Constraints
authors: Nicholas Teh Eugene Lim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fair allocation of indivisible goods under generalized assignment constraints, where each agent's bundle must fit within her budget, the sizes of goods may differ across agents, and unallocated goods go to a charity. A natural fairness notion here is feasible envy-freeness up to one good (FEF1), which requires an agent's envy towards any feasible subset of another bundle to disappear after some good is removed from this subset. While FEF1 allocations always exist, they could previously be computed efficiently only when sizes are common to all agents. We show that FEF1 allocations can be computed in strongly polynomial time, and more generally whenever each agent's value can be almost exactly maximized over her feasible bundles, a requirement that cannot be relaxed substantially. Our analysis relies on an essentially tight quadratic bound on how often each agent's bundle is repaired. Moreover, the allocation can be made approximately envy-free up to any good while retaining nearly half the Nash welfare of any given allocation. In contrast, requiring a single good to eliminate an agent's envy towards all feasible subsets of another bundle at once, which makes no difference without constraints, renders the problem NP-hard and may halve the attainable Nash welfare.
tldr: The paper gives a strongly polynomial-time algorithm for computing feasible envy-freeness up to one good (FEF1) allocations of indivisible goods under generalized assignment (budget) constraints, with tight repair-count bounds and Nash welfare guarantees.
motivation: FEF1 allocations are known to exist under generalized assignment constraints, but prior efficient algorithms only handled the case where goods have identical sizes across agents; the authors aim to remove this restriction.
method: They analyze an iterative allocation-and-repair procedure, proving an essentially tight quadratic bound on the number of times each agent's bundle must be repaired, requiring only that each agent's value be nearly exactly maximizable over her feasible bundles.
result: FEF1 allocations are computable in strongly polynomial time in general, the allocation can also be made approximately envy-free up to any good while retaining nearly half the Nash welfare, and the stricter 'single good eliminates all envy' variant is shown to be NP-hard.
conclusion: Feasible fair division under budget constraints is tractable for EF1-style fairness, but stronger fairness notions incur computational hardness and welfare loss.

title: Cyclicity Of Period Annuli Of Quadratic Codimension Four Centers
authors: Yulin Zhao Qi Meng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quadratic systems with a center fall into four classes: Hamiltonian [MATH], reversible [MATH], generalized Lotka--Volterra [MATH], and codimension-four [MATH]. Before this work, the cyclicity of period annuli under quadratic perturbations had been completely determined for [MATH], whereas only certain special cases had been resolved for [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH]. In this paper, we establish that the period annulus of every center in [MATH] has cyclicity three under quadratic perturbations, thereby proving \.{Z}o{\l}{}dek's 1994 conjecture for this class. The proof combines Picard--Fuchs equations with a Chebyshev criterion. Its key step is a strict Wronskian inequality for two ratios of elliptic integrals on their entire interval of definition. We establish this inequality by constructing a comparison function and excluding a first zero of the Wronskian. The Chebyshev property avoids the two additional zeros allowed by the second-order differential reduction used in earlier proofs.
tldr: The paper proves Zoladek's 1994 conjecture that every quadratic codimension-four center has cyclicity three under quadratic perturbations.
motivation: The cyclicity of period annuli under quadratic perturbations was known for Hamiltonian centers but only partially resolved for reversible, generalized Lotka-Volterra, and codimension-four classes.
method: The proof combines Picard-Fuchs equations with a Chebyshev criterion, relying on a strict Wronskian inequality for ratios of elliptic integrals established via a comparison function and exclusion of a first zero.
result: Every center in the codimension-four class is shown to have cyclicity three under quadratic perturbations, resolving the remaining case of Zoladek's conjecture.
conclusion: The Chebyshev property circumvents extra zeros arising from second-order differential reductions in earlier approaches, completing the cyclicity classification for quadratic codimension-four centers.

title: Adaptive Blockwise Tensor Trains For Stochastic Finite-Volume Methods With Uncertain Geometry
authors: William P. Gammel, Steven T. Walton, Stephen A. Andrews, Svetlana Tokareva, William T. Taitano
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic finite-volume (SFV) methods extend conservative, shock-capturing discretizations to hyperbolic systems with uncertain inputs by partitioning the parameter domain into finite-volume cells. However, their memory and computational cost grow exponentially with the number of uncertain parameters. Tensor-train (TT) formats can remove this exponential dependence, provided the ranks of the discrete solution remain small throughout the simulation. This requirement is frequently violated when the uncertainty is geometric. Mapping each realization onto a common reference domain introduces parameter-dependent metric factors, so that shocks and contacts propagate at different reference speeds and come to occupy different cells across realizations. The resulting rank growth is spatially localized - a structure that neither a single global TT nor a separate TT for each physical cell is able to exploit. We propose an adaptive blockwise TT representation in which the SFV solution is partitioned along its physical mode into contiguous blocks, each stored as an independent TT for every conserved variable. Blocks are split near discontinuities and in regions of large variance or rank, and merged where the solution is smooth. The mesh itself is never changed; only the grouping of cells into trains adapts. We embed this representation in a TT-based SFV solver combining WENO3 reconstruction in the physical and stochastic directions, positivity-preserving limiters, and strong-stability-preserving Runge-Kutta time integration, with nonlinear steps evaluated via cross approximation. A mean-conservative rounding that adds no rank, together with single-valued interface fluxes, conserves the parameter-mean mass and energy to round-off for any partition. The approach is demonstrated on a Sod shock-tube problem with uncertain wall positions.
tldr: The paper introduces an adaptive blockwise tensor-train representation for stochastic finite-volume simulations with uncertain geometry to reduce rank growth and memory cost.
motivation: Stochastic finite-volume methods suffer from exponential cost growth in uncertain parameter dimensions, and standard tensor-train formats struggle with localized rank growth caused by geometric uncertainty.
method: The authors partition the physical mode into contiguous blocks, each stored as an independent tensor train per conserved variable, with adaptive splitting near discontinuities and merging in smooth regions, embedded in a WENO3/SSP-RK solver with positivity limiters and cross approximation.
result: The method is demonstrated on a Sod shock-tube problem with uncertain wall positions, conserving parameter-mean mass and energy to round-off while controlling rank growth through adaptive blockwise partitioning.
conclusion: Adaptive blockwise tensor trains offer a practical way to exploit spatially localized rank structure in stochastic finite-volume simulations with uncertain geometry, though the work is outside quantum information science.

title: Solving The Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem With Polygonal Neighborhoods Using A Metaheuristic Enhanced With Block Coordinate Descent
authors: Rog\'erio S. Matos Ernesto G. Birgin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) in which customers are represented by planar regions, called customer neighborhoods, rather than fixed points. Visiting a customer consists of selecting a point within its neighborhood. Therefore, besides determining the sequence of customers visited by each vehicle, one must also determine the corresponding visit points. To better reflect practical applications, customer neighborhoods are allowed to be simple polygons, either convex or non-convex, and distances are measured using the Euclidean norm. Applications include aerial reconnaissance, wireless sensor data collection and inspection, and two-stage delivery systems. We propose a general variable neighborhood search framework in which each neighbor is represented by a collection of routes. Constructing a route involves two stages, defining a customer sequence and then determining the associated visit points. The latter task is solved by a block coordinate descent (BCD) procedure, the central methodological contribution of this work, which computes high-quality visit points at a cost low enough to be used repeatedly inside the search. In extensive experiments on newly generated and adapted benchmark instances, within the time limits considered, the proposed framework matches all solutions proven optimal by CPLEX and matches or improves the best solutions found by CPLEX in the remaining instances. For the instances adapted from the CVRP literature, it also improves, in every instance, a CVRP-based upper bound given by the solution of the original CVRP instance reported in the literature, which is feasible for the problem with neighborhoods.
tldr: The paper proposes a metaheuristic with block coordinate descent for solving capacitated vehicle routing problems where customers are polygonal neighborhoods rather than fixed points.
motivation: The authors aim to model practical routing applications such as aerial reconnaissance and wireless sensor data collection where service locations are regions rather than points.
method: A general variable neighborhood search framework is combined with a block coordinate descent procedure to jointly determine customer sequences and visit points within polygonal neighborhoods.
result: The method matches all CPLEX-proven optimal solutions and matches or improves best CPLEX solutions on remaining instances, also improving CVRP-based upper bounds on adapted benchmarks.
conclusion: The proposed BCD-enhanced metaheuristic is effective for CVRP with polygonal neighborhoods and provides high-quality solutions within practical time limits.

title: Demystifying Real-world Llm Service Freeloading
authors: Xinyi Hou, Shenao Wang, Wenhui Pan, Yanjie Zhao, Haoyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Third-party projects repackage free inference from LLM web applications and dedicated clients into independent APIs. We refer to such use beyond providers' permitted access, allocation, or redistribution conditions as LLM service freeloading (LSF). However, its scale and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We present a systematic measurement study of 513 open-source projects, tracing 1,588 inference paths across 64 upstream LLM services and characterizing their development, dependencies, and operating mechanisms. We find that 93.0% of repositories were created in 2026. Direct HTTP or WebSocket requests account for 83.2% of paths, making reproduction of product protocols the dominant invocation method. Projects adapt messages, reconstruct conversation state, and convert responses to support compatible APIs. Account selection or rotation appears on 304 paths (19.1%), allowing projects with multiple eligible accounts to distribute requests across their separate allowances. Our policy analysis finds that 58 of the 62 services with available terms explicitly prohibit at least one examined practice, including automated access, account sharing, or service redistribution. These restrictions cover both downstream API provision and the means of obtaining upstream inference. Our findings inform defenses against unauthorized consumption and redistribution of free LLM resources. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to the relevant providers.
tldr: A large-scale measurement study of 513 open-source projects that repackage free LLM web-application inference into third-party APIs, termed 'LLM service freeloading'.
motivation: Third-party projects illicitly extract free inference from LLM web apps and dedicated clients to build independent APIs, but the scale and mechanisms of this practice are poorly understood.
method: Systematic measurement of 513 repositories, tracing 1,588 inference paths across 64 upstream LLM services and characterizing dependencies, invocation mechanisms, and account-rotation strategies, supplemented by a terms-of-service policy analysis.
result: 93.0% of repositories were created in 2026; 83.2% of inference paths use direct HTTP/WebSocket requests rather than official APIs; account selection or rotation appears on 19.1% of paths; 58 of 62 services with available terms explicitly prohibit at least one observed practice.
conclusion: The findings characterize unauthorized consumption and redistribution of free LLM resources and inform defenses, with responsible disclosure made to affected providers.

title: From Conversations To Commitments: A Design Study Of Shared Records For Agent-to-Business Coordination
authors: Carlos Eberhardt (IBM Software, Rochester, United States Of America), Mansura Habiba
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Business commitments require accepted terms to be linked to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence. We examine how a shared, attributable interaction record can support these links across independently operated organisations. Talea combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution. We use its coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension in a design study of an airline booking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels. Four observations follow. First, AT Protocol provides mechanisms supporting five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls require additional enforcement. Second, the case's confidentiality constraints restrict each hotel's authorised view to its bilateral exchange; only the airline can correlate all three deals. Third, this leaves a possible benefit for late-joining participants inside the airline's trust boundary, but does not establish an advantage over an equally instrumented point-to-point design. Fourth, a deterministic release interface constrains fixed, approved payloads but cannot bound disclosure when negotiated values depend on private state. Finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks reproduce the specified behaviours and counterexamples when selected controls are removed. They do not measure comparative benefit or validate a deployed commercial system. The remaining hypothesis is that, within one trust boundary, shared records improve decision reconstruction and recovery under changing participation relative to point-to-point exchange with equivalent authority, reservation, retention and correlation evidence. We specify an experiment to test it.
tldr: A design study of a shared, attributable interaction record (Talea, combining signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution) for coordinating business commitments across independently operated organisations.
motivation: Business commitments need accepted terms tied to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence across organisational boundaries, motivating a shared interaction record.
method: Design study using a coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension, modelling an airline rebooking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels, with finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks.
result: AT Protocol supports five of six coordination requirements; confidentiality limits each hotel's view to its bilateral exchange, only the airline can correlate all three deals, and a deterministic release interface cannot bound disclosure when values depend on private state.
conclusion: No comparative benefit over an equally instrumented point-to-point design is established; the remaining hypothesis about shared records improving decision reconstruction within one trust boundary is left to a specified future experiment.

title: Besicovitch Pseudo Almost Periodic Stochastic Processes And Their Applications To Delayed Stochastic Neural Networks
authors: Yongkun Li, Yuwei Cao, Bing Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Besicovitch almost periodic concept is a generalization of the Bohr, Stepanov, and Weyl almost periodic concepts and, in a certain sense, has broader coverage and weaker conditions. However, the concept of pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes in the Besicovitch sense has not yet been systematically proposed, which limits the characterization of the complex oscillatory behavior of a broader class of stochastic non-autonomous systems. This paper proposes the concept of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes. As an application of this concept, we study the existence of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic solutions in distribution for a class of stochastic delayed neural networks in which all parameters except the time delays are pseudo almost periodic and establish stability criteria for such solutions in the [MATH]-th mean sense. The work of this paper fills the gap caused by the lack of the concept of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes and provides a new conceptual tool and analytical approach for characterizing the complex oscillatory behavior of stochastic differential equations and stochastic neural network systems.
tldr: The paper introduces Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes and applies them to prove existence and stability of solutions for delayed stochastic neural networks.
motivation: Existing almost periodic frameworks (Bohr, Stepanov, Weyl) lack a systematically developed Besicovitch-sense pseudo almost periodic stochastic theory, limiting the description of complex oscillatory behavior in non-autonomous stochastic systems.
method: The authors define Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes, then use fixed-point/analysis techniques to establish existence of solutions in distribution for stochastic delayed neural networks with pseudo almost periodic parameters, plus stability criteria in the p-th mean sense.
result: Existence of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic solutions in distribution is proven and stability criteria in the p-th mean are derived for the considered class of delayed stochastic neural networks.
conclusion: The work fills a conceptual gap by providing a new analytic tool for characterizing oscillatory dynamics of stochastic differential equations and neural network systems.

title: Crossed Homomorphisms On Leibniz Superalgebras
authors: RB Yadav Arpan Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we give characterisation of crossed homomorphisms of Leibniz superalgebras as Maurer-Cartan elements of an associated graded Lie algebra. This characterization enables us to develop a cohomology theory for crossed homomorphisms and to apply it to their formal deformation theory. We show that the infinitesimal of a deformation is a 1-cocycle and that linear deformations are classified by such cocycles. Furthermore, we introduce the category of crossed homomorphisms between two fixed Leibniz superalgebras.
tldr: The paper characterizes crossed homomorphisms of Leibniz superalgebras as Maurer-Cartan elements of an associated graded Lie algebra, building a cohomology and deformation theory for them.
motivation: Crossed homomorphisms generalize homomorphisms and appear naturally in deformation and cohomology contexts, but a systematic cohomological framework for Leibniz superalgebras was lacking.
method: The authors identify crossed homomorphisms with Maurer-Cartan elements of a graded Lie algebra, then use this identification to define cohomology groups and control the formal deformation problem.
result: The infinitesimal of a formal deformation is shown to be a 1-cocycle, linear deformations are classified by such cocycles, and the category of crossed homomorphisms between two fixed Leibniz superalgebras is introduced.
conclusion: The work provides a unified cohomological and deformation-theoretic framework for crossed homomorphisms of Leibniz superalgebras, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Why $2$, $3$, And $5$? Lambert Series, Prime Logarithms, And A $48$-Step Octave For Musical Tuning
authors: Shubho Banerjee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The primes [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] generate many familiar frequency ratios in musical tuning. We identify three mathematical properties that distinguish these primes in a construction based on modular transformations of Lambert series. We derive an exact identity for [MATH] for every odd prime [MATH], together with a separate identity for [MATH]. Within this construction, all transformed Lambert-series arguments can be chosen real precisely for [MATH]. In the identities obtained for these three primes, every series argument has magnitude at most [MATH], whereas the identity for [MATH] requires complex arguments and contains a more slowly converging series. The leading [MATH]-terms for [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] generate a [MATH]-step octave grid and recover its conventional prime mapping [MATH] exactly, without rounding, while including the leading [MATH]-term for [MATH] enlarges the grid to [MATH] steps. The identity for [MATH] introduces no auxiliary logarithms of larger primes, whereas for every prime [MATH], an exact computation identifies such logarithms in the construction. The Lambert-series remainders provide exact corrections for just intervals and musical commas. For a published theoretical model of [MATH] Hindustani shrutis, the additive [MATH]-step mapping assigns all [MATH] ratios to distinct positions, with corrections no greater than [MATH] cents in magnitude. These results establish precise arithmetic distinctions that parallel the prominence of [MATH]-limit tuning, without implying that number theory determines musical practice.
tldr: The paper derives exact Lambert-series identities for the primes 2, 3, and 5 and uses their leading terms to construct a 48-step octave grid for musical tuning.
motivation: The author seeks to explain why the primes 2, 3, and 5 dominate conventional musical tuning by identifying arithmetic properties that single them out within a Lambert-series construction.
method: Modular transformations of Lambert series are used to derive exact identities for odd primes, with real versus complex series arguments and convergence behavior analyzed for p = 2, 3, 5 versus larger primes.
result: The leading terms for 2, 3, and 5 generate a 48-step octave grid recovering the standard prime mapping exactly, while including p = 7 extends the grid; Lambert-series remainders give exact corrections for just intervals and commas, including a fit to a shruti model within a fraction of a cent.
conclusion: Precise arithmetic distinctions parallel the prominence of 5-limit tuning, though the author explicitly avoids claiming that number theory determines musical practice.

title: Using Block Coordinate Descent For Solving The Close Enough Traveling Salesman Problem
authors: Ernesto G. Birgin, Paula C. R. Ertel, Rogerio S. Matos
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Close Enough Traveling Salesman Problem (CETSP) is a variant of the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem in which the salesperson must visit some point within a disk associated with each customer. Evaluating a visiting sequence requires determining an optimal visit point within each disk. This building block of virtually every CETSP algorithm is typically computed either by solving a second-order cone programming (SOCP) problem with a general-purpose solver, which can be expensive, or by discretizing the disks, which sacrifices optimality. We propose a block coordinate descent (BCD) method that computes these visit points exactly, without discretization, optimizing one visit point at a time. We show that the resulting single-disk subproblem reduces to a one-dimensional minimization, and we characterize its stationary points through the roots of a quartic polynomial. Of the three resulting solution strategies, which agree up to machine precision, Newton's method is the most efficient. Compared with an off-the-shelf SOCP solver, BCD evaluates fixed tours more than an order of magnitude faster. Embedded in an iterated local search (ILS-BCD), it finds the known optimal solutions of 720 small benchmark instances and, on 62 large ones, outperforms all heuristics of their original study in 47 and matches the best of them in 11 others. Within the memetic algorithm MA-CETSP, replacing the general-purpose SOCP solver with BCD and adding an exact local search based on the single-disk solver yields a method that, over the best of 20 runs, is better than the original algorithm in 20 of the 62 large instances and equal in the others, and improves on its best published values in 21. BCD is a fast and exact building block for evaluating visiting sequences that can replace general-purpose SOCP solvers within CETSP algorithms and enables searches that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.
tldr: This paper introduces a block coordinate descent (BCD) method that exactly computes optimal visit points for the Close Enough Traveling Salesman Problem (CETSP) and embeds it into heuristic solvers.
motivation: CETSP algorithms repeatedly need to find optimal visit points within customer disks, which is typically done via expensive general-purpose SOCP solvers or lossy disk discretization.
method: The authors formulate a BCD scheme optimizing one visit point at a time, reduce the single-disk subproblem to a one-dimensional minimization, characterize its stationary points via quartic polynomial roots, and compare three solution strategies (with Newton's method found most efficient).
result: BCD evaluates fixed tours over an order of magnitude faster than an off-the-shelf SOCP solver, finds known optimal solutions on 720 small benchmark instances, and improves or matches best-known results on large instances within ILS-BCD and MA-CETSP frameworks.
conclusion: BCD is a fast, exact building block for evaluating visiting sequences that can replace general-purpose SOCP solvers in CETSP algorithms and enables otherwise computationally prohibitive searches.

title: On The Non Existence Of Minimal Non-uniquely Ergodic 4-IETs With Flips
authors: Gabriel Soler L\'opez Antonio Linero Bas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The existence of minimal non uniquely ergodic oriented IETs of n intervals requires that n>= 4 by Th. 2.12 from (W. A. Veech, Interval exchange transformations, J. Anal. Math., 1978); moreover, for n=4 there exist examples of minimal non uniquely ergodic 4-IETs with two independent invariant measures, see (M. Keane, Non-ergodic interval exchange transformations, Israel J. Math., 1977). For the non oriented case, also called IETs with flips, the first examples of minimal non uniquely ergodic IETs were built in (A. Linero Bas and G. Soler L\'{o}pez, Minimal non uniquely ergodic IETs with flips, J. Differential Equations, 2023). However, the examples are (10,k)-IETs (k is the number of flips, 1<= k<= 10). Since there are no minimal (n,k)-IETs for n<= 3, it is interesting to decide if, as in the orientable case, there exist minimal non uniquely ergodic IETs with flips and four intervals. Our Main Theorem answers this question in the negative.
tldr: The paper proves that no minimal non-uniquely ergodic 4-interval exchange transformations with flips exist, in contrast with the orientable case where such examples are known.
motivation: Minimal non-uniquely ergodic oriented IETs require at least four intervals and examples exist for n=4, while for IETs with flips the known examples needed ten intervals; whether four-interval flipped examples exist was an open question.
method: A purely mathematical/dynamical-systems analysis of interval exchange transformations with flips, using constructions and rigidity arguments from ergodic theory to rule out the four-interval case.
result: The Main Theorem establishes the non-existence of minimal non-uniquely ergodic 4-IETs with flips.
conclusion: The flipped (non-oriented) case behaves differently from the oriented case at n=4, closing a natural gap in the classification of minimal non-uniquely ergodic IETs.

title: Stochastic Optimization For Switch-System Identification Under Errors-in-Variables
authors: Yasin Garehmohammadlou, Mohamad Kazem Shirani Faradonbeh, Mohammad Khosravi, Digvijay Boob
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we address the identification of switched dynamical systems under errors-in-variables, where both input and output measurements are corrupted by noise, and the number of operating modes and subsystem orders are unknown. We propose a unified identification framework that simultaneously estimates the subsystem parameters, latent switching sequence, and model structure. The proposed formulation combines a variance-normalized data-fitting criterion with temporally regularized soft mode assignments and sparsity-inducing penalties for selecting the active modes and relevant input-output lags. To solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop an alternating algorithm that incorporates convex mode-assignment updates and proximal stochastic variance-reduced gradient optimization for parameter estimation. While the existing approaches in the literature require exhaustive searches over candidate structures, the proposed method performs structure selection within a single model. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate recovery of the underlying system structure and favorable computational efficiency compared with a generalized total least squares and dynamic programming approach, particularly as the number of candidate structures increases.
tldr: The paper proposes a unified stochastic-optimization framework for identifying switched dynamical systems when both inputs and outputs are noise-corrupted and the mode count and subsystem orders are unknown.
