motivation: Existing identification methods for errors-in-variables switched systems require exhaustive searches over candidate model structures, which is computationally costly as the structure space grows.
method: A variance-normalized data-fitting criterion is combined with temporally regularized soft mode assignments and sparsity penalties, solved by an alternating scheme with convex mode-assignment updates and proximal stochastic variance-reduced gradient steps.
result: Numerical experiments show accurate recovery of system structure and better computational efficiency than a generalized total least squares plus dynamic programming baseline, especially as the number of candidate structures grows.
conclusion: The approach performs structure selection within a single model, avoiding exhaustive search, and offers a practical tool for switched-system identification under noisy measurements.

title: Anderson-Accelerated Landweber Iteration With Regularization Guarantees For Nonlinear Ill-Posed Problems
authors: Jianming Gao, Xiliang Lu, Lin Tian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anderson acceleration (AA) can markedly reduce iteration counts for fixed-point solvers, but its unrestricted signed history extrapolation need not preserve the stability required for iterative regularization of ill-posed problems. We introduce a regularization-guaranteed Anderson-accelerated Landweber method (\RG) in which finite-memory AA generates a proposal while the committed iterate is a controlled perturbation of a certified Landweber anchor. Under a local tangential cone condition and a scale-normalized localization condition, we prove strong convergence of the exact-data trajectory to a solution, stability at every fixed iteration, finite discrepancy stopping, and strong convergence of the discrepancy-stopped noisy reconstructions to the same exact-data limit; local uniqueness is needed only if that selected limit is to be identified with a prescribed solution [MATH]. Under the additional benchmark source condition [MATH] and a standard range-invariance condition, we obtain the discrepancy-principle rate [MATH]. The rate proof controls data-dependent Anderson coefficients through fixed memory, a fixed-reference ridge in the small AA least-squares problem, and an outer correction budget with an [MATH] tail. The numerical examples verify the efficiency of the proposed method.
tldr: The paper proposes a regularization-guaranteed Anderson-accelerated Landweber iteration for solving nonlinear ill-posed inverse problems, with convergence and convergence-rate proofs under tangential cone and source conditions.
motivation: Anderson acceleration speeds up fixed-point solvers substantially, but its signed history extrapolation can destroy the stability that iterative regularization of ill-posed problems requires.
method: A finite-memory Anderson acceleration generates proposals while the committed iterate remains a controlled perturbation of a certified Landweber anchor; convergence, stability, and discrepancy-principle rates are proven under local tangential cone and benchmark source conditions.
result: Strong convergence of the exact-data trajectory, stability at each fixed iteration, finite discrepancy stopping, and convergence of noisy reconstructions to the same limit are established, along with the discrepancy-principle rate; numerical examples confirm efficiency.
conclusion: The method yields accelerated yet provably stable iterative regularization for nonlinear ill-posed problems, bridging acceleration heuristics with rigorous regularization theory.

title: A Nonlocal Allen--Cahn Model For Volume-Constrained Wetting And Its Multi-Structure-Preserving Discretization
authors: Yadong Liu, Nan Lu, Zhonghua Qiao, Yuze Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At finite interface thickness, small droplets can shrink or disappear during wetting relaxation even when the phase-field mass is conserved. We develop a nonlocal Allen--Cahn model that couples a nonlinear diffuse-volume constraint to dynamic wall relaxation through Onsager's principle. The constraint gradient vanishes at the pure-phase values and does zero work in the energy balance, preserving the original bulk and wall dissipation structure. We construct a Compatible Variational Chain-Rule (CVC) scheme using the same discrete derivative of the volume density in the correction and in the volume increment. The scheme exactly conserves the nonlinear diffuse volume and reproduces the bulk--wall dissipation identity for the original discrete energy. Under a coercivity condition, the energy also yields a mesh-dependent maximum-norm bound. Numerical tests show second-order convergence in space and time. In flat-wall tests, the proposed model improves small-droplet retention and geometric-volume preservation and reproduces equilibrium cap shapes and contact angles. Additional tests illustrate wetting on chemically heterogeneous and rough substrates.
tldr: The authors propose a nonlocal Allen–Cahn phase-field model with a nonlinear diffuse-volume constraint for volume-constrained wetting, together with a structure-preserving numerical scheme.
motivation: At finite interface thickness, small droplets can shrink or disappear during wetting relaxation even when phase-field mass is conserved, motivating a diffuse-volume constraint that prevents this artefact.
method: A nonlinear diffuse-volume constraint is coupled to dynamic wall relaxation via Onsager's principle, and a Compatible Variational Chain-Rule (CVC) discretization is built using the same discrete derivative of the volume density in both the correction term and the volume increment.
result: The scheme exactly conserves the nonlinear diffuse volume and reproduces the bulk–wall dissipation identity; under a coercivity condition a mesh-dependent maximum-norm bound is derived, and numerical tests show second-order convergence plus improved small-droplet retention and correct equilibrium cap shapes and contact angles.
conclusion: The model and scheme provide a robust, structure-preserving framework for simulating wetting on flat, chemically heterogeneous, and rough substrates.

title: Sections And Constant Fields Of Postcritically Finite Rational Maps
authors: Wayne Peng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We relate the constant fields of generic preimage towers to two invariants of geometric monodromy. Bounded section indices characterize branching of the closed action and imply a finite constant extension. Unbounded finite-level abelianization orders force an infinite cyclotomic subextension. For a quadratic rational map with hyperbolic orbifold, we compute the section indices and abelianizations at every sufficiently large level and obtain an infinite real cyclotomic subextension. We also give a branching criterion for quadratic maps with neither critical point periodic and formulate three conjectures about the discrete action, the constants, and the case of bounded abelianizations with unbounded section indices.
tldr: The paper studies constant fields of generic preimage towers for postcritically finite rational maps, relating them to geometric monodromy invariants such as section indices and abelianization orders.
motivation: Arithmetic dynamics seeks to understand the field-theoretic structure (constants, cyclotomic subextensions) arising from iterated preimage trees of rational maps, and to connect these to group-theoretic invariants of the associated monodromy action.
method: The authors relate constant fields of preimage towers to geometric monodromy invariants, characterizing branching via bounded section indices and infinite cyclotomic subextensions via unbounded finite-level abelianization orders, then compute section indices and abelianizations for quadratic maps with hyperbolic orbifolds.
result: They show bounded section indices imply a finite constant extension while unbounded abelianization orders force an infinite cyclotomic subextension, explicitly computing these for hyperbolic-orbifold quadratic rational maps and obtaining an infinite real cyclotomic subextension; they also give a branching criterion and pose three conjectures.
conclusion: The work establishes a dictionary between section-theoretic/abelianization data of preimage towers and the arithmetic of constant fields, opening conjectural directions on the discrete action and bounded-abelianization regimes.

title: Bgpnp: A Non-Euclidean Gradient Projection Newton Pursuit Method For Sparsity-Constrained Optimization
authors: Jiawei Chen, Huilin Han, Yibing Lv, Jen-Chih Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A non-Euclidean gradient projection Newton pursuit method is proposed for solving sparsity constrained optimization problem via the Bregman distance. The method is also denoted as BGPNP. The method firstly constructs a gradient projection step based on the Bregman distance to ensure that the iterates satisfy the sparsity constraint. Then, when the support set becomes stable or the gradient norm is sufficiently small, a Newton pursuit step is introduced to improve local convergence efficiency. The BGPNP is proved to possess a sufficient descent property and the non-increasing monotonicity of the objective function values. The full convergence and linear convergence rate of the BGPNP are established under appropriate conditions, which do not involve the symmetry coefficient of Bregman distance and the [MATH]-uniform condition. Moreover, the locally quadratical convergence rate of the BGPNP is also obtained. This method provides an effective algorithmic framework for sparse optimization in non-Euclidean setting. Numerical experiments on sparsity-constrained compressed sensing problems validate the competitive performance of BGPNP compared with existing leading solvers.
tldr: The paper proposes BGPNP, a Bregman-distance-based gradient projection Newton pursuit algorithm for sparsity-constrained optimization.
motivation: Sparsity-constrained optimization often benefits from non-Euclidean geometries, but existing projected Newton methods may require restrictive assumptions and lack strong convergence guarantees.
method: BGPNP combines a Bregman-distance gradient projection step to maintain sparsity with a Newton pursuit step for local acceleration once the support stabilizes or the gradient is small.
result: The authors prove sufficient descent, monotonic objective decrease, global convergence, linear convergence under weakened conditions, and local quadratic convergence; numerical compressed-sensing experiments show competitive performance.
conclusion: BGPNP provides an effective non-Euclidean algorithmic framework for sparse optimization, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Poisoning Self-Evolving Security Policies In Llm Agents
authors: Honglu Jiang Aymen Noor
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving defenses improve LLM-agent security by learning reusable policies from observed attacks. However, we demonstrate that this learning process itself can become an attack surface. Using SED (Self-Evolving Defense) in the AgentDojo benchmark, we construct a single prompt-injection episode that causes the defense to learn an over-broad policy and subsequently refuse legitimate requests. Across 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task, while unrelated-task performance remains unchanged and the original prompt-injection defense remains effective. The attack also transfers to gpt-oss-120b; however, its poisoning mechanism depends on a successful initial prompt injection and therefore fails to activate when the target agent resists the underlying injection. In contrast, integrity-oriented attacks targeting SED's judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in our evaluated settings, identifying over-refusal as the primary exploitable failure mode observed in our experiments. We further identify self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments without an attacker. Finally, contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate over-refusal, without compromising security in our evaluated settings.
tldr: The paper shows that self-evolving LLM-agent defenses can be poisoned by a single prompt-injection episode, causing the learned policy to become over-broad and refuse legitimate requests.
motivation: Self-evolving defense mechanisms learn reusable security policies from observed attacks, but the authors argue this learning process is itself an underexplored attack surface.
method: Using the SED self-evolving defense in AgentDojo, they construct a prompt-injection episode that induces an overly broad learned policy, test it across 10 Nemotron runs and transfer to gpt-oss-120b, and probe integrity-oriented attacks on the judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization components.
result: Every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task while unrelated-task and original injection defense performance remain intact; the attack transfers to gpt-oss-120b but requires a successful initial injection, and integrity-oriented attacks fail; self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments is also identified.
conclusion: Over-refusal is the primary exploitable failure mode; contrastive policy synthesis plus an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce but do not eliminate over-refusal without compromising security.

title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery In Windows Kernel Binaries
authors: Jongseong Kim, Hwiwon Lee, Dongjun Kim, Lingming Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.
tldr: DeepBinary is a new benchmark for evaluating frontier LLM agents on open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries, including validation of previously unknown 0-day bugs.
motivation: Existing security benchmarks focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, leaving closed-source production binaries — which dominate industry software — largely unmeasured, so it is unclear how capable frontier models really are at deep binary vulnerability discovery.
method: Agents analyze target binaries with a disassembler and kernel debugger inside network-isolated VMs, report vulnerabilities with crashing PoCs, and every report is replayed on fresh VMs and judged by an LLM for validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated via bug bounty value); 12 target binaries are evaluated across multiple open- and closed-weight models and coding agents.
result: The evaluated models collectively found over 200 vulnerabilities worth an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities, and the results expose large differences in models' binary analysis, experimentation, and long-horizon persistence.
conclusion: DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable and reveals fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.

title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference For Production Llm APIs
authors: Liang Song
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, [MATH], [MATH]) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, [MATH], [MATH]). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, [MATH] constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding [MATH], passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev [MATH]) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.
tldr: FlashProve-Next introduces a zero-knowledge, proof-based protocol that lets clients verify that a closed-weight LLM API actually ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget without modifying native bf16/fp8/mxfp4 serving.
motivation: Users of proprietary LLM APIs have no way to confirm that providers honored the promised model, precision, and compute budget, since existing verification either trusts hardware/third parties or re-proves a cost-inefficient integer surrogate that diverges from native floating-point serving.
method: The work combines Reed-Solomon weight commitments with hidden column openings, local per-operator rounding contracts that eliminate integer surrogates, cost-weighted spot-checking for non-interactive public verification, and executable verifiers mechanically checked in 28 Lean 4 modules.
result: The authors report zero false rejections over 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows on Blackwell hardware, a 450.2 s GPU proof for Qwen3-0.6B, scaling to Qwen3-4B and a live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 deployment, with a 14/14 cheating-detection matrix and 10.1 ms CPU proof verification.
conclusion: Verifiable inference for production LLM APIs is achievable at practical cost via cryptographic commitments and formally verified proof systems, though cross-architecture hiding and full native-precision coverage remain future work.

title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On The Security Of Cross-Model Latent Communication In Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Manit Baser, Vyoman Jain, Rachel Yeo Hui Min, Xianglin Yang, Meenatchi Sundaram Muthu Selva Annamalai, Dinil Mon Divakaran
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds. In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.
tldr: The paper introduces Chasm, a framework that characterizes security vulnerabilities in cross-model latent communication (KV-cache transfer via learned mappers) among collaborating large language models, and proposes a target-side cache guard as a mitigation.
motivation: Latent communication such as cross-model KV-cache transfer reduces prefill computation and communication overhead in multi-agent LLM systems, but it lets a target model consume context it did not encode itself, raising the question of whether its safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses still hold.
method: The authors define three new attack surfaces (source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism) and empirically evaluate prompt-injection transfer, jailbreak transfer within and across model families, and white-box optimization through the mapper, then design a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches.
result: Latent handoffs substantially undermine safety: a target model that natively follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections follows up to 44.2% when attacked via a mapper, jailbreak transfer raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a family and 69.2 pp zero-shot, and white-box optimization through the mapper reaches 92.5% versus 37.5% for ordinary GCG.
conclusion: Cross-model latent communication is a significant and previously unexamined security risk for aligned LLMs, and simple cache-level corrections can largely restore refusal behavior, though the handoff mechanism itself remains an attack surface requiring further study.

title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing For LLM-based Agents
authors: Peizhuo Lv, Tao Chen, Mengya Shi, Ziyu Lin, Yuxuan Chen, Ruigang Liang, Tianwei Zhang, Wei Dong, Xiaofeng Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage. This makes pre-deployment auditing essential for systematically identifying implementation weaknesses and validating whether they can manifest as concrete security risks in realistic agent workflows. Existing approaches either focus on specific vulnerability classes or lack the capability to validate whether identified static weaknesses correspond to executable exploits. In this paper, we propose AgentLens, a systematic auditing framework for LLM-based agents. AgentLens analyzes the target agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, and organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph that captures how these factors interact to expose potential security risks. Based on this graph, AgentLens derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and constructs realistic multi-turn audit scenarios that place these payloads in task-relevant contexts to validate whether suspected risks manifest as security-violating behaviors during execution. Across five widely-used agent applications, each with over 24,000 GitHub stars, AgentLens identifies 44 vulnerabilities, and every vulnerability is validated by being triggered during execution. Compared with the state-of-the-art approach (AgentFuzz), AgentLens detects 3.67[MATH] more vulnerabilities. To date, 12 reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs.
tldr: AgentLens is a graph-guided auditing framework that builds an Audit Knowledge Graph over LLM-agent implementations to derive and validate exploitable attack paths before deployment.
motivation: LLM-based agents couple model decision-making with external tools, files and APIs, creating implementation weaknesses that can lead to remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection and data leakage; existing audits either target narrow vulnerability classes or cannot confirm that static findings are actually exploitable.
method: The framework analyzes the agent's implementation, component interactions and built-in defenses, organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph, then derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and embeds them in realistic multi-turn audit scenarios for execution-based validation.
result: Across five widely used agent applications (each with over 24,000 GitHub stars), AgentLens found 44 vulnerabilities, all validated by execution, detecting 3.67x more than AgentFuzz, with 12 issues assigned CVE IDs.
conclusion: Graph-guided, execution-validated auditing substantially improves vulnerability discovery in LLM agent deployments, but the work lies entirely in software/LLM security and has no connection to quantum information science.

title: The Weak Negotiation Function
authors: L\'eonard Brice
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Subgame-perfect equilibria (SPEs) constitute a refinement of Nash equilibria, where the players are not allowed to resort to non-credible threats to discourage deviations. In graph games equipped with a broad class of objectives, SPEs are captured by a tool called the negotiation function. After giving a quick overview of what has already been achieved using this tool, we define a variant of it: the weak negotiation function. We show that weak SPEs, a standard relaxation of SPEs, can be captured by the weak negotiation function exactly like SPEs are captured by the negotiation function. This characterisation yields a new computational result: deciding whether a given game contains a weak SPE where each player's payoff lies in a given interval is an NP-complete problem if the game has mean-payoff objectives. We also provide a new proof that the same problem in B\"uchi games is in P. The proofs reuse many arguments from their SPE counterpart, demonstrating the robustness of the tool. We also use the weak negotiation function to present a new proof, significantly shorter than the known one, of the existence of weak SPEs in mean-payoff games. We argue that those new techniques should be reusable in other settings, in particular to prove an open conjecture about the existence of randomised [MATH]-SPEs in mean-payoff games.
tldr: The paper introduces a 'weak negotiation function' characterizing weak subgame-perfect equilibria in graph games, deriving complexity results for mean-payoff and Büchi objectives.
motivation: Subgame-perfect equilibria refine Nash equilibria by ruling out non-credible threats, and the negotiation function is the known tool capturing them; the authors seek an analogous tool for the weaker standard relaxation of SPEs.
method: The authors define a variant of the negotiation function — the weak negotiation function — and show it characterizes weak SPEs, reusing proof arguments from the SPE counterpart across several objective classes.
result: Deciding whether a game admits a weak SPE with each player's payoff in a given interval is NP-complete for mean-payoff objectives and in P for Büchi games, and a shorter proof of existence of weak SPEs in mean-payoff games is given.
conclusion: The weak negotiation function is a robust, reusable tool, with the authors arguing its techniques may extend to an open conjecture on randomised SPEs in mean-payoff games.

title: On A Problem Of Erd\H{o}s And Graham Related To Restricted Order
authors: Shi-Qiang Chen, Quan-Hui Yang, Lilu Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a set of nonnegative integers. We prove that if [MATH] has a finite order for every finite subset [MATH], then [MATH] has finite restricted order. This resolves a problem posed by Erds and Graham in 1980. We also establish a local to global principle to characterize restricted asymptotic bases of finite order.
tldr: The paper resolves a 1980 Erdős–Graham problem by proving that finite order of all finite subsets implies finite restricted order, and establishes a local-to-global principle for restricted asymptotic bases.
motivation: The work addresses a longstanding combinatorial number theory problem posed by Erdős and Graham concerning restricted order and asymptotic bases.
method: The authors use additive number-theoretic arguments to prove the implication from finite-order finite subsets to finite restricted order and to formulate a local-to-global characterization.
result: They show that if every finite subset has finite order, then the whole set has finite restricted order, resolving the Erdős–Graham problem; they also characterize restricted asymptotic bases of finite order via a local-to-global principle.
conclusion: The paper settles a classical problem in restricted additive number theory and provides a structural principle for restricted asymptotic bases.

title: hp-Adaptive Finite Element Modeling Of Static Cracks In Density-Dependent Media
authors: Vicente Valle Martinez, Saugata Ghosh, S. M. Mallikarjunaiah, Dambaru Bhatta
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The elastostatic crack-tip fields within a density-dependent continuum are numerically investigated under several macroscopic loading configurations. The governing nonlinear boundary value problem is formulated using an algebraically nonlinear hyperelastic constitutive relationship in which the material moduli are intrinsically coupled to volumetric strain. Existence and uniqueness of the weak solution to the nonlinear displacement-based variational formulation are rigorously established at the continuous level via the Minty-Browder theorem. The variational formulation is then linearized at the partial differential equation level to construct a continuous damped Newton-Raphson scheme. To accurately capture the severe field gradients and internal singularities inherent to this model, the resulting sequence of linear operator equations is discretized and solved via a conforming finite element method within an [MATH]-adaptive framework. A comparative analysis is conducted across five distinct boundary loading profiles (encompassing uniform, piecewise-slope, and concentrated point loads) applied to a stationary cracked geometry. Within each configuration, the density-dependent constitutive parameter is systematically varied to assess its regulatory impact on the fracture process zone, focusing on the spatial evolution of normal stress, normal strain, and strain energy density near the crack tip. Numerical results demonstrate that local kinematic deformability is strictly bounded by the strain-limiting nature of the continuum, whereby static equilibrium is sustained through severe, localized stress amplifications. Furthermore, the mechanical influence of the modeling parameter is fundamentally dictated by the topological interplay between internal crack geometry and the spatial distribution of applied macroscopic loads.
tldr: A numerical study of elastostatic crack-tip fields in a density-dependent hyperelastic continuum using hp-adaptive finite elements.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize how strain-dependent material moduli regulate the fracture process zone near stationary cracks under various loading configurations.
method: The nonlinear boundary value problem is formulated with an algebraically nonlinear hyperelastic constitutive law, proven well-posed via the Minty-Browder theorem, linearized into a damped Newton-Raphson scheme, and discretized with a conforming hp-adaptive finite element method.
result: Across five loading profiles, static equilibrium is sustained through severe localized stress amplification, with kinematic deformability bounded by the strain-limiting continuum and parameter influence governed by crack geometry and load distribution.
conclusion: The density-dependent model captures crack-tip singularities robustly, showing that the constitutive parameter's effect depends on the topological interplay of crack geometry and macroscopic loading.

title: Optimal Bounds For The Length And Number Of Unit Fraction Representations
authors: Wouter van Doorn Thomas F. Bloom
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper gives a human-written exposition and simplification of proofs that were recently posted by OpenAI. We prove that every [MATH] can be written as the sum of [MATH] many distinct unit fractions. We also prove that the number of representations of [MATH] as the sum of [MATH] distinct unit fractions grows doubly exponentially in [MATH].
tldr: This paper provides a simplified exposition of proofs about representing numbers as sums of distinct unit fractions and bounds on the number of such representations.
motivation: The work concerns a classical number-theoretic problem on Egyptian fraction representations, motivated by recent proofs posted by OpenAI.
method: It gives human-written exposition and simplification of existing proofs establishing bounds on the length and count of unit fraction representations.
result: The paper proves that every number in a specified class can be written as a sum of a bounded number of distinct unit fractions, and that the number of representations grows doubly exponentially.
conclusion: The contribution is expository and mathematical, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Block Coordinate Descent Method For Nonconvex Multiobjective Optimization Under H\"older Continuity
authors: Lizet Santa Cruz Calder\'on, John Frank Matos Ascona, Vitaliano de Sousa Amaral, Danilo Rodrigues de Souza
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a block coordinate descent method for unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems with possibly nonconvex objectives and H\"older continuous gradients, intended for large-scale instances, in which updating all the variables simultaneously is expensive. In each iteration, only one block is updated along a descent direction common to all objectives, obtained by minimizing the maximum of their regularized quadratic models. We show that, unlike the single-objective case, stationarity on each block does not imply Pareto stationarity, and that no method that updates only the blocks of a partition of the variables and is monotone in all the objectives reaches, in general, an [MATH]-Pareto stationary point. Therefore, when none of the blockwise stationarity measures exceeds the tolerance, the algorithm performs a joint step across all coordinates and terminates only at [MATH]-Pareto stationary points. We establish a complexity bound of [MATH] iterations, where [MATH] is the smallest H\"older exponent, the same order as that of methods that update all the variables, as well as bounds on the numbers of function and gradient evaluations, which also hold with one regularization parameter per block.
tldr: The paper proposes a block coordinate descent method for nonconvex multiobjective optimization with Hölder continuous gradients and establishes iteration and evaluation complexity bounds.
motivation: Large-scale multiobjective optimization can be expensive when all variables must be updated simultaneously, motivating blockwise updates.
method: In each iteration, one block is updated along a descent direction common to all objectives, obtained by minimizing the maximum of regularized quadratic models; occasional joint steps ensure convergence to Pareto-stationary points.
result: The authors show blockwise stationarity does not imply Pareto stationarity for monotone block-only methods, and prove an iteration complexity bound of the same order as full-variable methods, along with function and gradient evaluation bounds.
conclusion: The method provides a theoretically grounded block coordinate descent approach for nonconvex multiobjective optimization, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Estimation For High-Dimensional Hawkes Processes With Inhibition Via Cir Approximation
authors: Nadia Belmabrouk, Mohamed Ben Alaya, Xavier Erny
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop a parametric estimation method for a high-dimensional Hawkes processes with inhibition. The proposed approach relies on a quantitative approximation of the Hawkes process by a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) process. In particular, we establish an explicit convergence rate in the joint large-population and long-time regime. This result requires specific techniques to handle the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient of the limiting CIR process.Based on this approximation, we construct explicit and easily implementable estimators of the model parameters. We establish their consistency and asymptotic normality. We also conduct numerical experiments to illustrate our findings.
tldr: The paper develops parametric estimators for high-dimensional Hawkes processes with inhibition using a CIR process approximation.
motivation: Hawkes processes with inhibition are challenging to estimate in high dimensions, and the authors seek tractable estimators via an approximating diffusion.
method: They establish a quantitative approximation of the Hawkes process by a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process with explicit convergence rates in a joint large-population and long-time regime, then construct explicit estimators and prove consistency and asymptotic normality.
result: The proposed estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal, and numerical experiments illustrate their performance.
conclusion: The CIR approximation provides a practical and theoretically grounded estimation framework for high-dimensional inhibited Hawkes processes.

title: Tori Without Contractible Closed Geodesics
authors: Anton Petrunin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a Riemannian 2-dimensional torus has no contractible closed geodesics if and only if it admits a geodesic foliation.
tldr: The paper proves a geometric characterization: a two-dimensional Riemannian torus has no contractible closed geodesics if and only if it admits a geodesic foliation.
motivation: The author aims to clarify the relationship between the existence of contractible closed geodesics and the existence of geodesic foliations on Riemannian tori.
method: The work uses Riemannian geometry techniques for surfaces, likely analyzing geodesic foliations and closed geodesic structures on the torus.
result: The main theorem establishes an equivalence between the absence of contractible closed geodesics and the existence of a geodesic foliation on a Riemannian 2-torus.
conclusion: This provides a clean geometric criterion connecting contractible closed geodesics to geodesic foliations in dimension two.

title: Controllability Of The Cahn Hilliard System At Finitely Many Observation Points
authors: Greeshma K Sheetal Dharmatti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study approximate controllability of the Cahn-Hilliard (CH) system with prescribed targets at finitely many points in the spatial domain. Our aim is to design a L^2 control such that given a finite set of observation points and target values, the solution reaches arbitrarily close to the prescribed targets at these points. First we study the associated linearised system using variational methods and then extend the results to the semi-linear CH system using fixed-point arguments. Further, we investigate approximate controllability in more general setting where we allow the control to be measure valued (in specific, Dirac delta type controls). This formulation is more challenging to obtain requisite regularity due to the simultaneous presence of pointwise observations and pointwise controls. Hence we restrict ourselves to the study of linearised CH system and devise a control which exhibits approximate controllability. We achieve this by approximating measure valued control with L^2 controls and showing appropriate convergence.
tldr: The paper studies approximate controllability of the (semi-linear and linearised) Cahn-Hilliard system when targets are prescribed at finitely many spatial observation points, including measure-valued (Dirac-type) controls.
motivation: Pointwise observation and pointwise actuation in a fourth-order parabolic PDE are interesting mathematically but require careful regularity analysis; the authors aim to design controls that steer the solution to arbitrary targets at a finite set of points.
method: Variational methods establish controllability of the linearised system, a fixed-point argument extends the result to the semi-linear CH system, and measure-valued controls are handled by approximation with L^2 controls plus convergence arguments.
result: Approximate controllability at finitely many observation points is proved for both the linearised and semi-linear CH systems with L^2 controls, and for the linearised system with Dirac-type measure-valued controls.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous PDE-control framework for pointwise targeting in Cahn-Hilliard dynamics, though the simultaneous pointwise observation/control setting remains restricted to the linearised case.

title: Variance Reduction Note 6: The Convergence Of Saga
authors: Alina Lodhi Kamran Fareed
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: SAGA corrects a sampled component gradient with a table of previously computed gradients. Updating one entry at a time gives an unbiased gradient estimate at the cost of one new component gradient per iteration. This sixth note on variance reduction proves a linear convergence guarantee for a smooth finite sum with convex components and a strongly convex average. A two-component quadratic shows how the spread of the stored evaluation points determines the variance, even at the minimizer. We track the iterate and the table jointly to obtain a last-iterate bound, then relate its dependence on the sample size to the rate at which individual entries are replaced. For generalized linear losses the same gradient table can be represented by one scalar per observation and a running mean.
tldr: This note proves linear convergence for the SAGA variance-reduced stochastic gradient method on smooth finite sums with convex components and strongly convex average.
motivation: SAGA improves stochastic gradient estimates by storing previously computed component gradients, but its last-iterate convergence and dependence on table-update dynamics require further analysis.
method: The paper analyzes the joint evolution of the iterate and the stored gradient table, derives a last-iterate bound, and relates sample-size dependence to the rate at which table entries are replaced; a two-component quadratic illustrates variance from stored evaluation points.
result: A linear convergence guarantee is established, and the variance at the minimizer is shown to depend on the spread of stored evaluation points; for generalized linear losses the table reduces to one scalar per observation plus a running mean.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical convergence guarantees for SAGA and clarifies how the gradient table affects variance and last-iterate performance.

title: Beyond The Limits Of Welfarism: An Affordable Proportional Approval Voting Rule
authors: Anton Baychkov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two of the most widely studied voting rules in approval-based multiwinner elections are Proportional Approval Voting (PAV), which maximizes a welfare score over committees of a fixed size, and the Method of Equal Shares (MES), which gives voters equal budgets and selects candidates whose supporters can pay for them. MES guarantees priceability and laminar proportionality, both of which can fail for PAV. Can PAV offer similar guarantees without giving voters budgets? To answer this question, we go beyond the limits of welfarism by allowing PAV to select committees of varying size, while penalizing larger committees. Both our exact rule and its polynomial-time local-search variant produce outcomes that admit a priceable completion and, on laminar instances, a laminar-proportional one. Our analysis carefully separates the roles of two marginal stability conditions. At suitable thresholds, addition stability gives a strong proportionality guarantee in the form of EJR+, while deletion stability limits overrepresentation and ensures affordability. We use these conditions to derive welfare and coverage guarantees for different completions of our rules. The same welfare comparison also improves the best known lower bound on the utilitarian ratio of standard PAV.
tldr: This paper proposes an affordable, variable-size variant of Proportional Approval Voting that recovers priceability and laminar-proportionality guarantees while retaining welfare comparisons.
motivation: PAV maximizes a welfare score but fails priceability and laminar proportionality, which the budget-based Method of Equal Shares guarantees; the author asks whether PAV can achieve similar axioms without budgets.
method: By going beyond welfarism, PAV is allowed to select committees of varying size with a penalty for larger committees; an exact rule and a polynomial-time local-search variant are analyzed via marginal addition- and deletion-stability conditions.
result: The rules yield outcomes admitting a priceable completion—and laminar-proportional completions on laminar instances—with addition stability giving EJR+ and deletion stability ensuring affordability, plus improved welfare and coverage guarantees and a better utilitarian ratio lower bound for standard PAV.
conclusion: PAV-like rules can match key proportionality guarantees of budget-based rules without voter budgets, refining the understanding of marginal stability's role in social choice.

title: The Detour Is The Danger: Preserving Security During Llm Agent Recovery
authors: Boyang Ma, Jinku Li, Hao Wu, Sheng Gao, Man Zhou, Minghui Xu, Yue Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.33605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.
tldr: The paper identifies workflow security downgrade in LLM agents, where failure-induced autonomous recovery discards original security protections, and proposes ARGUS to preserve security obligations during recovery.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly replan after tool or skill failures, which can restore task functionality while silently bypassing security requirements. The authors aim to characterize and mitigate this recovery-induced security risk.
method: They perform fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment across seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains, then introduce ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework with resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement.
result: ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement in an 864-run evaluation, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion compared with blocking alone.
conclusion: Secure agent recovery must preserve security obligations across workflow changes rather than merely restoring task functionality.

title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers On Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
authors: Yan Lin, Zhongliang Guo, Jingyu Lin, Daizong Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.34181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.
tldr: The paper studies diffusion-based adversarial purification for vision-language agents operating on native-resolution multi-element inputs, showing that classifier-oriented purifier designs mislead agentic defense evaluation and design.
motivation: Content providers can perturb open-model vision-language agents via images or text strokes, and existing adversarial purifiers were designed and evaluated for fixed-resolution classifier/natural-image benchmarks rather than native-resolution agentic inputs.
method: The authors evaluate diffusion purifiers on an agent built with Qwen3-VL-8B under grey-box attacks at native resolution, compare against cheap input transformations at matched clean cost, and test on web-shop pages and a held-out set with a second VLM.
result: Resizing inputs to the diffusion model resolution severely increases clean TextVQA cost, while the Divide-and-Conquer purifier retains 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy on web-shop pages versus at most 40.0% for cheap transformations, with robustness attributable to global noise level.
conclusion: Agentic inputs should not be treated as classifier inputs, and the authors derive three defense requirements and release their evaluation protocol.
